By adapting recurrent quantum circuit patterns into quantum circuit layers, researchers have enhanced the efficiency of computing molecular properties. Typically, using symmetry in molecular orbitals has led to simplified circuit designs, but these often fail to generalize well to diverse molecular systems. Our approach transforms recurrent circuits into a more compact form, eliminating the need for symmetry constraints. We predict that these compact forms will equally well approximate the quantum many-body ground state, and our results on testing them with molecular systems support this prediction. Our work is the first to leverage recurrent patterns in quantum circuit layers for first-principles molecular calculations, and the compact forms we derived show potential in significantly reducing the circuit depth, thereby substantially decreasing the associated cost of computation. Our findings are further validated by demonstrating that the model's performance is largely resistant to the choice of hyper-parameters. Moreover, we observe a clear relationship between the complexity of molecular systems and the required depth of compact forms, and our results reveal a significant gap between current depths in practical calculations and a theoretical minimum, which motivles us to explore more advanced neural network architectures to bridge this gap. Using these compact forms, we are able to accurately predict the molecular properties of larger systems with up to 18 electrons and 40 orbitals, and our results are of the same quality as those achieved with the original recurrent circuits. Our work is implemented in the open-source PySCF package as the "pvcnn" module. Additionally, the associated code and data can be accessed through our repository at https://github.com/s-su/pvcnn. Specifically, the PySCF package can be downloaded from https://github.com/s-su/pvcNN, and the associated data can be accessed at https://github.com/s-su/pvcNN/tree/ data. Our investigation into average-case dynamics of generalized Chebyshev methods, along with their special cases - Newton's method and gradient descent, reveals that these algorithms exhibit non-alternating, ascending iterations. This method can provide superior average-performance than gradient descent while maintaining similar worst-case behavior. Furthermore, the study establishes the universality of generalized Chebyshev dynamics across various functional domains. To study the average dynamics of localized algorithms, we introduce a novel dynamic system, termed the Localization System, which facilitates mathematical analysis of these methods. This approach allows us to derive key insights into the average dynamics of optimization algorithms, yielding unexpected conclusions. To validate our theoretical findings, we verify the results through extensive numerical simulations. This research has significant implications in both optimization theory and the broader understanding of generalized Chebyshev methods. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/alberto915/GeneralizedChebyshev. Firstly, it presents average-case dynamics of optimization algorithms in a unified manner. Secondly, it highlights the significance of the harmonic mean, thereby providing an alternative perspective on the variance, finally, it proposes the Orientation Number as a novel characteristic that effectively captures the localization quality. These contributions possess inherent value and can be applied to various optimization challenges. Additionally, the concept of Average Orbits offers insights into the generalized Chebyshev iterations, while the Specialization Theorem bridges the gap between the localization quality and function characteristics. Moreover, we define new metrics, such as the Width and Variance, which complement existing localization metrics and provide deep insights into optimization algorithms. This study is the first to investigate average dynamics of optimization algorithms, achieving several significant theorems, alongside pioneering four new concepts, and introducing two novel parameters, which are crucial for understanding localized algorithms. A key issue with immersive technologies is maintaining seamless tracking of objects, such as human heads, within complex environments. Our invention, TRaP2D, is an advanced adaptive algorithm that uses probabilistic data association for tracking a mobile agent's position in three-dimensional space. Originally presented in 1994, the method has undergone significant enhancements to address issues of efficient computation, code availability, and extended compatibility with modern operating systems. A comprehensive high-performance implementation of TRaP2D is now accessible on GitHub, featuring direct access to pixel data for enhanced accuracy at high speeds. Our experiments demonstrate that this variant outperforms existing tracking algorithms by a significant margin. Our novel approach is an enhanced version of the 1994 adaptive algorithm and is a substantial improvement over previous implementations, which often suffered from inefficiencies, compatibility issues, and a lack of availability. A key advantage of TRaP2D is its ability to accurately and efficiently track low-resolution markers at high speeds of up to 120 frames per second on a standard desktop computer. This significant boost in performance enables a more streamlined and engaging user experience during immersive applications. Our evaluation shows that, even in the most demanding scenarios of five closely moving people, TRaP2D maintains an average error rate of just 0.4 pixels, while demonstrating enhanced robustness and accuracy in the most challenging conditions. As a result, this advanced algorithm is now readily available for use in immersive applications where precise and seamless tracking is essential. A comprehensive collection of test data is also provided to facilitate further development and research in head-tracking technologies. A key advantage of our approach is its adaptability, allowing it to accurately track markers of varying sizes under diverse conditions, while incurring minimal computational overhead. We prove the equivalence of orthomodular lattices and orthomodular spaces by establishing a one-to-one correspondence that preserves their respective structures. This correspondence maps each orthomodular space to a lattice and each lattice to a space in such a way that the lattice corresponds to the space's section lattice and the space corresponds to its lattice's free completion. Additionally, this correspondence preserves the lattices' orthomodular lattices and space structures, and it satisfies the uniqueness of lattice-space and space-lattice correspondences. As a result, orthomodular lattices and spaces become equivalent to projective lines, and this correspondence offers a generalized version of the Pappus-Chincarini configuration theorem for orthomodular lattices and spaces. Furthermore, this correspondence also applies to state spaces of quantum systems described by Hilbert spaces, and it reveals a previously hidden geometric structure common to all such spaces. Finally, this geometric structure provides a way to generalize familiar geometric concepts, such as circles and triangles, to quantum state spaces, and it potentially opens up new areas of research in quantum mechanics. In the context of traditional quantum logic, our findings imply the existence of a hidden geometric structure common to all Hilbert spaces, and they raise the possibility of exploring quantum logic in a way that exceeds the limitations imposed by the standard Gleason theorem. In the long term, this geometric structure may offer a way to extend the boundaries of quantum computing by utilizing geometric concepts, such as general geometric Desargues theorem, to devise new quantum algorithms. In the short term, this provides a way to use geometric concepts, such as general geometric Pappus theorem, to create novel quantum algorithms. As an example, we use the Lorentzian Seidenberg-Tate scheme to demonstrate the applicability of our findings to quantum state spaces with singularities. This is done by applying the Atiyah-Banach algebra techniques to quantum state spaces with singularities and to devise a new quantum algorithm based on the general geometric Pappus theorem. In the process, this also provides a way to extend the boundaries of quantum computing by using geometric concepts to devise new quantum algorithms in the standard Hilbert space framework. The use of AI-generated proofs is becoming increasingly common in various fields, yet their validity has not been extensively examined. In this study, we address the issue of verifying the accuracy of AI-generated proofs by considering them as input for peer review. We propose a system that facilitates the review process by comparing the structured representations of AI-generated proofs with those of human-authored proofs. These structured representations are obtained through the extraction of logical formulas from natural language expressions using machine learning-based tools. The system's effectiveness was validated in experiments involving law and mathematical proofs, which showed a significant improvement in the detection of AI-generated proofs when combined with human review. Additionally, the system was used to conduct a case study on the verification of proofs generated by a leading AI reasoning system. Our findings suggest that the integration of AI and human efforts in the peer review of proofs offers a promising approach to addressing the trust and validity concerns associated with the emerging use of AI in legal and academic domains. A highly efficient interior point method called Primal-Dual Interior Point Method, or PDIPM for short, has been developed. This method employs an optimal two-phase approach combined with early termination techniques to rapidly solve large-scale Linear Complementarity Problems, which are often encountered in interior point methods. By taking advantage of early termination, PDIPM can significantly reduce interior point iterations. Furthermore, the application of a nearly optimal search direction makes PDIPM well-suited for large-scale problems. The effectiveness of PDIPM was thoroughly verified through extensive numerical tests on various large-scale optimization problems. The results show that PDIPM consistently outperforms other methods, including Newton's method, the Interior Point Method of Zhang et al., and Primal-Dual Hybrid Newton Interior Point Method (PDHNNIPM). Notably, PDIPM was able to solve problems that other methods struggled with, and its average computational time was consistently the lowest. The source code for PDIPM can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/huynhquocduong/PDIPM. The repository contains detailed information on the method's implementation. In addition, the code can be run using MATLAB version R2018B or later on Windows or macOS platforms. The method can be used to solve large-scale Linear Complementarity Problems in the range of $n = 500$ to $10^5$. The reasoning behind this range is as follows: For problems with $n$ within this range, PDIPM was observed to be the most efficient. Furthermore, even when $n$ exceeds this range, PDIPM remains competitive and often reaches the desired termination criteria in some cases. The possible limitation of PDIPM could be its potential to be slowed down by the two-phase approach, which may not be noticeable for problems with a smaller number of components. However, as the problem size increases, the initial investment in time during the first phase actually results in a faster overall solution, which in some cases, allows PDIPM to outperform other methods. The numerical tests confirm this to be true. The main idea behind PDIPM's termination is to evaluate the convergence of iterations within a smaller, reduced system. This is made possible by the Two-Phase Approach, which allows PDIPM to check the completion of inner iterations in a smaller system. The reduced system is derived from the original Linear Complementarity Problem by applying an equivalence transformation, which enables PDIPM to terminate interior point iterations early. In an effort to mitigate this limitation, we are introducing the AI Incident Database (AIDD), a comprehensive resource for sharing knowledge on actual AI incidents. By crowdsourcing real-world examples of AI failures, AIDD will foster safer system development, inform improved designs, and foster a culture of responsibility. Ultimately, by sharing and learning from these experiences, AIDD aims to help prevent recurring errors and reduce the potential for future tragedies. You can access and contribute to the database at https://aiddatabase.org. It differs from Quipper-M, which relies on a free category technique, by using a typed category method. Both designs, Proto-Quipper-M and Quipper-M, share the property of generating non-cloneable quantum states when reduced. Proto-Quipper-M's key feature lies in its ability to construct quantum circuits through the use of typed recursive functions, enabling the straightforward compilation of recursive functions into efficient circuits. We demonstrate the benefits of Proto-Quipper-M by applying it to the design of quantum algorithms, particularly by using its category-based structure to adapt existing algorithms from the Quipper-M environment. Additionally, Proto-Quipper-M's high-level syntax facilitates the easy modification of algorithms, as evident in our modification of Shor's algorithm for factoring large numbers on a quantum computer. The Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) transformation offers a method to compare event times within point processes by converting individual event times into unified dimensions. This allows for simultaneous analysis of multiple event times, which can then be interpreted in terms of relative timing ratios. We've modified the widely used Cox process model to accommodate these transformed times, which we refer to as ILR Cox models. These models maintain the mathematical properties of the original Cox process models. The validity of the ILR Cox models was verified through simulation experiments on both discrete and continuous data. The benefits of using ILR transformations were most apparent in scenarios with small data samples or highly irregular event times, as the method outperformed traditional approaches to point process regression in terms of model fit. The performance of ILR Cox models was found to decline slightly in scenarios with large data samples and well-distributed event times. Despite this, the method represented a useful and versatile tool for analyzing point processes, particularly in situations where event times were of greater significance than spatial coordinates. The application of ILR transformations also facilitated new interpretations of point process models, such as uniformity models and Gaussian processes. The implementation of ILR Cox models is demonstrated through simulated data examples in R programming language. The related R code is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/krzysztofgrabski/ILR_Cox_models. This paper extends the framework for universal normalizing flows to include U(1) gauge theories. Fostering connections between probability theory, integrable systems, and gauge theories, the framework's framework treats partial differential equations as forward simulations of probability flows. As such, it naturally incorporates gauge symmetries via gauge transformations that remain simulated equations, while also generating rich families of integrable partial differential equations. Focusing on U(1) gauge theory, we formulate a normalizing flow representation of the Chern-Simons theory and develop the corresponding magnetic fluctuations on a plane. Notably, our results reveal that conventional and magnetic symmetries are automatically incorporated within the flow's framework. To verify the accuracy of our approach, we derive several exact partition functions and correlation functions, including those for multisoliton configurations, bound states, and magnetic vortex-antivortex pairs. Our analytical findings are in perfect agreement with existing predictions from the gauge theory. Moreover, the framework's versatility allows us to explore a broad range of U(1) gauge theories, even those that don't have known integrable counterparts. Moreover, our approach has a somewhat unexpected benefit: the generated action may be cost-effectively optimized via contrastive learning. To illustrate this, we examine the one- and two-loop variational problems for Chern-Simons and U(1) Yang-Mills theories. Our analysis shows that the flow's optimal action accurately reproduces the partition function and correlation functions generated at the two-loop level via perturbation theory. By leveraging gauge symmetry, our approach ensures that the optimal action remains gauge-invariant. Focusing on magnetic fluctuations of the Chern-Simons theory, our results reveal that the optimal action accurately reproduces our own flow-generated correlation functions, which in turn correctly predict the $1/N$ expansion predictions from the gauge theory. Moreover, our analysis shows that the optimal action is a gauge-invariant functional of the pure Yang-Mills theory's magnetic correlation functions. Lastly, our approach may be adapted to study any U(1) gauge theory's partial differential equations, whether they have an integrable counterpart or not. We've developed a system for identifying formatted text with a specific purpose, which is to link related information together. Formatted text is structured into elements like names, dates, and locations that follow standard formats, but due to typographical errors, it can be difficult for computers to recognize. We've tested different machine learning techniques by creating datasets with intentionally introduced errors, which reveal that biased training data can significantly enhance recognition accuracy, particularly when encountering unusual error types. We discovered that incorporating additional data, specifically designed to correct common mistakes, can significantly improve our results. When applied to a text recognition task, our system achieved an accuracy of 72.0%, surpassing the baseline of 67.2%. Furthermore, our evaluation shows that certain error types can be resolved more effectively than others, with the format-specific training data having a more significant impact on the machine learning models' performance. To facilitate future advancements in formatted text recognition, we have made our training data and source code publicly available. The public resources can be accessed at https://github.com/krishanruz/discrete_fer. We have submitted an paper on our study to the 9th International Workshop on Semantic Mapping, titled "Towards Discrete Formatted Text Recognition using Biased Training Data," which is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.04262. Measurements of t t ¯ quark production in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV were taken at the CERN LHC with the CMS detector, collecting data on 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. Top quark cross sections in leptonic and hadronic decays were measured in two separate analyses. The leptonic analysis, which relies on the detection of electrons or muons, showed a cross section of 832 ± 2 fb with an uncertainty of 15%, matching theoretical predictions within the framework of perturbative quantum chromodynamics. The hadronic analysis, which relies on the identification of jets, reported a cross section of 833 ± 18 fb with an uncertainty of 10%, also agreeing with theoretical predictions. These results, which consider various systematic uncertainties, included measurements of t t ¯ quark production at different energy scales using an extended k$_{\rm T}$ factorization scheme. This method was found to describe the transition from lower to higher energy regions of the measurements more effectively than traditional factorization schemes. Additionally, the distribution of the number of distinct jets in t t ¯ quark production was measured, providing further insights into the production mechanisms of top quarks. Lastly, the production of top quarks in association with vector bosons was measured, focusing on events containing one or two isolated photons. These measurements were in line with theoretical predictions for t t ¯ + V (V = W or Z) quark production, accounting for various backgrounds including t t ¯ + V (V = γ) production at the 30 fb level. Furthermore, the search for same-sign top quark production was conducted, finding no significant deviations from expected backgrounds. A limit on same-sign top quark production was placed at the 95% confidence level, quantified as 1.1 pb for t t ¯ + jets, in line with theoretical predictions for t t ¯ + V (V = W) quark production at the 30 fb level. Lastly, the search for excess events in t t ¯ + V (V = Z) quark production was conducted, comparing data and standard model expectations for t t ¯ + Z quark production at high energy levels, finding no significant anomalies. In the context of lasso regression with a complex data set, an increasingly popular approach involves utilizing parallel machines to divide and process 'homogeneous' data subsets. However, this strategy faces two primary obstacles: ensuring that the data subsets are indeed homogeneous, and providing an efficient way to divide the data into manageable parts. To overcome these challenges, we introduce an adaptive-sieving-based algorithm for solving the high-dimensional rank lasso problem in a large data environment. Our innovative method utilizes a special technique to isolate and separate non-homogeneous data subsets, while simultaneously reducing computational complexity by limiting the number of data subsets and ensuring that model coefficients remain consistent across all subsets, thereby allowing for efficient problem solving and coefficient estimation. Our experimental results, conducted using both synthetic and real-world data, demonstrate the superior performance of our adaptive-sieving-based algorithm compared to existing methods on large data sets. Our software implementation, known as SiVRAL, is available for public use at the following website: https://github.com/yang-yang/SiVRAL. Our theoretical analysis suggests that, in the best-case scenario, our algorithm achieves optimal performance, whereas, in the worst-case scenario, its complexity remains efficiently limited by a polynomial value. Furthermore, in terms of practical execution time, our approach significantly surpasses traditional methods, often by orders of magnitude. To date, our study appears to be the very first to formally analyze and document an algorithm of this type. Our research findings are expected to contribute to the development of scalable and efficient methods for solving complex data problems in large data environments. Our life cycle assessment methodology provides a framework for evaluating the environmental effects of AI services and other technologies, thereby facilitating informed design and development of future AI systems. The primary goal of process monitoring is to ensure that actual processes unfold as predicted. While many methods can identify deviations from anticipated processes, few validate their corrective actions in real-world contexts. Our research employs a previously unutilized dataset from a Swedish municipal administration to analyze both predictive and corrective processes. We evaluated and compared several predictive methods for uncovering irregular cases and subsequently employed a decision tree to simulate decision-making processes. To assess the efficacy of these methods, we simulated both predictive and corrective actions and compared them with actual behaviors. Our results demonstrate that using decision tree ensembles to simulate decisions provides a reliable means of identifying unusual cases and can also generate accurate decisions to mitigate problems. However, the accuracy of these decisions could be improved with the incorporation of basic inductive validation techniques. This real-world validation provides essential insight into the effectiveness of both prescriptive and predictive methods. A cutting-edge method for predicting and validating coupled problems in fluid dynamics has been developed. This approach involves utilizing the dual-weighted residual method to create an error estimation framework. By applying the dual-weighted residual method to an established model problem, we derive an error representation that can be used to determine reliable confidence intervals for the solution of interest. Specifically, we demonstrate the efficacy of this method in solving coupled problems involving fluid mechanics and advection-diffusion equations. Notably, our framework encompasses both offline and online components that adapt to optimize solution accuracy at minimal cost. Through a series of numerical experiments, we validate the effectiveness of our method in predicting errors and achieving tolerance-based solutions for these types of problems. Additionally, we highlight the benefits of our method in reducing the computational cost associated with achieving a highly accurate solution, thereby facilitating rapid prototyping and validation in practical applications. This work has far-reaching potential for the practical implementation of goal-oriented modeling and validation strategies in various fields of fluid dynamics. Graph packing issues have been extensively studied for various graph types, yet tight bounds remain elusive, particularly for circuits that avoid overlapping vertices. This research examines circuit packing within planar graphs of constant girth, revealing a novel approach to obtaining tight bounds through a packing lemma, which itself is proven using a novel untangling technique with general girth. This packing lemma is applied to derive tight bounds for circuits within graphs of constant girth as well as specific instances such as triangle-free graphs. A novel algorithm is also presented for determining a minimum-size circuit-packed tree in a given girth-constant graph, running in $O(\log^3{N})$ time. Furthermore, we extend our methods to other packing problems, including paths and trees, and establish a new connection between these problems and the minimum-cut linear programming relaxation introduced by Karger and Stein. Based on this connection, a new $O(\log^3{N})$ algorithm is presented for finding a minimum-size tree packed path in a given graph. Additionally, we propose several open problems, including determining whether the circuit packing problem can be solved in near-linear time and whether circuit and path packings can be obtained jointly in a given $g$-constant graph. These results contribute to the ongoing efforts in graph packing research. In our research, we explore the concept of opinion dynamics with the utilization of mean-field theory. Opinions are represented one-dimensionalally and dynamics are nonlinearly based on the opinion gradient. A new of regime-switching dynamics is discovered, leading to the formation of permanent social groups (order) and preventing the formation of freely moving populations (chaos). These transitions are caused by the interaction between opinion gradient and dynamics non-linearity, and are accompanied by the spontaneous emergence of order. We analyze the complexity of our system through calculating variance and entropy, and discover that it exhibits sudden changes around the critical points of order/chaos transitions. Moreover, our results are validated by performing extensive numerical simulations. By applying the limit cycle approximation, we successfully map the phase diagram and understand the underlying mechanism of order emergence, and how the system escapes chaos through the formation of opinion gradients. Additionally, our theory is applicable not just to the model we studied but also to a wide range of other opinion dynamics models. Lastly, we discuss the practical implications of our findings.

This delay is understood to be caused, at least partially, by the time it takes for mature mRNA to be produced from transcribed genetic material, as transcription does not immediately result in functional mRNA. Research is being conducted to determine the factors driving the transformation of transcribed genetic material into functional mRNA. One hypothesis is that the length and location of genes influence this transformation, so our team has used high-throughput data from the study of thale cress plants to test this hypothesis. By measuring the time between transcription completion and mature mRNA production for individual genes, our results show that longer genes experience a greater discrepancy between this transformation and transcription completion time. Additionally, our data highlight the varying efficiencies of different RNA processing mechanisms and suggest that chromatin structure has a limited impact on the time between transcription completion and mature mRNA production. Dropped objects pose a significant challenge for robots operating in unstructured environments, particularly in settings where vision is compromised by poor lighting, distance, or image quality. Existing research on detecting dropped objects often relies on a single sensory input, such as visual information, for object identification. In contrast, this study explores how integrating various physical properties, including gravity, friction, and inertia, can aid in sensing and recovering dropped objects. By leveraging these physical characteristics, a mobile robot can collect diverse data from its actuators, allowing it to perceive and respond to dropped objects through sensing multiple physical properties, even when vision is limited or unreliable. The research demonstrates that combining sensory information from these physical properties can effectively mitigate the ambiguities inherent in sensory data, effectively identifying a dropped object in various complex scenarios. The integration of sensing from multiple physical properties can effectively replace and adapt a more traditional, vision-based approach to detecting dropped objects. Firstly, we investigate how long, on average, SynGTE takes to produce a program, finding it can do so within a minute for a significant number of cases, and usually within 5 minutes or less overall. To provide more insight into SynGTE's performance, we gather and share data on several new metrics, including common issues encountered during synthesis, the impact of specifications, and the relationship between synthesis failure rates and program characteristics. Conversely, a subsequent evaluation assesses SynGTE's accuracy by questioning the validity of the specifications used in the previous study. By comparing synthesized code to actual implementations on the same tasks, we discover that SynGTE's generated code often demonstrates effectiveness but also makes mistakes similar to those encountered during the initial study, highlighting the challenge of creating perfect specifications. Both investigations offer valuable insights to guide future developments of SynGTE and the program synthesis field as a whole. Based on our findings, we propose several potential directions for further exploration and improvement. Ultimately, we conclude that SynGTE can be a highly useful tool for creating custom software, and we look forward to seeing the impact it has in this domain. In particular, we suggest that SynGTE could be employed in settings where manual code production is time-consuming, such as in program transformation, maintenance, and repair, by specifying the desired input-output relationships. Additionally, SynGTE has the potential to benefit from the growing availability of automatic grading tools, which could be used to evaluate and refine generated code more effectively. In the long term, we envision program synthesis techniques like SynGTE's to contribute to significant advancements in areas like software testing and validation. In fact, we already began exploring this possibility by using SynGTE to generate test cases, which revealed potential shortcomings in the specifications used in our initial study. This study aims to illustrate the varied roles reduction methods play in climate research, from eliminating irrelevant details to preserving essential interactions, and to encourage responsible use of these methods, especially through the reuse of existing conceptual models. To facilitate this, a proposed framework seeks to categorize reduction methods based on their place within the hierarchy of climate model scales and to promote the critical reflection of their applicability to climate modeling. Ultimately, the ultimate goal is to promote the responsible utilization of reduction methods, recognizing their potential to both illuminate and obscure the complexities of the Earth's climate, and to encourage the reflection of their limitations on climate modeling. To overcome these limitations, a BonnEye system was developed, consisting of a portable, real-time imaging device and associated software for automatically detecting tumor boundaries based on low-energy X-ray transmission data. The BonnEye algorithm was initially tested and validated on synthetic and actual low-energy X-ray projections from patients, and subsequently applied to low-energy X-ray images obtained during radiation treatment, with promising results, including accurate identification of tumor boundaries and verification that the tumor largely disappeared after treatment. The BonnEye system's effectiveness was further confirmed by clinical professionals, who noted the derived tumor contours closely matched those obtained from CT scans. Consequently, the BonnEye system can potentially enhance the accuracy of radiation treatment by supplying radiation oncologists with regularly updated tumor contour maps. Moreover, the BonnEye algorithm can also automatically identify lung regions, making it useful for various applications, including lung cancer detection and diagnosis. Further clinical trials are necessary to completely evaluate the BonnEye system's capabilities. In the analysis of compositional data, researchers typically work with high-dimensional information where each data point represents a combination of several components. This type of data is often encountered in fields such as biology, geology, and genetics. One commonly applied transformation in the study of compositional data is the standard normalization, which involves taking the natural logarithm of each component and adjusting for variation in relative abundance. This method has been widely utilized but is known to introduce complications in interdisciplinary research, particularly when combining datasets from various domains due to differences in normalization techniques. In this study, we introduce a distinct set of pre-processing strategies tailored to specific types of biological data, namely RNA-seq, mass spectrometry proteomics, and single-cell data. Our aim is to establish a unified framework for pre-processing biological data by examining the effects of different combinations of techniques on the representation of null models. Our investigation highlights the significance of methodological uniformity across datasets and suggests the adoption of a null-model-based assessment of data stability as a benchmark for validating pre-processing strategies. Although our focus is on biological data, the concepts we explore are applicable to the broader analysis of compositional data. This study is a continuation of previous work in the field and contributes novel insights to the field of data analysis. A related package, called compositionalData, is available for application in R. It includes functions for standard normalization, logarithmic transformation, and the calculation of null model probabilities. Additionally, the study delves into the statistical analysis of differences in pre-processing strategies using compositional null models and explores the effects of techniques like proteomics preprocessing on protein composition. The study's code and methods are fully transparent and can be accessed at a public repository. The core accretion model, a widely accepted theory for planet formation, suggests the existence of large, hot Jupiter planets with highly eccentric orbits that form through a process of rapid, runaway gas accretion. As smaller planets, like Earth, take longer to accumulate mass and thus gas, they are expected to have more stable orbits with lower eccentricities. Recent discoveries by the Kepler space telescope of numerous hot Jupiters with diverse eccentricities challenge this prediction, as studies also indicate that runaway gas accretion may not always be necessary to explain the observed orbital eccentricities of these planets. An alternative explanation is the gravitational interaction with a second, larger companion planet, suggesting that the distribution of orbital eccentricities is not solely the result of different migration mechanisms. As a test of this hypothesis, our research examines the distribution of orbital inclinations among planets with varying masses, expecting that runaway gas accretion would result in a subdivision among orbital inclinations due to a process known as tidal realignment. Similar to the case with eccentricities, the observed distribution of inclinations does not support this prediction, as nearly half of the measured inclinations are found to be very close to 90 degrees. This result can be interpreted as evidence that gravitational interactions with companion planets are common, affecting the migration patterns of planets through gas accretion and thus requiring further investigation into planet formation models. As a next step, our model involves three-body scenarios where a hot Jupiter planet and an outer companion planet interact through gravitational interactions, predicting a ratio of high to low inclination values of approximately three to one. Furthermore, our model indicates that orbital eccentricities are influenced to a lesser extent by the presence of companion planets, as hot Jupiters with high eccentricities may not necessarily be observed in their most energetic states. In the field of meta-reinforcement learning, our research focuses on addressing a fundamental challenge: designing a flexible decision-making system that can effectively navigate multiple tasks with varying structures. To achieve this, we have developed a novel meta-algorithm called Neural Episodic Framework (NEF), characterized by a dynamic memory that adapts to each task and facilitates the retention of unseen states, temporary variables, and partial observations. Through a process of episodic learning, NEF optimizes its internal representations to integrate task information from both observations and past experiences. Additionally, NEF's ability to maintain dynamic memories and modulate the focus on relevant experiences enables it to emerge both a policy that adapts to different tasks and a discovery mechanism that selects the most informative past experiences to inform the current task. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of NEF in solving a variety of tasks, including grid worlds, laser tag, and a range of other practical problems, and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art meta-reinforcement learning methods while exhibiting more efficient focus selection and improved predictive accuracy. Furthermore, NEF's dynamic memory is comprised of episodic memories, temporary variables, and a focus controller, and can be implemented using neural networks that map observations to memory activation vectors. In total, NEF offers a versatile framework for solving a variety of task adaptation challenges. As such, it provides a practical and efficient solution for a range of practical problems. In order to further investigate the underlying assumptions and capabilities of NEF, a series of theoretical and experimental analyses were conducted to evaluate and confirm that NEF is capable of solving a variety of generalization and prediction problems. As such, NEF serves as a robust tool for exploring the structure of reinforcement learning tasks and predicting behaviors from past experiences. Our research thus opens a new area of investigation, and we propose the name "Episodic Learning" for this particular category of learning problems. As such, we offer a formal definition for this particular category of learning problems. Based on the outstanding performance of NEF, and the significance of episodic learning, we expect that it will serve as a guiding principle for the development of future meta-reinforcement learning methods. Our results demonstrate that nilpotent algebras of step length 3 are not geometric and yield two separate cases for nilpotent algebras of steps 4 and 5, respectively. This study presents a new, user-friendly tool called SIFT-CPD for registering two CT images based on tissue density. Unlike other methods that rely on surface features, SIFT-CPD uses a comprehensive algorithm that accounts for variations in patient size, shape, and organ morphology. It employs the Scale-Invariant Feature Transform, combined with a probability distribution model for robustly detecting and matching image features. During the registration process, SIFT-CPD adjusts for differences in intensity contrast and local tissue patterns, ultimately aligning two CT scans with high precision. Our method was tested on a dataset of 20 patients with different sizes, shapes, and organ morphologies, and was compared to another popular registration technique. The results show that SIFT-CPD offers superior alignment and accuracy, and can be used as an efficient and reliable tool for various image-guided medical therapies. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to remarkable achievements, but
researchers have noted that over-representation in the output layer can hinder
predictive accuracy. To address this issue, a novel method called UOT-Pooling
utilizing the Unbalanced Optimal Transport framework has been developed. This
new approach not only facilitates the representation of diverse data
points via optimal transportation, but also enables the dynamic adjustment of
pooling sizes based on current and historical errors. Through this dynamic
adjustment, the UOT-Pooling method seeks to optimize the overall accuracy of
neural networks. In order to implement this new approach, an efficient
conic segmentation algorithm is proposed that quickly calculates the optimal
transport cost under various constraints. Comprehensive experiments have been
conductured using six benchmark datasets and revealed that the UOT-Pooling
method consistently outperformed the state-of-the-art techniques. As a result,
the UOT-Pooling method represents a pioneering direction in the field of
neural network optimization. This work has been made available on arXiv and will
be presented at ICCV 2021. The associated code can be found on GitHub. A
corresponding blog post has also been published on Tachyon.

Our findings reveal minimal evidence of AGNs following spiral arms. Instead, we found that 9 AGNs aligned closely with their host galaxies' major axes, while 11 AGNs aligned more loosely or even opposed their host galaxies' major axes. Furthermore, our analysis revealed a type 1 AGN orientation distribution significantly different from type 2 AGNs, with a near-circular normal distribution and no pronounced radio emissions' excess. In contrast, our distribution of type 2 AGNs showed a distinct, not circular normal distribution, with a significant excess of low-inclination objects and no radio emissions' excess. Our study confirms that 9 out of 20 AGNs aligned closely with their host galaxies' major axes and indicates type 1 AGNs oriented at low inclinations are less energetic than others. This research paper delves into the characteristics of flat general rotation surfaces from a geometric perspective. By defining the pointwise Gauss map and its properties, we establish a comprehensive framework for understanding these surfaces. Utilizing the pointwise Gauss map, we derive key conditions that govern the flat general rotation surface equation, which is expressed through the pointwise Gauss map's first fundamental form. Additionally, we identify and classify special cases of flat general rotation surfaces, including surfaces with a compact domain and constant 1-type Gauss map. Our approach also enables the identification of isoparametric surfaces within the flat general rotation class. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the pointwise Gauss map is a conformal projection when the surface is a flat general delimitator, which in turn yields a novel classification of flat general delimitator surfaces. Our findings also include a classification of minimal general rotation surfaces with a pointwise constant 1-type Gauss map. Our method involves a conformal projection of the pointwise Gauss map, which in turn enables the classification of minimal general rotation surfaces. Estimating scene geometry is a fundamental problem with numerous applications in computer vision. Recognizing the geometric structure of a scene is more inherently meaningful than categorizing it by labels. Thus, scene geometry estimation might be more effective in pre-training models for downstream tasks. Unlike traditional image classification, which relies on one input sample, estimating scene geometry requires extending existing knowledge to anticipate the geometric relationships between objects in novel scenes. Consequently, this task demands more extensive use of prior experiences, making it more suitable for training general-purpose vision models through self-supervised pre-training. In this research, we introduce a novel self-supervised pre-training method centered on estimating scene geometry. Our approach involves extending existing geometric knowledge from 2D images to 2D slices of 3D scenes. A corresponding geometry estimation task is defined as predicting the 'future' 2D slice of a scene, given the current 2D slice. A new dataset, named SBS, with an accompanying method to create more challenging 'future' predictions, is developed. Our method of estimating scene geometry and associated dataset significantly outperform current self-supervised state-of-the-art pre-training methods on pre-training and downstream tasks of object pose estimation and image classification. Moreover, our method of estimating scene geometry and associated dataset exhibit minimal to no training data dependencies, making them highly versatile. This study examines the effectiveness of LSTM in enhancing Japanese word segmentation using character-based models, particularly in cases where words are compound and not clearly defined in a dictionary. Data from the KAKENe project provided 42,928 Japanese compound words, making up around 0.37% of the language's total vocabulary. To address the data scarcity, a strategy involving multiple forward passes was employed to increase the sample size for training. Furthermore, an attention mechanism was incorporated to analyze the internal state of LSTM at different time intervals. Experimental results show that a model using three-layer LSTM with attention surpassed the baseline accuracy of 57.3% by 8.8%, reaching 66.2%. To validate the model's generalizability, evaluations using tenfold cross-validation were conducted. Additionally, when the model was applied to a larger dataset containing 434,921 compound words from Wikipedia, it achieved an accuracy of 54.1%. Overall, the LSTM-based approach outperformed existing models using hidden Markov models and recurrent neural networks. However, it's worth noting that the model still struggled with data scarcity by comparison with more information-rich languages like Spanish. Future plans include collecting more data and exploring the use of pre-trained word embeddings. Moreover, the implementation of the model will be made publicly available on the GitHub platform. Finally, evaluations of the model's performance using various accuracy metrics such as precision, recall, and F1-score are planned for future development.

This study investigates the most frequently shared external resources on the Stack Overflow platform. With a large number of developers contributing to the site, the value of shared resources, particularly those from the internet, is considerable, with a significant portion of the site's content originating from external sources. Despite the significance of these resources, there has been no comprehensive analysis of them in the literature. We extracted a random sample of 1,504 questions that included external resources from the Stack Overflow dataset and employed a combination of quantitative and qualitative methods to analyze them. Our analysis reveals that images are the most shared resource type, with 55% of questions featuring at least one image. Additionally, external resources are often repeated in answers to the same question, with 61% of questions having at least one resource shared multiple times. To understand why users contribute external resources and the challenges they face, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 15 active Stack Overflow contributors. Our results indicate that the benefits of sharing resources outweigh the drawbacks, with 80% of interviewees agreeing that the rewards exceed the costs. While the rewards are high, the risks and difficulties associated with sharing resources are substantial, with 93% of interviewees acknowledging these challenges. We identify and name a new concept, "Resource Reuse," and outline areas for further research to improve the site's functionality to enhance the user experience of resource contribution. Our analysis sheds light on the significance of shared resources on Stack Overflow, highlights current limitations, and points out opportunities for improvement to create a more efficient contribution system. Based on our findings, we propose modifications to the site's functionality that can boost contributor satisfaction and the overall quality of the site. To bridge this gap, we combine two effective psychological mechanisms - self-affirmation and value-affirmation - to create an innovative intervention aimed at increasing people's commitment to climate change action. Our intervention, comprising a series of online affirmations and a subsequent values-based activity, has shown significant potential in enhancing personal values, leading to significant increases in both climate-related identity and behavior as well as personal values, as evidenced by our study results. Our study's findings underscore the significance of personal values in inspiring climate change action and illustrate how psychological mechanisms can be strategically combined to foster desired outcomes, including action intended to benefit the global community. Furthermore, our study offers a model for designing value-based interventions aimed at promoting positive behaviors on an individual level. In terms of future research opportunities, our study presents several possibilities for exploring the long-term effects of our intervention as well as investigating potential differences in intervention outcomes based on varying levels of initial climate change identification. Additionally, our study presents a chance to adapt and refine the intervention for use with diverse audiences, potentially through the incorporation of machine learning tactics to tailor the intervention to individual needs. Our solution involves enhancing the precision of disease symptom extraction by leveraging a new generalization technique through adaptive data weighting. This method allows the same set of diseases to be learned from unlicensed data, even when there's an imbalance in the availability of disease samples. Our study indicates that adaptive data weighting is a powerful tool for mitigating disease imbalance and can be applied to various scenarios of extracting symptoms. Autonomous vehicles can learn to drive skills through reinforcement learning, but prior studies have found that a significant amount of data needs to be digested by the agent for an acceptable level of performance. This research builds upon existing reinforcement learning approaches by demonstrating that recurrent neural networks incorporated into the agent can significantly improve performance and reduce data requirements in partially observable environments. It is shown that recurrent neural networks can be effectively incorporated into the agent by testing them in a simple role as a recurrent neural network actor or a combination of actor-critic role with a static policy, a predictive model, or a memory-augmentation role. These contributions are validated by successfully applying the approach to a challenging autonomous driving task in the Gazebo simulator. The results indicate that recurrent neural networks can improve performance and reduce data requirements by efficiently incorporating past experiences into the agent, thereby facilitating the learning of complex skills relevant to autonomous driving. The approach is expected to be adaptable to various domains. The proliferation of deep annealing neural networks (DANN) has shown remarkable potential in enhancing the performance of various annealing neural networks (ANNs), which in turn has led to a surge in power consumption on custom-designed hardware. This study counteracts this issue by introducing an efficient and general-purpose classifier network, dubbed template-based neural network (TNN), with the capacity to rival ANNs in both performance and flexibility. Notably, our TNN model can function as both a solution to the weight machine learning problem and a general-purpose classifier, distinct from DANN and ANNs. Moreover, we developed a sampling-theoretical method to generate training data for the TNN and conducted comprehensive experiments on various datasets, which resulted in outstanding classification accuracy, accompanied by the associated generalization errors, all of which demonstrate the "achieving-it-all" theorem for the TNN. Furthermore, we successfully implemented the TNN on custom-designed hardware, specifically an analog neuromorphic device, to achieve state-of-the-art performance, thus validating the efficiency and robustness of the TNN. Interpreting machine learning models, especially black-box algorithms like Random Forest, can be challenging. Previous methods have shown some success in extracting meaningful information, yet they often fall short of providing a comprehensive understanding of how input features influence the model's output. In this research, we present a novel technique called Disentangled Attribution Curves (DACs) that aspires to improve feature importance by pinpointing the partial effects of each feature, distinct from their interactions. Our proposed method is then applied to the bike-sharing dataset, revealing notable insights. Our findings suggest that DACs offer more precise and interpretable results, primarily due to the disentangled nature of the curves, which aligns with expected patterns. In contrast, traditional feature importance methods, such as Permutation Feature Importance (PFI), fail to account for partial interactions and return flat curves for certain features. Furthermore, DACs have the potential to identify features with redundant information, such as days of the week and months, both of which demonstrate similar and anticipated effects on the model's output. While DACs achieve accuracy of 92.5\% using a subset of relevant features, the full model struggles due to the negative impact of redundant and highly-correlated features. Ultimately, DACs provide a groundbreaking approach for understanding the complexities of black-box models, revealing the intricate roles of individual features and their interactions. Our method's simplicity and versatility make it easily applicable to various datasets, such as the iris, breast cancer, and housing price datasets, which are analyzed in the supplementary material. To protect against adversarial attacks in federated learning, researchers use private technologies such as homomorphic encryption, secret sharing, and multi-party computation for federated learning. However, current solutions either have significant computational overhead or have limitations in their protection capabilities. For instance, homomorphic encryption has considerable computational costs and cannot safeguard data when the adversary is the user, while secret sharing and multi-party computation can be costly due to data retasking and network traffic. Existing solutions also have restrictions in their classification accuracy and additional bandwidth requirements. We aim to address these shortcomings with a novel approach that combines secret sharing and homomorphic encryption in a nested manner. This nested approach enables the secure computation of user gradients and contributions from adversaries, while allowing for the recruitment of more users and the efficient classification of short models. This new approach offers more comprehensive protection, faster computation, and greater support for users than existing solutions. We conduct extensive experiments to validate our claims, using datasets from the Standard dataset collection and evaluating our approach against 6 prominent attacks. The results show that our approach successfully resists all the attacks, while also achieving superior accuracy and reduced computation overhead compared to state-of-the-art techniques. For instance, our approach offers 100% protection against POA and HME attacks, delivers 101.34% less computation overhead than HE-based approaches, and requires 101.34% fewer bytes of network traffic than multi-party computation-based approaches. This new approach is capable of providing advanced protection, outperforming existing solutions in efficiency, and recruiting a greater number of users than previously possible. This research presents a new approach to verifying that an Arduino driver functions as expected when installed on a microcontroller. Our method utilizes a simulation environment that mimics the interaction between the computer host and the Arduino board, allowing for testing of the driver through input/output interactions. The simulation consists of three interconnected components: a remote driver running on the Arduino that facilitates data exchange with the host, a local emulator running on the host that simulates the host's output to the Arduino and processes its input, and a bridge that coordinates remote and local interactions. To validate our approach, we formally proved that the remote driver's behavior is equivalent to the emulator's, based on the specification of their concurrent execution. Additionally, we successfully tested the driver using our simulation environment, demonstrating its effectiveness. Notably, our method does not rely on symbolic execution and can handle drivers written in C. The advantages of our approach include improved reliability, faster testing, and lower costs, as well as simplified validation processes for drivers and models of microcontrollers. The project has been implemented using Arduino's IDE and the Arduino Due board, with all relevant code and documentation available online. The time complexity of our method was found to be linear in the number of input values. While the space complexity is also linear, it may become Scary of O(n) in the worst case due to the inherent limitations of the Arduino environment. Our approach is innovative in its use of simulation-based verification, and it fills a significant gap in existing research by testing driver output without the need for modification. As a result, it has the potential to be a pioneering work in this area. Based on our performance analysis, the time complexity of the algorithm was found to be proportional to the number of input values, at O(n), making it efficient and scalable. Similarly, the space complexity was found to be linear, at O(n), although it is possible that it may become a higher order of magnitude in the worst case due to the constraints of the Arduino environment. As a result of this analysis, our approach has the potential to be used in the testing of real-world drivers, as demonstrated by the inclusion of the i2c_tool driver that was successfully verified in this research. Furthermore, the project has significant practical implications as a result of its wide applicability, its innovative use of simulation-based verification, and its potential to be a pioneering work in this area. As a result of this research, an open-source implementation, as well as additional documentation and project details, are now available online at the URL listed in the acknowledgements

This paper presents an evaluation of two novel runtime filters, Timeloops and Descent, which enable the isolation of critical system APIs from untrusted applications written in languages such as PHP, Python, and Ruby. A comparative study between Timeloops and Descent has been carried out using real-world examples, including PHP applications in which system APIs can be invoked unintentionally, leading to security vulnerabilities. The evaluation examines two critical aspects: the ease of integration with existing code bases and the resource utilization associated with each filtering approach. Unlike Descent, which requires significant modifications to code and relies on sophisticated analysis for API isolation, Timeloops achieves this goal with minimal code adjustments and leverages existing runtime mechanisms. Furthermore, Timeloops has been successfully integrated into the PHP development environment, allowing for both static and dynamic code analysis. As a result, Timeloops provides a practical means of limiting system API usage and preventing accidental security vulnerabilities in applications written using interpreted languages. high-dimensional data points describing the genetic activity in each cell. Due
to the inherent properties of this data in Euclidean space, it has become common
to apply traditional Euclidean distance metrics in classification and
dimensionality reduction tasks. However, studies have shown that grouping cells
based on similarities in the expression of specific genes across different
samples can often be achieved with much lower dimensional representations.
 Consequently, our study sets out to investigate the effectiveness of using
these lower-dimensional space forms for classification, utilizing both well-
known dimensionality reduction techniques and more custom approaches. The
results reveal that features derived from PCA, tSNE, UMAP, and GMM in these
lower-dimensional space forms offer substantial performance improvements over
standard Euclidean space classifications, in addition to providing substantial
dimensionality reductions. Furthermore, combining these dimensionality reduction
techniques with supervised classifiers such as Logistic Regression and SVM
results in significant improvements in classification accuracy in scRNA-seq data,
in some cases with reduced dimensional representations up to 99.77%. Therefore,
our research highlights the benefits of utilizing these lower-dimensional space
forms over traditional Euclidean distances in classification tasks. Lastly,
our study also introduces an open-source Python package, scReducer, which can be
used to replicate the classification results in this study and additional
reduction techniques not covered here. This package is accessible via
https://scinder.github.io/scReducer/. For data analysis, we utilized Python
version 3.7 along with relevant bioinformatics and machine learning libraries. The project's main goal is to analyze how stars interact with each other in close approaches to a supermassive black hole under different hypothetical scenarios.  These scenarios include a mass-dependent interaction where the mass function of stars varies, and a model of star clustering.  The project utilizes a method to determine the mass function of stars based on their near-infrared magnitudes and incorporates various templates of star clustering.  The project then calculates the rate of close approaches between stars, both with and without considering their prior encounters with the black hole, using a Monte-Carlo method.  The results of these calculations are used to determine the coefficient of restitution for star-black hole and star-star collisions.  The project finds that taking into account the mass function of stars significantly affects their coefficient of restitution, while clustering has a negligible effect.  These findings imply that a model of mass function is necessary to accurately model the scattering of stars in the environment of a supermassive black hole.  These results can be applied to study the scattering of stars in galaxies with a wide range of masses.  The project also finds that accounting for prior encounters of stars with the black hole has a negligible effect on their coefficient of restitution.  These findings can be applied to studies of the growth of supermassive black holes, allowing for the inclusion of statistical mechanics principles in models of star-slinging phenomena.  The project's code and results are made available to the public through a repository on the GitLab platform. This work investigates the application of stochastic Model Predictive Control (MPC) to systems affected by uncertainty. The key challenge in utilizing MPC is to manage the trade-off between tracking performance and enforcing feasibility, given that the system's behavior is unpredictable. To address this, our study proposes a novel online algorithm that generates robust control moves while accommodating uncertainty, with the goal of achieving optimal tracking performance. In contrast to conventional MPC methods, our approach does not require knowledge of uncertainty bounds but rather leverages an uncertainty metric that serves as a convenient substitute, thereby enabling efficient computation. The proposed method is further demonstrated through simulation studies on multiple systems, including a mass-spring system and a quadcopter aircraft. The results confirm the effectiveness of our approach in achieving efficient and robust performance, even when uncertainty is high. Notably, our method exhibits computational efficiency comparable to or better than existing methods, with a computational complexity of $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$. The developed code is publicly accessible through the URL provided in the reference. Additionally, potential future applications and extensions of our work are presented. As such, this paper is suitable for researchers with a advanced level of understanding of stochastic MPC. \linebreak Further details can be found in the document.

Sundials are ancient timekeepers that can be found in both urban and rural areas of Indonesia, dating back to the pre-clock era. As direct sellers of clockwork technology, sundials offer a unique glimpse into the history of their respective locations. Despite their significance, sundials have largely been overlooked in academic circles, with only a handful of studies on sundials from Indonesia and Europe published in notable journals. To address this gap, we propose a citizen science initiative that enables the global community to contribute to the documentation and research of sundials in Indonesia. By combining crowd-sourced data collection, field research, and expert analysis, we aim to shed new light on the sundials of Indonesia. This includes exploring their historical context, calculating their celestial parameters, and understanding their relationship with local cultures. Ultimately, this project will demonstrate the potential of interdisciplinary research driven by citizen science to transform our understanding of ancient history. If successfully implemented, this project can serve as a model for similar endeavors in other countries. To achieve this goal, we require funding of 500,000,000 IDR over a period of 24 months. The project team consists of three researchers with a proven track record of achievement in various fields. Further details of the proposal are presented below. Background: Indonesia is home to numerous sundials, with the oldest dating back to the 16th century in the region of Java and the Younger Dryas in Sumatra. As timekeepers, sundials offer a unique glimpse into historical events, while their statistical analysis provides valuable insights into celestial parameters. Recent breakthroughs in machine learning and AI have created new opportunities for advanced pattern recognition, while advances in GPS technology allow for more precise measurements of temporal relationships. Objectives: To collect and document historical information on sundials in Indonesia through a citizen science approach, to calculate their celestial parameters, and to explore their cultural significance in relation to local histories. Methods: A comprehensive literature review on sundials will be conducted, coupled with field research to collect data on their spatial distribution, temporal relationships, and cultural context. Using advanced computer algorithms, we will accurately determine their celestial parameters, while employing traditional recording methods will document their historical and cultural importance. To ensure the sustainability of this project, we will maintain an online platform for continued data collection and research. Results: Preliminary findings from our field research show promising results, with new insights into the spatial distribution and temporal relationships of sundials in Indonesia expected to emerge from this study. Conclusion: This project will contribute to the development of new new methods for documenting and analyzing

In TFIET, a method for dynamic expansion of 5G DED2D and future DED+2D networks, user devices receive data and energy through nearby users with greater resources. This is achieved by equipping a subset of users with energy and data transfer capabilities, which allows the network to dynamically expand and connect distant devices. This approach uses joint data and energy routing techniques to minimize costs while ensuring that all devices are connected and satisfied with their service requirements. This paper investigates TFIET under two scenarios: TFIET-D, which assumes that connected users can transfer data and energy, and TFIET-N, which assumes that energy transfer is possible but data transfer is not. The highest energy savings can be achieved in TFIET-D, which also offers the fastest data rates, but both methods can adapt to different service requirements. The largest data rates are achieved in TFIET-N when there is a lack of energy-harvesting users, which indicates the need for additional energy-supplying users in this scenario. The energy savings in TFIET-D far exceed those of TFIET-N, which is due to the energy transfer between users in the latter method. The TFIET-D scenario can also support various service standards, which further indicates its potential for use in future-proof networks. This work investigates the near-future networks that will be used in the long-term, which will eventually transition to DED+2D with mobile energy suppliers. This is achieved through the deployment of flying base stations that provide energy and data to connected users, which in turn supply energy and data to distant devices. This is the main focus of our companion paper, FFIET. Both TFIET and FFIET investigate dynamic expansion of future networks with energy and data transfer capabilities. While TFIET focuses on DED2D and DED+2D, our companion paper investigates the fixed versions of these networks, which is essential for understanding the long-term vision of these networks and how they will function in the long-term. The extent to which these changes affect individual circumstances largely depends on factors such as their geographical location, age, and professional experience. Although various studies have examined the labor market's response to the adoption of automation in non-laboratory settings, there is a notable lack of research exploring the impact of automated laboratories on their staff. To fill this knowledge gap, a study was conducted using in-depth interviews with laboratory staff, focusing on their perspectives on the consequences of automated laboratories on their working lives. Key areas of investigation included the laboratory environment, staff management policies, employee concerns, and possible solutions to mitigate these changes. Findings indicate that laboratory staff are concerned about the potential consequences of automated laboratories, including reduced job security, changed working conditions, and the need for adapted work routines. This article formulates a revised version of Asser's conjecture and investigates its tenability. We define a set, $\mathcal{S}$, which comprises spectra obtained from undirected bipartite graphs, and a conjecture is stated which asserts that the set $\mathcal{S}$ is complete. A program aimed at verifying this conjecture involves characterizing the elements of $\mathcal{S}$ using criteria that are both necessary and sufficient. We establish that each element of $\mathcal{S}$ can be identified with a function from the set of natural numbers to the set of non-zero integers, which generates the spectrum through a specific graph construction, and this function must satisfy certain conditions. Furthermore, a random model is introduced which allows us to explore the possible functions that correspond to elements of $\mathcal{S}$, and we are able to compute the probability that a randomly selected function generates a spectrum that belongs to the set $\mathcal{S}$. We are then able to determine the probability that a randomly selected graph is bipartite and belongs to the set $\mathcal{S}$. This model is shown to be related to another problem, in which we investigate the properties of a certain probability measure, known as $p_n$, which is defined on the set of functions from the set of integers to the set of non-zero integers, and which assigns a probability of $1/2$ to functions that are symmetric. A series of theoretical results are established which describe the properties of the function $p_n$. These findings are further generalized in the study of the sign patterns that correspond to the spectra of the Bertrand-Rademacher random walk. The study investigates the probability that a randomly selected sign pattern belongs to the set $\mathcal{S}$. The findings are then used to determine the probability that a randomly selected graph is bipartite and belongs to the set $\mathcal{S}$. Consequently, these results provide insight into Asser's original conjecture and the properties of the set $\mathcal{S}}$. In scanning transmission electron microscopy, electrostatic phase plates are used to modify the electron probe size, though doing so poses the challenge of maintaining probe current. To address this issue, this work investigates how the design of phase plates affects electron probe size and current density. Various designs of unipolar and bipolar phase plates with different fill-factors and pixel patterns were analyzed, indicating that increasing fill-factor generally decreases the probe current while altering pixel patterns has a minimal impact. Furthermore, a method to estimate phase plate transfer functions was developed using simulations, demonstrating good agreement with experimental results. Using this information, bipolar phase plates were designed to minimize size and current density variations, ultimately successfully implementing a bipolar modulator with a high fill-factor of 93.75%. Despite initially exhibiting a high current density, this design showed potential for improvement through optimization of the modulator design, ultimately demonstrating the capability to balance ideal probe size and current density with a high fill-factor. We derive exact formulas for the expected number of distinct positions in $d$-dimensional binary random walks after $2n$ steps. These formulas are obtained by expressing the random walk as a generator for the $d$-dimensional lattice in the semi-group algebra generated by the integers, and then applying a general result on the generated sub-lattice's cardinality. Furthermore, we find that the expected number of distinct positions increases exponentially in $d$, with a rate tied to the entropy of the Fibonacci Pascal triangle. By contrast, one-dimensional random walks exhibit entropy growth akin to the binary uniform measure on the integers. Additionally, our approach yields a straightforward algorithm for sampling $d$-dimensional random walks, with a novel correlation insight that significantly improves the efficiency of sampling $d+1$-dimensional random walks by projecting $d$-dimensional walks. A related open-source implementation is available at https://github.com/rl2/RandomWalkCounting. All code can be generated directly from the Python arXiv certificate arxiv-2002-05029.zip. Our study is motivated in part by the application of numerical integration, and one such example is the study of the critical threshold for the d-dimensional ginzburg-landau model on the d+1 dimensional lattice. We provide the critical threshold to be precisely $n^{1/d}$ for the $d$-dimensional model and present numerical integration results for the average distance of the random walk from the origin in the $d$-dimensional model. Lastly, the relatively simple structure of the generated sub-lattice allows us to establish a probabilistic interpretation of the $d$-dimensional random walk by considering the distribution of $d$-dimensional lattice points generated by $d$-dimensional random walks. This generation process can be viewed as a random walk within the $d$-dimensional lattice that is augmented with an additional dimension in which time progresses, offering an alternative perspective on the $d$-dimensional random walk. Conversely, the random walk within the augmented $d+1$-dimensional lattice corresponds to the generated sub-lattice's $d$-dimensional section, thereby establishing a direct connection between the random walk and the generated sub-lattice's properties. To establish the general result on the generated sub-lattice's cardinality, we first derive exact formulas for the expected number of distinct positions in $d$-dimensional random walks within the augmented $d+1$-dimensional lattice.
