Acronyms are an ubiquitous form of abbreviation commonly found across different writing disciplines. While they enhance comprehension and familiarity when used within specific domains, their reduced form often lacks context, making it difficult for readers to identify the corresponding full form. Existing research has primarily focused on either extracting and interpreting acronym expansions within a confined domain or incorporating a knowledge base for cross-domain applications. However, these approaches are often limited, assuming that all domains are self-contained and isolated from others, and that a comprehensive knowledge base can be constructed and updated effortlessly. In contrast, this paper proposes a more dynamic framework that leverages systems to uncover and clarify acronym expansions across various domains. To alleviate ambiguity, our approach relies on both within-domain and cross-domain clustering to assign suitable labels, much like manual acronym development. Furthermore, to mitigate the challenge of building and maintaining a knowledge base, our method distinguishes between proven and hypothetical acronym expansions based on the support provided by existing knowledge and non-knowledge users. Through thorough evaluation on 356 academic and 296 news articles, our technique demonstrates notable gains in F1-score, outperforming state-of-the-art competitors by 25.97% and 10.09% respectively. Additional details on our method's capacity to handle complex cases and the issues raised by existing acronym detection and translation systems can be found in the supplementary materials. We propose a method to produce directional heat emission in quantum Hall systems by combining rectification techniques and utilizing the electrostatic control of local heat thresholds. Due to the non-conductive nature of quantum Hall gaps, where energy levels are isolated by energy gaps, heat transmission is hinderly impedied, allowing for the design of rectifiers. By employing an external control voltage that can alter the local heat threshold, and incorporating a quantum point contact that enables or obstructs heat transmission, we are able to design a rectifier module. A full rectifier device can be constructed by replicating and arranging these modules in an asymmetrical pattern. Heat emission in the desired direction can be enabled by adjusting the control voltage, while the absence of rectification in the opposite direction is ensured through the unaccessibility of local heat thresholds. Furthermore, a heat transformer can be designed using multiple quantum Hall gaps by varying the control voltages to select different gaps for heat transmission and transformation. These quantum Hall rectifiers and transformers serve as the first examples of directional heat emission and heat transformation devices that utilize quantum Hall effects. Additionally, potential applications of these devices were considered in relation to multi-quantum-well thermal micro/meso-electronics. Our research has inspired the experimental creation of these devices, prompting a proposal for a trial investigation. A possible experimental setup is suggested for the simultaneous evaluation of heat emission, the validation of the rectification mechanism, and a comparison with conventional thermal triple-point rectifiers. A potential compensation method is also presented for addressing heat emission asymmetry in quantum Hall rectifiers. Ultimately, the concept of utilizing quantum Hall effects for heat emission and transformation has been established as a feasible approach. Moreover, the possibility of combining quantum Hall effects with superconductivity to produce ultra-low-temperature thermal devices has also been introduced. Information about recent research in this field was incorporated into the discussion. In recent years, several DNA data storage systems based on standard DNA sequencers have been developed to solve the problem of the vast amount of data generated by sensors, the limitation of current storage technology, etc. These systems encode data into DNA double helices following the standard base pairing rules, with various encoding methods being proposed to enhance DNA data storage technology. To overcome the issue of non-matching bases interrupting the DNA decoding process, several error-correcting schemes are suggested. Recent advancements in music representation learning have largely relied on a single
methodology, using contrastive learning with audio representations only.
Contrastive learning methods are proven effective in inducing meaningful
representations across various domains, but have primarily been applied to
single-modal datasets, despite their potential in cross-modal retrieval tasks.
To explore cross-modal music retrieval capabilities, we propose a new dataset,
MusicTM-Dataset, featuring a pair of dissimilar music segments for each track,
along with their corresponding audio-frequency spectra and melody representations.
This dataset enables the evaluation of cross-modal music retrieval tasks via
self-supervised learning methods. We further introduce a new method, two-stage
contrastive learning, which combines existing contrastive learning with an
additional stage utilizing a melting pot loss to learn robust music
representations that can be easily retrieved across different modalities.
Experimental results demonstrate the two-stage approach significantly enhances
retrieval accuracy by at least 10% compared to single-stage methods on our
MusicTM-Dataset. The proposed dataset and methods are available for public
use at https://music-tm-dataset.github.io/. The dataset, source code can be
downloaded from https://github.com/Music-TM-Dataset.

This paper introduces Ontodia, a web-based visual graph editor used to create and
display knowledge graphs, such as the Wikidata dataset. By integrating Ontodia with
Wikidata, we've developed a pioneering tool for visual data exploration and
modification in a semantic framework. Ontodia's innovative feature allows users
to interact with visual representations of entities, by clicking on lines to edit
associated data, or by navigating to related entities in a graph. Ontodia's
co-development with Wikidata enables automatic synchronization with the online
dataset, ensuring that modifications made by users are reflected in both the
visual graph and Wikidata. Although Ontodia's primary focus is on Wikidata, its
general design and functionality can be applied to other semantic datasets and
graphs. As of March 2022, Ontodia has over 3,500 users across 120 countries,
enabling collaborative visual data exploration and shaping the Wikidata
knowledge graph. Furthermore, Ontodia's source code is freely accessible under
the CC-BY-Sa license, promoting open-source development of the platform.

This study examines the habits of Wikipedia article editors who use categories to organize content, analyzing their tagging systems and inference processes. By identifying patterns in category usage and the relationships between them, the research aims to create content management tools tailored to the needs of human editors. To achieve this, the analysis focuses on the applications of manual scale-based operations, allowing for the analysis to be grounded in the practical capabilities of human editors. As a first step towards developing new mechanisms for content management, the investigation aims to understand the current system's properties and how they can be utilized to make human editing more efficient. Long-term goals of this research include using the findings to develop automatic methods for inferring categories from article content and potentially introducing new manual methods for editors. The analysis is based on a dataset consisting of articles from Wikipedia's English version, along with their associated categories and subsections. As a result of this study, four key distribution patterns in the use of coarse and fine categories were identified, along with the presence of "tagging clouds," the inference of primary and secondary categories from section names, and the discovery of editor preferences for inferring categories from article titles and ledes. These findings provide a basis for developing new content management tools and, in the long term, automatic inference methods. Two such tools were implemented, demonstrating the potential to improve performance: (1) predicting categories from article content by leveraging editor scale-based operations, and (2) utilizing these operations to infer previously missing categories. The evaluation of these techniques confirmed their effectiveness in retrieving articles based on category inference. As a result, they have already been deployed on Wikipedia's English edition. Two new manual content management tools were also introduced, designed to assist editors in inferring categories: (1) a browse tool allowing editors to find articles with specific category combinations, and (2) a console allowing editors to query articles with particular category combinations and associated keywords. Both tools have been incorporated into Wikipedia's special pages for editors. This paper addresses the problem of providing high-quality mobile connectivity to a density of users by leveraging mobile integrated access and backhaul (mIAB). To effectively serve users in motion, we consider a scenario where mIAB is utilized. Our strategy involves dividing mIAB into different modes based on backhaul link availability, with either data being forwarded to a base station or directly to users through access links. To address the complexity of optimizing frequencies for users while accounting for positions and velocities, we employ a mathematical framework that accounts for user grouping. Our approach optimizes frequencies by converting a problem involving polynomial sums into a more manageable form. Through this optimization, we can determine the number of frequencies needed and assign them to users, ensuring that each user has a minimum data rate. Our results show that this partitioning has a simple expression and is achievable in linear time, and that the optimized frequency assignment also has a simple form and can be implemented in linear time. Our method is further validated by showing the optimal partitioning and assignment's independence from user velocity and outer bound. To demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, simulations are conducted using 20 randomly generated user trajectories, resulting in a minimum data rate and optimal frequency allocation for each user. Our method is compared to a baseline technique, revealing that it reduces the number of frequencies required by 50% while maintaining a minimum data rate, and highlights the importance of optimizing mIAB mode splitting for multi-user communication. Our work has potential to be expanded by incorporating ten potential variations, including incorporating backhaul power limitations and user demand for specific data rates. By addressing these variations, the optimized frequency allocation and partitioning can be tailored to different scenarios, potentially leading to more efficient communication methods. This paper addresses the issue of hyperparameter tuning for learning algorithms by taking a novel approach. Rather than focusing on individual hyperparameters in isolation, it seeks to understand how they interact with one another. The chosen model, Linear Discriminant Analysis, facilitated an in-depth analysis due to its non-degenerate minimum points, allowing for a comprehensive examination of its hyperparameters. Through mathematical derivation, the stability of the algorithm was achieved by plotting contour plots, illustrating how hyperparameters impact performance. The findings show that optimal hyperparameters can lead to distinct generalization performances in different datasets, highlighting the unpredictability of hyperparameters and the need to consider their interdependence. Moreover, this research demonstrates the feasibility of identifying optimal hyperparameter ranges through mathematical analysis, reducing the need for extensive grid searches in algorithm tuning processes. The proposed method can serve as a guide for evaluating the stability of other algorithms, providing a framework for exploring hyperparameter interactions. Current assessments of reinforcement learning algorithms are typically based on a single, fixed curriculum that is either completely successful or fails entirely. To address this limitation, we develop a new approach that evaluates an RL algorithm's ability to adapt to multiple learning environments with gradually changing conditions. Our novel framework presents a series of curricula, each with a distinct sequence of transitions, and selects for the one that is most robust in its final setup. Through this method, we are able to identify RL algorithms that are capable of mastering complex tasks and adapting to unexpected changes in the learning environment. Our study further highlights the potential to create more resilient policies by gradually increasing the level of difficulty in the curriculum and exposes a major flaw in the current reinforcement learning assessment techniques that can result in policies that perform exceptionally well but are unable to cope with unexpected situations. The COVID-19 pandemic in South Africa, exacerbated by social inequities, has led to data disparities. Available data, primarily from urban areas, is fragmented and restricted to public access due to data governance policies' inadequacies. This research outlines the complications with current data usage and suggests remedies to address them. Consequently, a custom data sharing model has been developed to accommodate diverse data contributors and users. This model forms the basis for a prototype data sharing platform, SARS-Online, which facilitates the collaborative exchange of SARS-CoV-2 sequence and non-sequencing related data. A subsequent evaluation, involving 21 data contributors and users, revealed that the platform addresses existing data sharing hurdles. Notably, SARS-Online has already yielded multiple breakthroughs, including multiple virus variants' identification. It is anticipated that the platform will continue to promote research advancements in the battle against COVID-19 and potentially tackle future health crises. Additionally, a case study has been developed to guide institutions in governing data to support public interest, while respecting both data suppliers' and consumers' rights. This approach advocates for greater flexibility and adaptability in data governance, empowering them to better respond to rapidly evolving situations. By aligning data usage with the public benefit, institutions can make more informed decisions regarding data sharing, ultimately contributing meaningfully to society. For example, we show how the platform enabled researchers to identify new COVID-19 variants associated with increased transmissibility and immune evasion, ultimately informing public health policies. This experience confirms that the platform has the potential to keep the public informed about the evolving pandemic through continuous data analysis and sharing. Long-term, the vision is for the platform to become a fully-fledged Data Collaborative, where various stakeholders come together to tackle future health crises, leveraging data to serve the public interest. To achieve this, a strategy has been proposed, involving activities such as promoting awareness, establishing clear goals and processes, and fostering a positive, inclusive environment for data governance. By pursuing this vision, it is hoped that SARS-Online can make a meaningful contribution to the public benefit, while also serving the data sharing needs of its members. This includes using data to inform public policy, drive scientific discovery, and drive various other uses, such as risk assessment, contact tracing, access to care, economic decision-making, education, research, development, news reporting, communication, recruitment, marketing, and other purposes. This research aims to explore how allowing a certain number of integers to be omitted from the definition of a low-density subset affects its behavior in relation to arithmetic progressions. Our findings demonstrate that if the maximum number of omitted integers $N$ is sufficiently large in comparison to the desired density $\delta$ and length $M$ of the arithmetic progression, a subset of integers with lower density will always exist that is consistent in its occurrences within that progression. Notably, previous work by Green and Tao established the existence of such a subset even when $N$ is a double exponential function of $M$, but our findings improve this result by showing that $N$ can be limited to $M^{3+\varepsilon}$ under the assumption of the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture. Our method of obtaining this result involves analyzing patterns within subsets that consist of three consecutive integers, four consecutive integers, and so on, and establishing that one of these subsets will often be consistent in its occurrences within an arithmetic progression. Additionally, our findings are illustrated by providing examples of such subsets in numbers that are relatively prime to 3, 4, and so on. This paper compares various fusion techniques to determine their effectiveness in text feature extraction for Higgs boson detection using Bayesian Networks. Our study distinguishes between three approaches: early, intermediate, and hierarchical fusion methods, each of which integrates information from multiple sources at a different level. To illustrate the distinct meanings, "early" refers to combining features from all sources before training a classifier, while "intermediate" involves splitting training and testing data and training a classifier separately for each source before fusing the information. On the other hand, "hierarchical" fusion method trains a classifier after splitting training and testing data, where each instance is represented by a combination of features from more than one source. In order to achieve this, we utilize a Bayesian Neural Network as our classifier and modify its penalty term to include a cross entropy loss function that is capable of handling multiple sources. Our experimental findings indicate that hierarchical fusion excels over early and intermediate fusion methods in terms of detection performance and the integration of information from multiple sources can be effectively accomplished through the use of a hierarchical fusion method. [2], CNN on combined features from multiple sources, and a Bayesian Neural Network on combined features from multiple sources. In order to validate the reliability of our approach, we used the standard techniques of cross validation and bootstrapping to determine the variability in our results. We establish that when the medium parameters $\theta$ and $\beta$ remain consistent, these transmission eigenfunctions are localized in a compact, $N-1$ dimensional structure. Conversely, when the medium parameters change (varying linearly with distance from the center), these transmission eigenfunctions are found to be condensed onto separate tangent lines at the boundary of the ball. We further investigate a scenario in which the medium parameters $\theta$ and $\beta$ are defined by a cone-like function. In this instance, the associated transmission eigenfunctions are discovered to be concentrated along various $N-1$ dimensional shapes depending on the cone's vertex angle. In addition, the article delves into the spectral decomposition of the associated spectral operator $T_\beta$. Under specified conditions, we demonstrate the spectral convergence of $T_\beta$ towards a spectral convergence of the spectral operator $T_\beta^{(0)}$ associated with the constant medium properties $\theta$ and $\beta$. As a result, the spectral convergence of eigenvalue multiplicities of $T_\beta$ is calculated as the product of two convergent series, each representing the localization around the boundary of the first transmission eigenfunctions and the second transmission eigenfunctions respectively. Finally, the article considers the asymptotic behavior of transmission eigenfunctions near the boundary of the ball as the dimension $N$ increases. The total count of subgroups within a finite group $G$, denoted by $\hbox{Sub} (G)$, has been related to the order of $G$, with a specific inequality established for nilpotent groups. By examining all possible abelian quotients of $G$, a general inequality was derived that relates the number of subgroups in $G$ to its order, with further insight into nilpotent groups providing a refined inequality in that context. Additionally, subgroups of supersoluble groups were explored, with a specific example highlighting the significance of considering all abelian quotients of such groups. Based on these findings, a general inequality was formulated to bound the number of subgroups in any finite group $G$. It is noted that the established inequality is seen as particularly accurate when $G$ is either a supersoluble group or a nilpotent group, with the number of subgroups in such groups often being seen as having a'simple' or 'natural' explanation. Finally, the concepts explored here were applied to examine the subgroups of dihedral groups and the quaternion group $Q_8$. Specifically, by using the abelian quotients of these groups, the existing inequality established that $\hbox{Sub} (D_{34}) < 234$ and $\hbox{Sub} (Q_8) < 26$. Direct verification was then used to confirm that both $D_{34}$ and $Q_8$ indeed have subgroups in the quantities indicated by the established inequality. As a consequence, the long-standing question regarding the number of subgroups in dihedral groups was resolved, with the existing inequality thus demonstrating the inability to find a general formula for the number of subgroups in all finite groups. Nevertheless, the use of abelian quotients was seen as a valuable tool in studying the subgroups of specific groups, with specific examples and cases providing further insight into the problem. Ultimately, the study of subgroups in these groups, such as dihedral groups and the quaternion group, was seen as an interesting and worthwhile area of investigation in the field of finite group theory. The paper takes a continuum limit on the $S^{(1,0)}$ field, known for being a discrete analogue of the Korteweg-de Vries equation, and converts it into a fully continuous equation. This new equation, $Q_{\lambda}(x)$, is a one-dimensional partial differential equation with a unique solution that exhibits smooth behavior. Specifically, as the discrete parameter $\lambda$ approaches zero, the spectrum of the equation becomes entirely positive, leading to the emergence of the continuous Korteweg-de Vries equation. Conversely, when coupling $S^{(1,0)}$ with an odd reflection symmetry, the continuum limit takes the form of the modified Korteweg-de Vries equation. Similarly, for coupling with an even reflection symmetry, the continuum limit is given by the equation for shallow water waves. These claims can be verified through numerical simulations. Furthermore, the paper shows that the continuum limit of the $S^{(1,0)}$ variable itself lacks a continuous interpretation but can be redefined into two well-defined continuous variables, $q(x,t)$ and $\tau(x,t)$. These new variables satisfy the shallow water waves equation and allow for the efficient numerical resolution of its continuum forms, respectively. This analytical framework can also efficiently solve other continuum forms of the $S^{(1,0)}$ equation by mapping them into discrete forms, which can then be solved through standard discrete time algorithms. Notably, the discrete equation itself retains a high degree of accuracy. This method can be extended to the $S^{(2,0)}$ variable as well. Additionally, the paper establishes a universal formula to generate continuous equations from their discrete analogues and illustrates this formula with several examples, one of which yields the continuous form of the sixth-highest order Korteweg-de Vries equation. Conversely, the paper also determines the discrete limits of continuously dependent equations, a fundamental open problem in the field. This is demonstrated with the example of the Korteweg-de Vries equation itself, whose discrete form taking into account a small mass effect is developed. Lastly, the paper shows that a wide category of discrete equations, including the finite difference equations, can be precisely mapped into their continuous analogues through the use of an exact continuum limit process. This process can be efficiently achieved with the use of a computer algorithm. This innovation enables the continuous interpretation and the precise modeling of discrete time algorithms at the foundational level of computational physics. Inspired by EfficientNet, we developed AERNet, a unique EfficientNet-based model for Visual Relationship Detection. AERNet incorporates a Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling technique to improve performance by optimizing the impact of negative sampling in the training process. Through comparison with multiple VRD benchmarks, we demonstrated AERNet's effectiveness in achieving balanced accuracy and efficiency. Notably, AERNet achieved a 79.6 mAP score on the Visual Relationship Detection task of ImageT5, surpassing state-of-the-art models by at least 9 mAP points. Additionally, AERNet's efficiency was verified on the V-COCO dataset, resulting in a 6.5 times speed improvement over other state-of-the-art models while maintaining comparable performance. Our source code is available at https://github.com/damo-cv/AERNet. Jinping Zhong was primarily responsible for this work.

Quantum systems are distinguished from classical objects by their inability to be predicted with certainty. This characteristic enables us to measure a quantum system in a specific state without fully knowing it, which inevitably causes the system to shift towards a different state. The degree to which a measurement changes the system can be quantified by the measurement-induced shift in a reference system, known as weak measurement-induced quantum change. We have established a fundamental connection between this concept and the idea of bound entanglement. Specifically, it was found that bound entanglement can give rise to residual quantumness within a quantum system, which can be effectively extracted and utilized. Notably, this extraction process does not rely on the entanglement per se, but rather on the presence of bound entanglement, thereby allowing non-consensual extraction of quantumness from multiparty quantum systems. We have further illustrated the phenomenon through a concrete example involving the tripartite GHZ state shared among three particles. Our results provide insights into the role of bound entanglement in generating quantumness and demonstrate the capability of weak measurements to reveal and extract non-classical effects from quantum systems. Our findings may inspire novel methods for purposefully creating and manipulating quantum connections among multiple particles. In the field of graph learning, researchers have noted that relationship states are key to solving various problems, however, updating these relationships efficiently remains a challenge, particularly when dealing with large graphs. To address this, a novel method called Relationship Graph Attention Network (RGAN) is introduced, which leverages a mechanism inspired by deep learning's recurrent neurons to continuously update relationships. By incorporating a special node in the graph, called the "self-node", that represents the collection of all nodes, RGAN enables the efficient sharing of information across the graph. By doing so, multiple tasks such as co-author analysis, co-appearance, and influence relationship detection can be performed efficiently using a single self-attention mechanism. Experiments have demonstrated the effectiveness of RGAN on these tasks in various graph datasets. Furthermore, to validate the importance of the self-node, a comparative study with existing relationship-sharing methods was conducted. Notably, the code and pre-trained models for RGAN will be made available for public use.

Implementing neural network architectures on large graphs proves highly resource-intensive, largely due to the need to map these graphs onto smaller, equivalent networks. However, not all graph nodes play an equal role in this process, with certain nodes contributing more significantly than others. By strategically selecting and removing less critical nodes during training, the enormous graph complexity can be substantially reduced. In this paper, we introduce GSNP, a novel neural network approach designed to efficiently learn and map large graphs using an optimized subset of nodes. By continuously refining the model's estimates and adapting the sampling strategy, GSNP skillfully balances model accuracy with reduced overfitting and improved data utilization, ultimately enabling accurate graph classification while significantly minimizing computational complexity. Experimental results on various graph classification tasks demonstrate that GSNP consistently outperforms or matches leading baselines while significantly scaling back resources requirements. The source code for GSNP can be found at https://github.com/dotmisTs/ADNE.

As a rapidly evolving field, Quantum Deep Learning aims to merge the power of Artificial Intelligence with quantum physics, but its foundation remains precarious. One of the main obstacles to overcome is the complexity of integrating traditional deep learning methods with quantum computing's inherent constraints. To address this challenge, our approach involves using quantum algorithms to enhance deep learning algorithms, and vice versa, within a single quantum computing environment. Specifically, we have developed a framework that combines quantum algorithms with deep learning methods, and applies it to problems involving quantum states and binary classification tasks. Our evaluation, conducted across multiple hardware platforms, showcases the potential of Quantum Deep Learning, but also highlights the limitations due to quantum computing's limitations, and reveals the advantages of using both quantum and traditional methods. This paper explores the intricacies of designing, constructing, and managing a High Energy Muon Collider, which poses significant technical challenges due to its high energy levels and complex muon production and focusing system. Unlike electron colliders, a muon collider requires an intricate system for capturing and cooling the short-lived particles, posing substantial difficulties in its planning and execution phases. With numerous complex components involved in the project, the risk of errors, mismanagement, and budget overruns increases exponentially, highlighting the critical importance of regulating costs and scheduling in the project. Given the magnitude of these challenges, some experts question the feasibility of building such an infrastructure at all. However, recent breakthroughs in magnet and superconducting technology hold promising potential for simplifying the design and making the project more viable. Despite this, significant research is still needed to confirm the practicality of a High Energy Muon Collider, which could serve as a future landmark in the history of particle physics. In the context of this study, we examine how such a project might be approached, focusing first on the current status and then detailed design of such a facility. We examine the dispersion relations for scalar and vector modes within various theoretical frameworks that incorporate relativistic fluids with viscosity, such as hydrodynamics and AdS-CFT correspondence. Our analysis shows that, while certain aspects of the fluid's behavior are protected by conservation laws and thus identical across different approaches, the dispersion relations for the scalar and vector modes exhibit distinct variations. Notably, our findings highlight the presence of an infrared divergence in the dispersion relation for the scalar mode, suggesting that it may not be adequately described within the context of relativistic fluid dynamics. Furthermore, we derive a non-trivial lower bound on the rate of entropy production, which we determine to be a constant multiple of the energy density. Our results are also expanded to include fluids with local thermal equilibrium, which is characterized by space-time variations of temperature and viscosity that follow specific scaling behaviors. Additionally, we use the AdS-CFT correspondence to directly compute the Green's functions for the scalar and vector fields within type-II superfluids, with viscosity represented by a quantum coherence factor that controls the fluid's counter-currents. We use these results to determine the dispersion relations for the scalar and vector modes, which we find to differ significantly from those obtained through hydrodynamics. Notably, our findings suggest the presence of a'meron' mode within the theory, which contributes to the energy of the counter-current, and identify the infrared divergence present in the dispersion relation for the scalar mode as a consequence of the fourth power divergence of the counter-current's log-mass. Finally, we use the AdS-CFT correspondence to determine lower bounds on the growth of entropy production and the scalar mode's momentum, which we find to be proportional to and respectively. Additionally, our analysis suggests the presence of a boundary layer within the gradient expansion of hydrodynamics, which contributes a counter-term to the energy-momentum tensor that prevents divergences and allows the gradient expansion to be performed directly to the required order. This counter-term is found to match exactly the counter-term necessary to remove infrared divergences from the dispersion relations for the scalar and vector modes. This suggests the presence of a 'boundary layer' within the AdS-CFT correspondence, which contributes a similar counter-term with the same coefficient. This counter-term is itself identified as a contribution to the energy-momentum tensor that is not typically considered to be a 'counter-term', but rather a genuine contribution that varies linearly with the boundary layer and is thus distinct from 'counter-terms' that typically fade as one approaches the boundary. Primordial black holes, formed by gravitational collapse of denser regions, are potential detectors for photon spectra across various energy ranges. A recent study demonstrates that the Hawking radiation spectrum of these black holes exhibits an increased peak in lower energy ranges for lighter mass species. This shift is driven by the larger number of lighter states, leading to a greater occupation number and therefore a more intense photon flux. This phenomenon can be observed in multiple contexts, including dark matter searches, astrophysical processes, and particle physics experiments, and may significantly influence data analysis outcomes. For example, primordial black holes could produce an anomalous signal within the axion experiment Axion Direct, potentially complicating dark matter detection efforts. Similarly, lighter mass black holes may generate an increased photon flux in dark matter direct experiments, outweighing the production rate by orders of magnitude. Conversely, this effect can provide an opportunity to refine existing bounds on dark matter masses, and potentially expand the sensitivity of current experiments to darker particles. To further investigate these findings, a publicly accessible note has been included, outlining a simplified method to obtain the Hawking radiation spectrum. This method accelerates and stabilizes the numerical determination of the spectrum, and may be applied in various black hole and dark matter studies. Building on the concept of Boolean circuits, we develop a novel method to evaluate circuits, aiming to accelerate processing speed. In contrast to traditional Boolean circuit evaluation, which follows a top-down approach, our technique, called 'Evaluating Circuits Quickly' (ECQ), executes a sequence of operations simultaneously through pipelining. ECQ utilizes a network of simple computation units to evaluate a circuit's edges and intermediate nodes concurrently. ECQ operates by fixing a circuit's input values and running a series of ECQ steps, diminishing the circuit's size at a constant rate. ECQ's performance can be further enhanced by applying advanced techniques such as circuit rearrangement and computation unit optimization. We present detailed results from tests on a wide range of circuits, showcasing ECQ's efficiency and its significant speedup capabilities. Moreover, ECQ is accompanied by a user-friendly interface, allowing users to easily evaluate and compare the evaluation times of various circuits. Our study also includes a video illustrating the ECQ process in action, available at https://youtu.be/HH6HTD3Gm7M. All source code and project materials are publicly accessible at https://github.com/alexalex112/ECQ. As a key outcome of this research, we launch the CECP (Circuit Evaluation and Performance) project, an ongoing endeavor to investigate methods for efficiently evaluating circuits, backed by an extensive collection of test data. Ultimately, our work addresses an essential question: how much can we speed up circuit evaluation using diverse techniques? Our answer, encompassed within the CECP project, indicates a substantial speedup of at least an order of magnitude for numerous circuit evaluation methods. Moreover, our analysis uncovers a thought-provoking connection between circuit design and its evaluation, suggesting that reformulating the problem into a different circuit structure can lead to substantial performance gains. With CECP, we introduce a novel approach called 'performance flux,' representing how different circuit design methods impact evaluation times. Our research includes a comprehensive catalog of evaluated circuits, accompanied by performance data for further study. Additionally, our work highlights an interesting observation: despite considerable efforts, we have thus far discovered only a minimal set of over 180 speedup techniques, leaving immense potential for further research in the field. In conclusion, our goal is to stimulate discussion on the relationship between circuit design and evaluation, fostering a shared knowledge bank of methods to evaluate circuits efficiently. To achieve this, we plan to expand the CECP project by inviting contributions from the community to share their circuit evaluation methods, promoting collaboration and mutual benefit.

Building upon this notion, this paper presents a novel approach called Refine-SAN, an efficient and efficient object-sensitive hyperspectral segmentation method. Session-based recommendation systems are particularly effective in scenarios where users' preferences are uncertain or unavailable. These systems generate recommendations by serially presenting user choices to a model, which learns to predict the next item based on the current session sequence. Traditional methods employ straightforward data augmentation by presenting user choices as the next item in the sequence. Nonetheless, this approach is impaired by the limited variety of user choices and is difficult to expand upon. In an attempt to address this, we will be presenting Augmenter, a novel self-supervised learning method that employs a two-stage strategy to create more realistic and diverse augmented data. First, Augmenter fine-tunes a pre-trained session-based recommendation model to generate representative item sequences on unseen data. It then utilizes these sequences as training data for an enhanced self-supervised learning model. In a second stage, it utilizes this new model to create additional augmented data. Through rigorous evaluation on three real-world datasets, we achieved notable improvements over existing self-supervised learning methods, with performance enhancements averaging 26.4% and 13.5% respectively. This auxiliary data can then be discarded once training completes, which poses an unnecessary computational burden. In this study, we demonstrate that auxiliary variables are indispensable for optimal performance and highlight their significance in selecting relevant features for each object category. By incorporating an additional loss function that encourages auxiliary variables to be discarded after training, we can achieve a desirable outcome where auxiliary variables are eliminated while maintaining optimal performance. This approach is particularly useful in reducing computation required for inference and can also prevent overfitting by removing unnecessary data. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets validate the efficacy of this method, resulting in improved performance and accurate elimination of auxiliary variables in various object categorization tasks. In particular, auxiliary variables were successfully eliminated for image data using our method, which confirmed their role in selecting selective features and revealed the specific features being extracted and utilized by different categories. Furthermore, our method showed potential in modeling complex human actions by incorporating visual data, highlighting its applicability in multiple applications. By visualizing the learned features, we achieved a comparative understanding of the auxiliary variables involved in modeling different actions versus individual objects, which significantly differed in their characteristics. Additionally, our method achieved state-of-the-art performance in object categorization tasks using RNNs with auxiliary variables, which outperformed previous work on multiple benchmarks while also facilitating the efficient removal of auxiliary variables for both visual tasks and action recognition, which is a valuable capability. Based on these findings, we propose a new name for this approach: Lightweight Shared Representations (LISR). In non-Hermitian systems such as the Hatano-Nelson chain with additional randomness, the response to external currents is impeded due to skin effect. This study investigates how the extended chain behaves under magnetic fields and electric currents. By examining the non-Hermitian Hamiltonian with two types of disorder, we found that the skin effect is influenced by correlations and anti-correlations within the disorder. Notably, the anti-correlated disorder results in the reduction of skin effect and the presence of localized waves at the edge of the system. The extended chain exhibits fragility similar to its Hermitian counterpart, albeit with different characteristics. The findings of skin effect and fragility are further supported by observing exceptional points, delocalization transitions, and entropy distribution within the system. The present investigation highlights the distinct properties of extended non-Hermitian systems and their potential to contribute to the development of topological photonics. The study also suggests that the induction of disorder can lead to the emergence of new states rather than destruction, offering a positive outlook for topological material research. The novel concept of fragility provides a framework for evaluating and comparing non-Hermitian systems, thereby paving the way for experimental validation of topological phenomena in non-Hermitian systems. The extended Hatano-Nelson chain offers an ideal model for experimenting with topological photonics, while the discovered exceptional points and delocalization transitions hold promise for observational evidence. The ability to manipulate skin effect through disorder correlations provides another area for exploring conditional coherence. The presence of localized waves in the system presents an opportunity for exploring entanglement through Bose-Einstein condensation. This paper presents the open-source library LibOPT, a comprehensive tool for benchmarking optimization algorithms. LibOPT encapsulates various optimization techniques and a range of standard benchmarking functions, as well as an automated benchmarking system that facilitates reproducible results across different platforms. To promote collaboration and shared knowledge, LibOPT's source code is freely accessible via GitHub, and the library is available for download at an dedicated website also. Currently, LibOPT implements 55 benchmarking functions and 15 different optimization methods, and future enhancements are planned to expand its functionality. Our software is designed to be user-friendly, and easily adaptable for introducing benchmarking and optimization to undergraduate students. By utilizing LibOPT, the process of performing benchmarking becomes streamlined, and an extensive list of related references is provided. As a key feature, LibOPT automates the following tasks: dimensionality reduction, generating random datasets, running predefined optimization processes, and producing summary reports in LaTeX and PDF formats. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we present a general introduction to optimization and benchmarking, as well as a detailed case study involving one of LibOPT's implemented functions. Firstly, we introduce the CMA Evolution Strategy and illustrate its use on one of the benchmarking tasks, and secondly, we provide an overview of the MetaOpt framework and show a benchmarking analysis comparing it to LibOPT, using the BlackBox GlobalOptBproblem task. In conclusion, our goal is to promote LibOPT as an essential tool for optimization researchers by facilitating collaboration, and by providing a framework for developing, accessing, and using benchmarking functions, and we envision a future where new optimization methods developed in the field could be incorporated into LibOPT. This, in turn, would allow for a comprehensive comparison of all available optimization techniques, and would ultimately contribute to the advancement of optimization research. In the long-term perspective, our goal is to expand LibOPT to cover solving real-world problems efficiently, and creating an automated process for converting optimization software into a usable web-service. This, in turn, could be employed by practitioners for solving their particular optimization challenges. Our sources are freely accessible at https://github.com/optprogs/libopt for the LibOPT source code, and at http://www.optprogs.org/libopt for the library website. We have derived the transitivity degree for specific cubic hypersurfaces as well as quadric hypersurfaces within complex affine 7-dimensional space. Furthermore, we have established the transitivity degree for a particular family of cubic hypersurfaces in the complex 5-dimensional projective space. These findings are based on certain specific assumptions regarding their invariant rings, which we demonstrate to be sufficient. We also resolve a query from [Bakhanov-Sogonov-Quaide 2020] by computing the transitivity degree for a specific family of quartic hypersurfaces. Additionally, we provide a step-by-step description of a geometrically motivated algorithm for computing the transitivity degree of any smooth algebraic variety defined over the real numbers. We then apply this algorithm to determine the transitivity degree for specific families of homogeneous polynomials in the projective space. This paper presents a novel framework for developing collision avoidance strategies for mobile robotic arms, taking into account their spatial structure. By representing the robot as a set of connected spheres, referred to as the poly-spherical model, we expand upon existing collision avoidance methods which primarily focus on fixed-base robots. Our approach generates valid collision avoidance trajectories for the end-effector by optimizing its position and orientation, while constraining related joint angles, to ensure associated key points (KPs) within the poly-spherical model remain outside of obstacles. Our solution incorporates the robot's kinematic chain by utilizing a modified reachable region and incorporating obstacles, represented as Gaussians, to effectively restrict end-effector placement. Our approach is evaluated through both simulation studies and practical experiments, indicating its superiority over existing arms collision avoidance strategies. The developed algorithm is compared with the Efficient Path Plan using Poly-Spherical Model (EPP-PSM), the current state-of-the-art, and significantly outperforms it, achieving a notable speed-up in computation time. Human language is inherently diverse in form and substance due to variations in vocabulary, context, and intent across different interactions. Effective comprehension of meaning necessitates an understanding of both the literal and contextual meanings of text, making natural language processing essential. Traditional NLP methods are constrained by the need for extensive, finely graded labeling to learn from, which is often costly and impractical to achieve. Human operators can efficiently provide coarse labeling for tasks like sentiment analysis, but NLP models often struggle to learn from this coarsely labeled data. Our proposed method, MEDIC, utilizes coarse labels to learn the differences between distinct labels and contextual meanings. MEDIC represents labels as vectors in a semantic space by identifying and leveraging contextual cues within labeled examples. During training, the model updates the label vectors based on the similarity between the context and the target label. In doing so, the model learns to recognize meaningful contexts for each label, facilitating better task performance. Our experiments demonstrate that MEDIC outperforms baseline systems using fine-grained data on two CoNLL-2016 SemEval tasks and yield state-of-the-art results on Quora Question Pair classification. Additionally, our work highlights the importance of labeling variety for NLP task performance. Large distributions of coarse labels can sometimes improve task outcomes, even when the labels are not highly specific. Our analysis suggests that the key factor is the variety of contexts associated with each label, rather than the labels themselves. In the study of polynomial systems, Gröbner basis algorithms have become fundamental tools for solving systems through elimination methods. As applications expand into fields like non-linear control theory and parametric mixed-integer programming, the complexity of polynomial systems increases substantially. In this context, using Gröbner bases for verification purposes becomes impractically costly. To address this challenge, introducing various heuristics aims to make elimination methods more efficient while ensuring a trade-off in reliability. Certain algorithmic architectures, such as PHC, Bertini, and polymake, offer such heuristics, although they lack a unified framework. Our work introduces SAGEBASE, a family of Gröbner basis algorithms capable of handling large polynomial systems through various heuristics. By integrating SAGEBASE into existing elimination methods, we enhance the computation of polynomial system solutions. Furthermore, by leveraging sign-based methods, we achieve an extensive validity range for the solutions obtained through elimination algorithms. This validity extends to the solutions computed by PHC, Bertini, and polymake, significantly including those obtained using heuristic-based approaches. Our work includes a comprehensive comparison of 15 sign-based Gröbner basis algorithms implemented in SAGEBASE and discusses their validity of output. To facilitate this research, we make available the SAGEBASE library and the Gröbner basis algorithms developed, in addition to the computational results obtained. Our aim is to provide an easily accessible reference on the usage of SAGEBASE for the computation of polynomial system solutions. We also intend to promote the application of Gröbner basis algorithms in various fields of research. In particular, we make available the SAGEBASE library, the Gröbner basis algorithms developed, and the computational results obtained, with the hope of fostering the collaboration necessary to expand the capabilities of SAGEBASE in the future. A novel radial basis function (RBF) interpolation method is presented, which parallels the classical linear interpolation formula but utilizes a non-linear RBF approach. Unlike earlier RBF interpolation techniques, this innovation maintains the convexity and monotonicity properties inherent in linear interpolation. By expressing the quadratic interpolation formula as a linear combination of linear interpolation formulas for sub-domains, a corresponding RBF representation is achieved that retains the monotonicity property. Furthermore, assuming an 'influence zone' for each node where the corresponding weight is positive, convexity is also ensured. For the standard Gaussian kernel, however, this 'influence zone' constraint leads to a nodal mesh that forms a Delaunay triangle mesh, thus precluding the use of unstructured meshes. An alternative 'influence zone' approach is proposed for the Gaussian kernel that relaxes this constraint, at the cost of precise monotonicity. These findings facilitate the development of a nodal mesh for quadratic interpolation that is applicable to any dimension greater than or equal to two. Additionally, an implementation is described that exploits the symmetry and uniformity properties of the nodal mesh to generate a canonical mesh, thus simplifying the nodal coordinates in the RBF interpolation formula. This implementation has been successfully tested on a range of test cases. In particular, it outperformed the standard MW4 mesh in terms of reliability and efficiency, while also demonstrating the feasibility of using the nodal mesh for quadratic interpolation in three dimensions. In contrast to linear interpolation, this RBF approach does not require specialized kernels for achieving monotonicity and convexity, thus highlighting its relative robustness and ease of use. In conclusion, the proposed nodal mesh for quadratic interpolation offers a versatile, easily implementable solution that can be used with ease in two, three, or higher dimensions. Moreover, this approach can be used to extend linear and quadratic interpolation to function of higher dimensions by employing appropriate 'influence zones' for weights, thus providing a potential path for generalizing higher-dimensional interpolation using quadratic RBFs. In particular, a five-dimensional nodal mesh for quadratic RBFs was successfully demonstrated, thus illustrating the feasibility of this interpolation method for such high dimensions. Finally, the efficiency and robustness of this quadratic RBF nodal mesh were validated through a range of high-dimensional test cases. In particular, significant errors were found in the standard MW4 mesh for dimensions greater than four, while the proposed quadratic RBF nodal mesh was found to be substantially more reliable and efficient in these higher dimensions. This study examines the focus of climate change research in leading economics and science publications from 1887 to 2015. Our analysis also contrasts the interest of policymakers in climate change with that of the general public. Our findings are based on text samples from the Science Citation Index, the Royal Economic Society's Economic History Series, and data on U.S. Congress members' research. Our results show that climate change was largely ignored by economists but received significant attention from scientists and policymakers from the 1960s onwards. Unlike the general public, whose interest in climate change was limited in the past but has since increased, policymakers' interest has shown a steady and unique progression over time. Additionally, our data suggests that policymakers' awareness of climate change was initially driven by nuclear threats but later became linked to energy concerns. The power of gravitational lensing allows us to observe distant objects more clearly and study their diverse "spectral maps" - the various wavelengths of light emitted from these objects. Using the highly magnified galaxy, RXJ0911-09, which has been lensed by a foreground gravitational well, we obtained extremely precise "spectral maps" - covering a broad spectrum from 1 to 21 microns - of six highly energetic, distant AGNs located within this galaxy. In natural language tasks, the ultimate goal is to achieve high accuracy while ensuring that machine learning models produce understandable outputs. There's been significant progress in this area, but existing models often prioritize accuracy over interpretability. In this research, we present a new approach called Linguistic Interpretability through Regularization (LIR), which helps models develop coherent, easily understandable representations of language. By drawing on insights from how humans learn languages, we've created an innovative method of thought process refinement that boosts a model's ability to grasp language effectively. We've carefully crafted a comprehensive framework that integrates four distinct components to drive linguistic interpretability, and our findings show that this approach leads to significant improvements in both accuracy and coherence. To test the versatility of LIR, we've applied it to both a semantic task and a natural language inference task, and our results consistently outperform state-of-the-art models in both areas. Notably, our findings also suggest that regularized representations tend to center around neutral phrases, and our models are often correct in their classifications in the absence of contextual information. By pushing the boundaries of what is possible in natural language processing, we hope that LIR will inspire the development of more user-friendly, coherent models of language. In the future, we plan to apply LIR to even more challenging tasks and to explore its potential for improving model performance over time. Gravitational wave memories, which are physical phenomena that could be observed through their effects on interferometers' residual bias in gravitational wave data, have sparked interest in understanding the complete gravitational wave radiation field. Previous research has focused on the non-momentum and co-momentum polarizations of gravitational waves, finding them to contribute equally to the memory effect. Contrasting this, the momentum polarization of gravitational waves does not contribute equally, but rather, its sum with the co-momentum polarization exhibits contrasting frequency behavior. When combining all four polarizations, the resulting sum shows diminishing contributions with increasing frequency. Building upon prior methods, we have identified that the momentum polarization of gravitational waves can lead to significant memory effects, and, using mathematical techniques, we have demonstrated that the total gravitational wave memory background, as well as its Fourier transform, can be represented by four distinct integrals, each corresponding to the different polarizations. Additionally, we have established that, unlike the ordinary gravitational wave background, the gravitational wave memory background exhibits a differing frequency spectrum. It displays zero frequency components that are proportional to $t^{-2}$, as opposed to the $t^{-3}$ proportionality observed in the higher frequency components. The distinction between these different frequency components could potentially be observed in future gravitational wave observations. Given that the gravitational wave memory background can be represented by four distinct integrals, each alternative integral being a different gravitational wave contribution, we have identified that one of these integrals, specifically the integral corresponding to the cross-momentum polarization, is not represented by prior research. As such, our work provides a more comprehensive understanding of the gravitational wave memory background. Finally, we confirm that the gravitational wave memory background, when summed correctly, does not contribute as equally as the usual gravitational wave background, but rather, the gravitational wave memory background, specifically the cross-momentum polarization terms, can exhibit considerable contributions in specific contexts. The understanding of these gravitational wave memories may lead to observable indications in the study of gravitational waves. The calculations for these gravitational wave memories can be found in the attached mathematical documents. The documents provide the mathematical explanations for the gravitational wave memories, discussing the different frequency behaviors, the gravitational wave memory background, and the existence of significant cross-momentum polarization terms. As such, the documents are essential for the study of gravitational waves, membranes, and the related gravitational wave membrane background. The associated gravitational wave computations can be found within the documents, specifically in the following documents: gravitational-wavememorycrossmomentum-20191120.pdf, gravitational-wavememorycrossmoment

As wireless communication systems become increasingly ubiquitous, guaranteeing data integrity is a top priority to prevent system failures. Traditional data transmission methods involve encoding data multiple times to ensure receipt, however, this comes at the cost of reduced data efficiency. To address this challenge, we present an innovative approach, known as the Efficient Semantic Protection (ESP) system, which offers high levels of data reliability with minimal data loss. To achieve this, we leverage the capabilities of non-binary code combining with logical code combining to protect data. Furthermore, we incorporate the use of compressed binary escapers to optimize data transmission efficiency. We evaluate the performance of the ESP system using the log-normal channel model and compare its results to conventional protection methods, demonstrating that ESP surpasses traditional approaches in terms of reliability while maintaining competitive transmission efficiency. To showcase its practical applications, we test the ESP system in two real-world scenarios: protecting data subject to arbitrary losses and scenarios with losses of at least k bits. Experimental results confirm the ESP system's superiority in both cases. Additionally, we provide the open-source software implementation of the ESP system, along with simulation tools, on GitHub for public access. https://github.com/InfNetUCF/ESP. Open issues can be found on the repository's description.

This paper presents a drone swarm framework that utilizes an evolutionary algorithm to optimize swarm behavior. By deviating minimally from the centroid, the swarms operate efficiently and adapt easily to changing environments and unforeseen events. The proposed framework evaluates drone states in relation to the centroid, assigning penalties according to their distance and orientation relative to the centroid, in addition to utilizing a fitness metric. Following generation, the worst-performing individuals are replaced with new ones through genetic variation, and the process is repeated until convergence is achieved, and the best individuals are selected as the swarm's current state. The approach demonstrates effective centering and can adapt to various tasks, as exemplified by a, (simulated) target-tracking, and (real-time) altitude adjustment, exemplars. The framework's efficiency is validated through comparative analyses with genetic algorithms and a, (simulated) neural network, operating in a, 20-dimension state space. The results show that the framework can maintain a tight swarm with a minimal number of drones, and it outperforms the comparisons in swarm cohesion, fitness, and task completion metrics. The framework has been successfully tested in both simulated and real-world settings, and it provides a foundation for creating drone swarms capable of various applications. The approach can potentially be applied to other problems, and it offers a versatile tool for optimization tasks. The code is freely accessible at https://github.com/AutonomouSly/EEF_Swarm. In the context of a connected chain graph, G(n), consisting of n vertices, its Seidel matrix is found to have exactly one eigenvalue of -1, and the remaining eigenvalues are located on the unit circle. The problem's objective is to determine the minimum Seidel rank of G(n), denoted as s(G(n)), with the given condition that n is an even number. By applying the quantum computation algorithm, specifically the Abelian-Stabilizer-Generation problem, it has been proven that s(G(n)) is equal to n when n is not a multiple of 4, and s(G(n)) is equal to n - 2 when n is a multiple of 4. The proposed method also allows for the efficient computation of the Seidel matrix's eigenvalues of G(n) by utilizing the matrix product of a specific Pauli group operator and the quantum permutation matrix of G(n). This product represents a quantum algorithm that computes the Seidel matrix of G(n) in a quantum environment. As an extension of this work, it has also been possible to compute the Seidel matrix's eigenvalues of G(n) by applying a classical algorithm based on the Weyl's classical result. Consequently, it has led to the development of an explicit formula for the Seidel rank of G(n). The approach presented in this study may be generalized to compute the Seidel matrix's eigenvalues of other class of chain graphs with flag complexes having specific properties. Furthermore, it may be possible to extend the results obtained here to the quantum environment by utilizing the principles of quantum computation. DB3 employs an entropic model to guide the distillation process by simultaneously optimizing student and teacher models through iterative decision-making, unlike conventional knowledge distillation which relies on pre-defined network properties. We introduce a novel loss function that combines information gain with cross-entropy, facilitating a range of optimization methods beyond gradient descent. By integrating non-uniform temperature scaling into the loss function, our approach resolves existing issues with inconsistent model comparisons and unreliable distillation results. We also present an adaptive mechanism for dynamically adjusting distillation burdens on multiple students, thereby mitigating overfitting associated with DB3 by balancing model growth and distillation effects. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods in improving distillation quality using a ResNet, MNIST dataset, and CIFAR10 dataset. The source code for our approach can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/hpghying/DB3.git. To address these challenges, we propose a novel tracking method that utilizes future information to anticipate and predict occlusions, utilizing the physical principles of inertia. This approach involves incorporating the center of mass of the person, which serves as a constant inertial mass, to track the entire body. Specifically, we leverage the visual flow generated by moving objects, which is captured by a novel flow estimator, to guide the tracking of individual hands. To facilitate efficient tracking, we employ a streamlined hand detection method that reduces the complexity of identifying hands in complex scenarios. This is achieved through the combination of a single convolutional operation with a specific query, which is represented as a set of key points adjusted in real-time. This simple yet effective approach enables fast and light hand tracking in scenarios with hand-object interactions. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art hand-tracking methods in scenarios with hand-object interactions and rivals their performance in other scenarios. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly affected state-of-the-art end-effector pose estimation results, yet these models demand extensive data for proper training. In the context of industrial robotics, a common issue arises from the limitations of training datasets, which often fail to account for minor discrepancies in tool geometry, leading to decreased calibration precision. Our proposed approach addresses this challenge by leveraging a depth camera to refine the output of a one-stage deep learning model, specifically designed for end-effector detection. Unlike more complex pose estimation methods, our approach relies solely on depth information, making it particularly suitable for applications involving hard or soft fuzzy grippers. Our experimental findings demonstrate that the integration of depth information significantly enhances the precision of end-effector position calculations, with notable improvements in orientation calculations as well. Moreover, calibrations involving slight deviations in tool geometry become more robust, and calculating the size of the end-effector is no longer required. Our approach can be implemented using any modern depth camera on widely available off-the-shelf hardware. In experiments to identify the underlying causes of interference in wireless networks, data collection is often laborious and time-consuming. As a result, researchers usually collect data from individual network nodes, referred to as 'focal units'. To increase efficiency, researchers might collect data from a smaller, selected group of nodes that exhibit unusual usage patterns or interference levels. Our study investigates the effectiveness of this approach and aims to determine the optimal criteria for choosing these group members, enhancing interference detection while minimizing additional data collection. We conducted an experiment using 2, 4, 6, and 8 focal units and found that using 4-6 units consistently provide the best outcome. Additionally, we found that focusing on nodes with high usage or interference does not always yield the best results, and that considering the variance in usage or interference alone is insufficient; rather, we need to select nodes that exhibit extreme patterns in both dimensions to optimize interference detection. Notably, we found that this approach is effective not just for our experiment but also when simulating scenarios with varying densities of interfering nodes. Our work highlights the importance of selecting relevant data collection units for capturing network interference and informs the design of more efficient and adaptive data collection methods for wireless networks. This study investigates how self-interacting dark matter influences a star's cooling process. Using a simplified model, we simulated a star's cooling under various conditions of dark matter interaction and found noticeable effects that require further attention to be considered in cosmological analyses of dark matter. Additionally, we identified potential observational methods to verify our findings. Lastly, we compared our model's assumptions with currently accepted cosmological models to estimate the possible impact of dark matter interaction on star cooling. Conversely, we also looked at how self-interacting dark matter could affect star formation rates in galaxy clusters, considering it as an additional factor. This study's findings are organized into two parts, with the first focusing on individual stars and the second on star clusters. The latter is summarized separately. On the other hand, diffused matter interaction has a more pronounced impact on cooling but requires further observational verification. Although dark matter interaction has a noticeable impact on individual stars, its effect on clusters is largely dominated by feedback from central galaxies. Nonetheless, we found that dark matter interaction could impact cooling in smaller subclusters, potentially making it visible in future X-ray observations. The ShapePipe pipeline is a cutting-edge approach to measuring galaxies' shapes accurately, utilizing multiple techniques to minimize measurement errors and produce the most reliable results. This comprehensive tool is used in the third generation of the Kilo Degree Survey (KIDS) weak-lensing data analysis and has played a crucial role in analyzing data from numerous other surveys, including CFHT's VIKING and CFHTKIDS. A key innovation of ShapePipe is its "booster" tools, specialized methods that enhance the accuracy of galaxies' shapes by applying diverse measurement techniques and combining them using careful analysis. In our latest update to ShapePipe, we've further refined this "pipeline" method, incorporating new and improved techniques for measuring galaxies' shapes and performing rigorous internal consistency checks. The revised pipeline has shown exceptional performance in analyzing galaxies' shapes from the KIDS dataset, outshining all previous versions and producing more accurate and reliable results. Our detailed analysis examines the benefits and limitations of each stage of the pipeline, and we have carefully assessed and validated the results using a comprehensive set of simulated data. The revised ShapePipe tool and its supporting data are now publicly available for researchers to use and build upon. Additionally, all analysis code used in our study has been posted on GitHub, and a copy of the repository has been saved in the repository's snapshot from 21 November 2020. Furthermore, the updated code includes several important changes that were introduced after that date but were not documented previously. This research investigates a Tsallis holographic dark energy model with an interacting coupling parameter in a FRW universe.  By introducing a variable $b(A)$ as a replacement for the constant dark energy and holographic dark energy interaction parameters, we can analyze how it changes over time.  By equating the Hubble parameter to the holographic dark energy scale, we derive a power law equation for the Hubble parameter, which allows us to determine how the interacting parameter $b(A)$ varies with the scale factor $A$.  Our results indicate that, at late stages, $b(A)$ approaches a terminal value, which is related to the scale factor by the equation $b(A)\simeq 2/(1-A^{2/3})$.  Our findings also suggest that the Tsallis holographic dark energy model is capable of providing a suitable cosmological description, as it is in agreement with the observed data for the parameters age of the universe and Hubble constant.  Our analysis further verifies that our model is compatible with the criteria of holographic dark energy, as well as with the requirements of the dark energy and Hubble parameter data constraints.  Our study also investigates the interaction tendency between dark energy and Hubble dark energy, which reveals that our model is capable of explaining an interacting tendency at early stages, while exhibiting no interaction at late stages, thereby resulting in a transition of the interacting tendency at the critical scale $A_{crit}\simeq 0.615$.  Consequently, our model is capable of providing a precise description of the Hubble expansion, as it is in agreement with the data for 366 data points, has a reduced chi-square value of $Chi^{2}=0.00824$, and has a reduced chi-square per degree of freedom of $chi^{2}/dof=0.02244$.  Our study demonstrates that our model is a reliable method for understanding the characteristics of the Hubble expansion, as well as the interacting tendency between dark energy and Hubble dark energy, thereby indicating that our model is a useful tool for studying the characteristics of the universe.

Our work demonstrates that, contrary to a long-standing misconception, these fluctuations can actually lead to more stable cooling rates in such ensembles. This, in turn, has significant implications for applications where high-precision conditions and minimal damping are required, such as in quantum simulation and timekeeping experiments. Our research, therefore, presents a new and more accurate model for laser cooling that takes into account the effects of heavy tails in cooling processes. Additionally, our work has a broader impact, as the model can also be applied to other areas where such fluctuations are present, such as in biology and finance. Our study, "Heavy tails in laser cooling: Understanding the role of fluctuations," has been published in Physical Review X, and a detailed explanation, along with associated code, is available at https://doi.org/10.1070/AB0046WTVC01. Our previous work on this subject can be found at arXiv:2102.02976, and is related to a subsequent study, arXiv:2106.11655. This research investigates how different training heuristics in deep learning, such as regularization of model parameters, influence the complexity of models being learned. Initial experiments indicate that regularizations including weight decay, gradient clipping, and batch normalization all reduce model complexity. To quantify model complexity, we used the maximum eigenvalue of the Hessian matrix of the loss function at the optimal model parameters. Findings suggest that gradient clipping has an immediate effect on the Hessian, while batch normalization's impact on model complexity is delayed until after training. To validate these results, we created a new benchmark consisting of 121 datasets from the OpenAI Espresso framework in combination with 11 small-sized CNN architectures, and tested them under various training conditions. Our analysis further explores the relationship between optimization techniques, learning rates, and the uniqueness of Hessian eigenvalues. Ultimately, we provide insights on the effects of hyperparameters on the learnability of models and the uniqueness of Hessian eigenvalues. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexrame/hess-ml. Our paper is hosted on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.02167. The Espresso benchmark can be found at https://espresso.openai.com/. The study consists of experiments on 121 datasets from the OpenAI Espresso framework in combination with 11 small-sized CNN architectures, and our analysis further explores the effects of various optimization techniques, learning rates, and the uniqueness of Hessian eigenvalues. Additionally, our model complexity metric was successfully applied to large-scale training jobs on the V100 GPU, and our study demonstrates the influence of batch size on model complexity. Our study is the first to examine the unique characteristics of Hessian eigenvalues in deep learning models, and our results indicate a significant disparity in the number of non-zero Hessian eigenvalues for different datasets, training configurations, and models. Our study is the first to explore the effect of model complexity on the data distribution in deep learning, and our results indicate a positive correlation between the number of Hessian eigenvalues and the data size for our benchmark.
