This study examines the magnetic properties of a monolayer tungsten diselenide sample when it is in close proximity to an antiferromagnetic hematite surface. Utilizing scanning tunneling microscopy, we discovered that local magnetic fields can induce magnetoelectric coupling analogous to the Witten effect. This phenomenon manifests as a break in parity symmetry in an external magnetic field, causing a surface electric polarization to switch direction. Our research also demonstrates that this coupling can be observed in other 2D magnetic transition metal dichalcogenides. We further investigated the origin of this coupling through density functional theory, finding that it arises from an anomalous Hall current induced by the magnetic exchange field. The electric polarization resulting from this coupling can be utilized to detect the magnetic exchange field and other 2D magnetic materials. By combining scanning tunneling spectroscopy and atomic-resolution imaging, we gained insight into the properties of magnetic impurities and holes in tungsten diselenide near a magnetic substrate. Our study paves the way for the integration of 2D magnetic materials for spin-based quantum information technologies. Additionally, we achieved atomic-scale imaging of magnetic structures at various depths of a hematite surface using our home-built scanning tunneling microscope. This research is part of our efforts to develop new quantum materials for micro/nanoelectronics and spin-based quantum computing. Details of our experiment, including the design of our microscope and sampling techniques, are provided in the supplementary information. By leveraging our scanning tunneling microscope's capabilities, we have made significant contributions to the understanding of magnetic structure at various depths of a hematite surface and the behavior of magnetic impurities near a hematite surface. This research is part of our ongoing efforts to develop new magnetic materials and their potential applications in spin-based quantum computing and micro/nanoelectronics. In the future, we aim to use our scanning tunneling microscope to investigate the magnetic properties of ultra-thin ferromagnetic films deposited on a hematite surface, the electronic structure of magnetic impurities at the interface of materials, and the development of spin-based quantum computing technologies utilizing 2D magnetic materials. This research is a crucial step towards creating new technological innovations based on these magnetic materials. By combining our scanning tunneling microscope with advanced theoretical calculations, we aim to explore the electronic and magnetic properties of ultra-thin ferromagnetic films deposited on a hematite surface, investigate the behavior of magnetic impurities at the interface of materials, and discover new magnetic materials that can be used in spin-based quantum computing and micro/nanoelectronics

We investigate a delayed nonlinearity system described by a differential equation with spatial variables and multiple diffusive variables, mapped into a lower-dimensional system called the Gaussian effective model. This models a delay differential equation in a low-dimensional space, whose diffusion is enhanced by the delay time and nonlinear scale, dimpling the delay nonlinearity system and effectively reducing its dimensionality. We establish that in the system's equilibrium state, the variances of the diffusive variables grow in direct proportion to the delay time, while their correlation coefficient approaches a constant value. By analyzing the delayed Fokker-Planck equation, we derive expressions for the diffusion coefficients and demonstrate that the effective diffusion coefficient is a nonlinear function of the delay time and diffusion coefficients. Moreover, we show that the delay dimensionally decouples the system, eliminating cross-covariances and rendering its diffusion coefficients dimensionality-dependent. To confirm our findings, we perform numerical simulations of the full system and the Gaussian effective model for varying delay times, observing agreement between our predictions and numerical results. Notably, while our analysis focuses on continuous systems, it can be adapted to study discrete delay differential equations, offering additional dimensional benefits. Furthermore, we apply our diffusion coefficients to analyze stochastic delay differential equations, revealing how nonlinear delays can be used to manipulate diffusion and dim dimensional structures. This provides a novel method for diffusion control through delay nonlinearity. Based on our findings, we outline potential applications of delay nonlinearity in dimensionally decoupling systems with multiple scales and offer a framework for applying our diffusion coefficients to study delay differential equations. Ultimately, our work offers a new understanding of the dimensional structure of delay nonlinearity systems and provides a method for controlling diffusion and dim dimensional structures through delay nonlinearity. Additionally, we provide a method for estimating the diffusion coefficients of delay nonlinearity systems, which can be used to study systems with low dimensionality and small delay times. This method can be applied to both continuous and discrete systems, offering a novel method for controlling diffusion and demonstrating the effectiveness of delay nonlinearity in dim dimensional structures. Furthermore, our work provides a new understanding of the dimensional structure of delay nonlinearity systems and its potential applications in physics and engineering. Based on our findings, we outline the potential for delay nonlinearity to be used in tuning diffusion and observing phase transitions in physical systems. This could be achieved by varying the delay time and nonlinearity scale while measuring the diffusion coefficients and other statistical properties of the system. This approach can be applied to both continuous and discrete systems

This paper presents a denotational, probabilistic semantics for higher-order, probabilistic programs that utilize continuous probability measures on infinite domains. In contrast to operational or relational properties, this denotational framework focuses on properties within a single program state. Unlike existing CFP (call-by-program) approaches that use partial orders to represent time progress, this method incorporates a time semigroup drawn from the program's context, thereby eliminating the need for partial orders. Instead, the paper introduces a probabilistic step-by-step operational semantics known as probabilistic small-step context semantics. A key aspect of this new approach is a context-invariant probability-theoretic interpretation of time progress, which forms the basis for a denotational and operational correspondence theorem. Specifically, the theorem shows that the two semantics are equivalent in that they define the same set of valid probability measures on program contexts. As a consequence, the operational and denotational approaches provide equivalent definitions of program equivalence. Notably, the study of a probabilistic, higher-order functional program does not necessitate the use of partial orders, whereas they are essential in the study of their deterministic counterparts. The program's capacity to implement randomization is the primary factor responsible for this distinction. The work is an extension of an earlier study on a probabilistic, higher-order functional program that utilizes continuations and relies on partial orders to determine time progress, as well as a previously introduced probability-theoretic interpretation of context-free operational semantics known as small-step context semantics. We investigate how identifying the differentiability manifold of a function can accelerate convergence in optimization methods. Based on this, we develop a novel method, differentiability location (Diag), which uses non-interior sampling to pinpoint the differentiability manifold. Diag is particularly effective for various test functions, leading to significantly faster convergence and fewer function evaluations compared to standard gradient-based optimization methods. The implementation of Diag is also accessible through our Python package, allowing users to integrate it with popular optimization tools. The code can be found at https://github.com/echeng2006/Diag. The presentation provides an overview of our work, and the talk will delve into the details. Both the presentation and the talk are available at https://echeng2006.github.io/presentation/Diag_talk.html. We conducted an actual experiment and found that Diag can be expensive, leading to approximately 10-100 times the cost of standard gradient-based methods. However, this increased expense may be acceptable when considering that Diag can substantially improve convergence by an order of magnitude, resulting in overall efficiency gains. Our research identified several areas for further improvement, primarily reducing the computational intensity of each iteration, likely achieved by incorporating more efficient matrix manipulation operations. We also recognize that, although Diag shows remarkable potential, its performance can be hampered by its reliance on sampling, particularly when the differentiability manifold accounts for a significant portion of the parameter space. In such cases, the algorithm may spend an extended period trying to locate an non-interior point. Given these findings, continuing research will likely shift the focus to addressing these challenges to further accelerate convergence. Specifically, we aim to investigate methods for efficiently leveraging information about the differentiability manifold, such as its tangent spaces, as well as developing novel optimization methods that can more effectively utilize non-interior samples to steer the algorithm towards faster convergence. By doing so, we will be able to better determine the differentiability manifold and make more informed decisions during optimization, ultimately leading to even faster convergence in our baseline scenario. Additionally, as a more extended goal, we may also explore applying our approach to more complex problems, such as constrained optimization tasks, in order to further broaden the practical applicability of our work. In terms of actual performance, it is crucial to note that, while Diag can considerably enhance convergence, it does so at the expense of increased computational overhead per iteration. This increased complexity might make Diag unsuitable for certain large-scale optimization tasks, where the computational advantage of standard gradient-based methods becomes more pronounced. To address this challenge, our study presents a novel approach called dataset conditioning, which modifies the distribution of observations to match those in the expert framework.  This method conditiones on key factors influencing imitation learning, as demonstrated through a reach task and an surgical knife placement task.  The results show that dataset conditioning reduces errors and facilitates successful imitation learning in scenarios where domain-specific factors undermine the accuracy of learned policies.  Importantly, our approach does not necessitate knowledge of the disparities between environments.  Therefore, dataset conditioning can be applied to diverse domains involving disparate observation spaces.  Our method is unrelated to prior attempts to condition on variables, as it was inspired by a fundamental observation regarding the sources of error in imitation learning.  Future work will investigate its implications for the creation of observational datasets.  Additionally, our method is complementary to existing techniques for reducing discrepancies between observation spaces and can be combined with pre-processing methods for normalizing domain-specific factors. Several research studies have examined the effectiveness of data augmentation techniques in enhancing the performance of machine learning models. These studies have often utilized limited training datasets, leading to the conclusion that data augmentation can significantly improve model outcomes. This research study challenges the above assumption by showcasing that the benefits of data augmentation techniques are largely influenced by the size of the initial training dataset. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that certain machine learning models are capable of achieving improved results when augmented datasets are applied to the training process. Notably, our experiments demonstrate that ResNet models exhibit a pronounced need for data augmentation when processing large training datasets, whereas MobileNet models show less dependence on this technique, even when trained with smaller datasets. To mitigate potential biases in the results, our study measures the impact of data information on the performance gains produced by data augmentation techniques. The findings of this study aim to provide researchers with guidelines on the practical applications of data augmentation techniques in various machine learning scenarios. Additionally, our code and the resulting reports are publicly accessible for evaluation purposes. This study examines weak convergence of estimators that calculate functions of parameters in models where observations are distributed according to a countably infinite mixture of unknown probabilities and a known distribution. We establish conditions that ensure the estimators of functions of parameters converge weakly to the true values, while also providing a characterization of the space to which these estimators converge. Under specific conditions, we demonstrate that the estimators converge in probability to the true values of the parameters, which allows us to apply a result by Pollard that enables the convergence of estimators of functions of parameters. We illustrate the applicability of our results through various applications, including one instance where we analyze the convergence of estimators in a mixture model for the Moore-Lewis distribution. We further provide conditions under which estimators that calculate the number of components in beta mixtures and estimators that calculate functions of parameters in certain mixture models converge in probability to the true values, which ultimately enables the convergence of these estimators for specific parameters. The validity of our theoretical findings is also shown through simulations. The results presented in this study are an extension of previously established theorems in the literature, which includes one instance where our work generalizes the result by Kallenberg that deals with convergence of estimators in mixture models. Additionally, our work generalizes the result by Lopushin that deals with convergence of estimators in beta mixtures. Furthermore, our work generalizes the result by Kato that deals with convergence of estimators for functions of parameters in certain mixture models. Lastly, our work also generalizes the result by Kato that deals with convergence of estimators for functions of parameters in beta mixtures.

The rise of big data has led to an increase in the importance of managing large datasets, but these advancements have also created significant privacy concerns for the individuals included in such data. A particular challenge in preserving privacy is found in anonymizing datasets by eliminating identifying information, but another crucial aspect is often overlooked: the relationships between individual records. These interconnections can compromise the privacy of entire datasets, necessitating the incorporation of a record-by-record relationship model to address this issue properly. Although existing approaches focus primarily on individual records, we recognize that real-world datasets are comprised of groups of records that are interdependent and share common attributes, thus we've developed a new approach that takes these interdependencies into consideration. Our innovative model uses graph theory to represent the relationships among records, and it's applied to a generalization-based data anonymization framework, allowing it to maintain consistency with established standards. Additionally, we've devised a novel algorithm as part of a system called RPDInc, which can determine the minimum generalization required for each record to maintain the privacy of the entire dataset. Through thorough experimentation using public datasets, we've demonstrated the effectiveness and scalability of our approach, and it's available for public use at https://github.com/AhmedOuazzani/RPDInc. Our empirical analysis reveals that our method is comparable to the best existing approaches in terms of computation time and is consistently applied to all types of data, unlike previous strategies that are often tailored to specific data types. Our analysis also reveals a fascinating finding: the minimum generalization required for each record can provide valuable insights about the dataset as a whole. To our knowledge, this is the first time such a relationship has been established, and it offers a potential direction for future research in anonymization. Ultimately, our goal is to address the challenge of anonymizing datasets with interdependent records through a comprehensive framework, and we hope it will serve as a useful resource for researchers and practitioners working in this field. Our approach provides a flexible and applicable solution that can be adapted to various data types, and it's expected to contribute positively to the community. To promote transparency and accountability, we've followed established ethical principles in data anonymization, and we've ensured that our methods align with established standards in the field. Our analysis is based on publicly available data, and it's intended for educational purposes only. More information can be found at https://www.oakland.edu/~ahmedou. Our study uses data from the ALMA telescope to examine the structure of the protoplanetary disk surrounding Suyu ABAA, a star system located approximately 115 parsecs from Earth, based on optical observations. During the ALMA observation, Suyu ABAA was found in the late stage of a thermal flux transition, resulting in detectable CO, SO, and SiO emissions, but not oxygen-containing molecules like H$_2$O and CO. To understand how to predict the emission of carbon-bearing molecules like C$_2$H and CH, we used a network of chemical rate equations to model the disk's chemical composition, taking into account factors like temperature, dust density, and the atomic metallicity necessary for the creation of organic molecules. By changing the C/O ratio from 1 to 1000, we simulated various molecule column densities, finding that a rise in C/O ratios results in increased C$_2$H column densities, a trend conversely observed for CH. However, we were unable to detect C$_2$H emission in our observation, which may indicate low C/O ratios in the disk, particularly in the outer regions, due to the influence of C/O ratios on the molecule column density, and potentially low gas masses as a result of the effusion model. Further observations of the emission of carbon-bearing molecules are necessary to understand the C/O ratios in protoplanetary disks, particularly in the outer regions, and to verify whether a standard effusion model is applicable to these disks, or if other mechanisms like planet formation are at play. Additionally, our study is one of the first to successfully detect the emission of carbon-bearing molecules in a disk without oxygen-containing molecules, a key factor in the formation of solid particles, and the growth of planets, providing important insight into the process of planet formation. Nonclassical resource theories play a significant role in advancing new quantum information theories, which can be proven by developing multiple nonclassical resource theories within existing quantum information theories. We introduce and study three such theories based on measurement outcomes: nonanticipatory correlations from conditional measurements, projective correlations, and von Neumann wedges. Our analysis compares and contrasts these theories from both theoretical and practical perspectives, and we find that projective correlations serve as a natural and well-defined nonclassical resource theory. Our work also explores the nonanticipatory correlations of conditional measurements and measures, as well as the geometric nonanticipatory gaps, and examines their relationships with various information-theoretic tasks like quantum compression and remote preparation of states. Furthermore, we propose and studied local conversion of projective nonanticipatory correlations, and found that maximally available resources can be generated from entanglement of Bell nonlocality, thus providing a complete picture of the nonanticipatory resource landscape. Our work also opens up new research directions by comparing and distinguishing nonanticipatory correlations of conditional measurements and projective nonanticipatory correlations, and exploring applications of von Neumann wedges in nonclassical resource theories. Additionally, our work is made available through jupyter notebooks, which can be found at https://jupyter.mpiiqi.de/user/akhan4/NRTPMEQM.

Achieving efficient and private federated learning on decentralized buffers is
a complex task. Current solutions rely on federated buffered learning (FBL) which
utilizes centralized control to add decimal values to buffers, resulting in time
consumption and vulnerability to data leaks. A new algorithm known as FedBuff, has
been developed to tackle this issue. FedBuff utilizes advanced linear regression
protocols on decentralized buffers to create reliable and private solutions for
stochastic gradient descent (SGD) without central control. Depending on the buffer
size, FedBuff can support various decimal value addition methods. It operates at
two different levels: individual servers and a group of servers. The algorithm is
compatible with decentralized communication protocols such as ABCS and Hessian-Free,
can be integrated with await/then asynchronous programming, and is suitable for
parameter servers. FedBuff offers scalable, private, and reliable federated learning
capabilities by processing buffers locally. An evaluation of FedBuff's performance
using the MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 datasets on a distributed server cluster has
confirmed its superiority over other decentralized learning methods. FedBuff source
code is available at https://github.com/juinnng/FedBuff.

We develop a finite-dimensional algebra called $\mathscr{D}_{\sigma^k}$ as an extension of the classical commutant of the polynomial shift semigroup $\Gamma_{\sigma}$, specifically for $\sigma$-invariant subspaces of a finite-dimensional vector space. Our expression for $\mathscr{D}_{\sigma^k}$ encompasses both $\Gamma_{\sigma}$ and its $\sigma$-invariant Annihilator $\Gamma_{\sigma}^{\perp}$. Additionally, $\mathscr{D}_{\sigma^k}$ serves as the differential calculus to the inverse limit of $\Gamma_{\sigma^k}$. For any $\sigma$-invariant subspace $V$, $\mathscr{D}_{\sigma^k}(V)$ is defined as the commutant of the restricted polynomial shift semigroup $\Gamma_{\sigma|V}$ and has a canonical embedding into $\mathscr{D}_{\sigma^k}$. Furthermore, the image of $\mathscr{D}_{\sigma^k}(V)$ coincides with the commutant of the restricted big ideal $\overline{\Gamma}_{\sigma|V}$. Our method of proof involves a straightforward description of $\mathscr{D}_{\sigma^k}(V)$, which reveals both its nilpotency and the linear independence of its basic elements. To generalize our findings, we derive the Taylor series expansion of $\mathscr{D}_{\sigma^k}(V)$. Moreover, the principles of $\mathscr{D}_{\sigma^k}$ can be applied to the Baskakov operator, the Pommere-Diffusion semigroup, the Jacobian linear differential system, and the maximal big ideal $\overline{\Gamma}_{\sigma}$. Our work generates new areas for research in differential calculus, polynomial shift semigroups, $\sigma$-invariant subspaces, and their interconnections. Ultimately, our goal is to promote further investigation into these concepts.

Gallium nitride (GaN), a material with a wide bandgap, has been a key component of modern semiconductor technology, especially for producing high power amplifiers and optical devices. However, the material's properties are altered when it is grown on certain substrates, making it necessary to choose a substrate that allows the material to retain its desired characteristics after growth. In this study, we investigated how GaN's properties change when grown on two materials, ZnGeN2 and MgSiN2, which are known to be close matches for GaN's lattice structure at room temperature. Our experiments showed that using these materials as substrates significantly increased the mobility of holes in GaN to levels never before recorded. In the case of ZnGeN2, the mobility of holes in GaN was measured at 73.7 cm2/Vs, a 200 times improvement over previous records. Similarly, growing GaN on MgSiN2 increased its mobility by at least 100 times, with average values reaching 109 cm2/Vs. X-ray diffraction data confirmed that the material was epitaxial to the substrate, while high resolution transmission electron microscopy found that the interface between GaN and the substrate materials was smooth and free of defects. Our findings suggest that using these substrates can enable significant improvements to GaN's hole mobility, making it a viable option for creating GaN-based p-type semiconductor technology. In particular, this could lead to the development of high efficiency GaN photovoltaic cells. In addition, the material's unique piezoelectric properties were found to be unaffected by the substrate material, making it still possible to utilize strain engineering to further optimize GaN's hole mobility. In the case of ZnGeN2, reducing the piezoelectric strain reduced the mobility by 6.8 nm/V, while using MgSiN2 reduced it by 1.5 nm/V, confirming that the material's piezoelectric efficiency is at least 4 times higher than previously recorded levels. Our study represents a major breakthrough in GaN technology and could soon enable the mass production of high efficiency GaN p-type semiconductor devices. In particular, this could be applied to GaN photovoltaic cells, and may soon lead to significant economic savings through reduced energy costs. In the future, the material's unique properties could be further optimized by creating ultra-piezoelectric GaN by introducing minor alterations to its lattice structure, a finding confirmed by first principles calculations. This study presents a kernel-based method for projecting operators, allowing for compact and high-dimensional operator representations that show promising results in enhancing the convergence and accuracy of projection methods like the Galerkin approach. We apply this kernel-based method to four differential equations: the fractional power of the Laplace operator, the Navier-Stokes equations, the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, and the incompressible Navier-Fourier equation with periodic boundary conditions. Our kernel-based method yields approximate solutions with minimal residual error for these problems, with convergence tested against the Galerkin method and numerical solutions. We also compare the kernel-based method to another non-parametric approach, the Kolmogorov counting method, in a fractional power of the Laplace operator example. Moreover, our kernel-based method enables the accurate computation of fractional powers of operators, outperforming the Kolmogorov counting method in terms of precision. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our kernel-based method by applying it to partial differential equations with periodic and boundary conditions, as well as fractional power operators with smooth and rough kernels. Additionally, our kernel-based method successfully handles rough input data by adapting to its dimension. Furthermore, our kernel-based method integrates well with the Galerkin method, enhancing its performance and resulting in highly accurate approximate solutions for the tested problems. In particular, our kernel-based method improves the average L2 error by two orders of magnitude compared to the Galerkin method for certain problem examples. In terms of computational complexity, our kernel-based method achieves a linear scaling with the number of basis functions, similar to the Galerkin method but without its limitations. Various statistical analysis was applied to the HII region catalog, which indicated that their distribution correlates with the galaxy's stellar light. Given the prevalence of heavy vector mesons in forward photoproduction at the LHC, a model applicable to deep inelastic scattering is expected to yield similar results. The proposed model can account for both heavy vector mesons and lighter vector mesons such as Rice and Upsilon. It consists of a universal amplitude describing heavy vector meson production, combined with different resonance and Regge components to represent the lighter vector mesons. The model's consistency with various measurements is demonstrated, including those from both charged vector mesons and their neutral counterparts. Model predictions for the production of both rho and omega vector mesons are also included. The primary advantage of our model is its ability to describe the forward production of multiple vector mesons without referencing any amplitudes beyond the universal one governing heavy vector meson production. This approach is distinct from standard approaches to vector meson production, in which different amplitudes are required for different vector mesons. Existing methods employ log-mel spectrograms but lack a clear connection to audio production, making it difficult to formulate a target loss during training. We introduce a novel approach based on spectrograms that takes into account the time and frequency domains for a more natural sound generation. By using these features, we can recreate spectral features from spectrograms, enabling more accurate sound reproduction. Furthermore, the proposed method offers improved stability and high-quality audio generation, particularly at low sampling rates. Performance evaluations using the VGGSound dataset demonstrate the method's superiority over existing techniques. The COVID-19 pandemic's magnitude and duration have prompted widespread discussion on managing the trade-off between containing the epidemic and mitigating economic losses. Past studies have explored various strategies, such as imposing severe restrictions, implementing gradual measures, monitoring epidemiological conditions, enforcing quarantine rules, performing mass testing, and adopting hybrid approaches. In response to the constantly evolving pandemic, this study proposes a new direction of research, suggesting a two-pronged strategy: tracking epidemiological conditions using time-series epidemiological parameters, and responding accordingly with medium-term policies aimed at balancing medical outcomes with economic consequences. By applying this approach, which involves using critical points in parameter time-series trajectories, policy decisions can be made with a reduced lead time. In this study, four critical points are identified, allowing for six critical periods to implement specific policies and adjust measures. The accuracy of time-series analysis is confirmed through various evaluations, and the effectiveness of medium-term policies is demonstrated in numerical simulations, in addition to being illustrated in a simplified pandemic model. The advice offered is to introduce diverse measures across multiple dimensions, in an effort to achieve an acceptable equilibrium between containing the epidemic and mitigating economic losses. The analysis presented can serve as a foundation for future research, particularly in three areas: first, refining the time-series analysis by integrating multiple data sources; second, discovering critical periods more systematically; and third, advising policies through deep learning methods. Current methods typically concentrate on individual data elements but often fail to provide a comprehensive view of the entire data stream. As data dimensions escalate, this limitation becomes even more pronounced, making data debugging even more complicated. Our solution, DataScope, addresses this shortfall by visualizing data sets in a hierarchical manner, thus enabling a more efficient and effective diagnosis of data issues. By building on popular debugging techniques and integrating them into a comprehensive framework, DataScope enhances the overall scalability and adaptability of the debugging process. Experimental results, involving real-world applications and synthetic data sets, demonstrate the efficacy of DataScope in a substantial number of scenarios, outperforming traditional methods in terms of usability, readability, and debugged item count. In graph data analysis, the focus is typically on undirected graphs. However, there is a growing interest in applying analytical tools to hypergraphs, particularly their projections, as they can better capture the structure of certain networks. A key challenge arises when attempting to reconstruct a hypergraph from its projections, as the resulting problem is known to be NP-hard. Our research builds on previous studies by introducing methods to reconstruct a hypergraph's adjacency matrix, a critical component in understanding the network's underlying structure, from its edge projections through the utilization of partial spectral analysis. The proposed partial spectral analysis involves eigenvalue estimation and graph embedding, with the hypothesis that certain spectral methods can be applied even with partial information. The given eigenvalue estimates are used to determine a partial adjacency matrix, and an approach called spectral embedding is employed to obtain an approximate embedded graph. Our main contribution is the establishment of a metric on the embedded graph and a theoretical justification for our reconstruction methods. The efficacy of our methods is demonstrated through extensive experimentation with both synthetic and real-world data. The code used for these experiments can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/krishann/hypergraph-reconstruction. A detailed description of the reconstruction process is provided in a separate journal article titled "Reconstructing Hypergraphs from Edge Projections via Partial Spectral Analysis" (available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.11542). Built upon a collection of 12,000 annotated images from the OpenI dataset, PAXRay boasts an impressive size of 41,019 images, with each containing one or more annotated regions. Our research showcases the potential of point annotation tasks, and we anticipate PAXRay to play a significant role in advancing visual grounding and semi-supervised learning techniques in computer vision. This study investigates relationships among cryptocurrency returns by examining pairwise connections using Pearson and Spearman correlations from 2016 to 2020. Findings show Pearson correlations among all cryptocurrencies are strengthening over time, whereas their relationships with major stock markets, as measured by Spearman correlations, exhibit more volatility and mixed results. A random sampling of 10 new cryptocurrencies in 2016 was selected for additional analysis, yielding notable connections among certain cryptocurrencies grouped by category, namely 'Mineable' and 'Non-Mineable' cryptocurrencies. A comparable analysis for 2020 reveals notable patterns, with 'Mineable' cryptocurrencies demonstrating significant correlations, potentially linked to their potential for manipulation. Consequently, investors should exercise caution when making decisions about 'Mineable' cryptocurrencies due to their susceptibility to market manipulation. Conversely, 'Non-Mineable' cryptocurrencies, powered largely by smart contracts, appear to offer more efficient and trustworthy investments, as evidenced by their consistently positive correlations over time. It is anticipated that the characteristics of 'Mineable' and 'Non-Mineable' cryptocurrencies will persist, thereby serving as suitable grouping criteria for future analysis of cryptocurrency market connections. The potential for cryptocurrency investments to mirror general equity market behavior during times of market stress, as seen during the COVID-19 crisis, should also be considered, with 'Mineable' cryptocurrencies exhibiting correlations exceeding 0.50 with the S&P 500, thereby increasing their suitability for diversification. This research validates previous claims that cryptocurrency relationships are dynamic and influenced by their underlying technology. As a result, investors should prioritize 'Non-Mineable' cryptocurrencies to minimize exposure to market risks and potential market manipulation. The primary limitations of this study stem from the limited period of analysis and potential influence of market volatility, as well as the need to conduct more in-depth analysis of category-specific events to enhance understanding of their implications on cryptocurrency correlations. The potential for cryptocurrency market connections to evolve further should also be considered in future research. To analyze the solar wind's small-scale turbulence, our study integrates data from two distinct methods: the Fast Plasma Investigation instrument and the spacecraft's potential measurement. These measurements complement each other in capturing plasma density fluctuations. The comparison between them reveals that the density fluctuations measured by the spacecraft potential are similar to those measured directly by the FPI, especially in terms of their spectral indices. However, the potential measurements tend to underrepresent the largest-scale density fluctuations. Our study also examines the ratio of perpendicular and parallel to the solar wind's velocity, revealing a consistent pattern of an increased ratio as the scale size decreases. This pattern is observed in both the inner and expanded views of the FPI. Our findings are consistent with earlier studies and support the concept that solar wind turbulence is composed of both ions and electrons. Our study further develops this model by incorporating the observed scale size dependence of our results. Our observations are also compared with numerical simulations, revealing agreement with the Boltzmann model up to a certain scale size. However, at smaller scale sizes, the measured fluctuations begin to deviate from the model, indicating the influence of electrostatic waves. Our findings suggest that at scale sizes of approximately 30 cm, the solar wind's turbulence transitions from being dominated by magnetic fields to a combined effect of magnetic fields and electrostatic waves. Our study demonstrates that combining data from the Fast Plasma Investigation instrument and the spacecraft's potential measurement yields a more comprehensive understanding of solar wind turbulence at small scales. Our results offer new insights into the nature of solar wind turbulence at small scales, paving the way for future research into this topic. Our study also enables the integration of our findings with earlier studies, as well as numerical simulations, to further the understanding of solar wind turbulence. Our findings can be applied to other astrophysical plasmas through the analysis of their magnetic field fluctuations. Our study offers new perspectives on the scaling of our primary observations, as well as the type of electrostatic waves observed, leading to a revised model for the interpretation of our data. A key factor limiting free-electron laser undulators is the divergence of extremely short, high-energy pulses emerging from the interaction zone. Our proposed chirp-taper method can mitigate this issue by aligning the pulse's phase and group delay to concentrate energy at the center, thereby reducing divergence and delaying the onset of side lobes. This technique, applicable across various undulator designs, has been successfully demonstrated in two different schemes - one for ultraviolet and soft X-ray FELs, and another for the hard X-ray regime - with substantial improvements in pulse quality and overall performance. Our findings are expected to benefit existing FEL facilities and inform the design of future systems. \\

In this study, we explored the application of a chirp-taper method to limit the spread of extremely short, high-energy pulses produced by free-electron laser undulators. A key limitation of this technology is the divergence of these pulses outside the interaction zone. To mitigate this issue, we developed and tested two variants of the chirp-taper method - one for ultraviolet and soft X-ray FELs and another for hard X-ray FELs - using the FLASH super-ACcelerator and the HZG soft X-ray SASE Co-Loader facility at DESY. Notably, the implementation of this technique led to a 20 times improvement in pulse energy concentration in the interaction region for both test cases, with potential to significantly enhance the performance of this technology and others like it. \\

To develop and refine this innovation, we utilized cutting-edge computer software, including ASTRA, UPARK, and Track3D, in conjunction with detailed knowledge of free-electron laser physics and technology. A major advantage of this approach is its versatility and adaptability to a wide range of existing FEL facility configurations. For example, the implementation of this technique could lead to a 20 times improvement in pulse energy concentration in the interaction region for both test cases, with potential to significantly enhance the performance of this technology and others like it. \\

In conclusion, the proposed chirp-taper method offers a versatile and effective solution to limiting the spread of extremely short, high-energy pulses produced by free-electron laser undulators. With its potential to significantly enhance the performance of this technology and others like it, this approach could play a key role in optimizing existing FEL facility performance and informing the design of future systems. Further study of this technique is recommended to explore its full capabilities and applications. \\

In the districting context, fairness analysis often involves evaluating plans generated from pseudo-populations created through latitude exchange, a variation of spatial exchange algorithms.  Although Simulated Annealing can accelerate convergence in local optima, its role in analysis has been limited.  This study leverages Simulated Annealing to both generate and evaluate districting plans, incorporating constraints based on population size and fairness considerations.  Two fairness metrics are utilized - equality of opportunity and discrete Kolmogorov-Smirnov.  Results indicate that equal optimal plans exist for fairness metrics based on spatial exchange and latitude exchange.  However, equality of opportunity plans may differ significantly from those optimized for Kolmogorov-Smirnov fairness.  This study suggests the potential for districting plans to compromise on fairness for simpler metrics to prioritize others.  This research addresses the open question of whether fairness optimal plans can be obtained through continuous adjustments.  Additionally, equality of opportunity plans generated through latitude exchange show little variation when the population is minimized.  Conversely, discrete Kolmogorov-Smirnov fairness plans display significant changes as the population undergoes exchange.  Ultimately, these findings highlight the importance of precisely defining districting objectives to achieve optimal results. A novel method is presented that employs an efficient, structured approach to training a discrete navigation agent to make informed decisions. This approach maximizes the mutual information between actions and observations, leveraging an approximate posterior distribution estimated through experience. A key innovation is utilizing a structured representation to incorporate prior knowledge about the environment, thereby reducing the need for extensive experience to inform navigation. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our approach results in more efficient learning and improved performance in multiple environments. Moreover, adding prior knowledge leads to substantial training time reductions. Code is available at https://github.com/ruinard/MI-Navigating-Agent.

Specifically, we found that the rate at which these binary remnants form is too low to account for the observed gravitational wave events detected by LIGO and VIRGO within their detection range. However, this population of binary remnants holds great promise for future discoveries, particularly at higher redshifts. Our findings suggest that the rate of binary remnant formation peaks around a redshift of 24 with an estimated value of 0.64 ± 0.13 year^{-1} Mpc^{-3}, primarily consisting of systems containing strontium-like ions. We also determined that approximately half of these binary remnants are contained within a mass range of 15-70 M⊙, a range where the binary systems' orbital separations significantly affect their initial formation probabilities. Consequently, low-mass and high-mass binaries do not merge by the time the universe reaches an age of one-tenth of the Hubble time, whereas massive systems with close companions have a higher likelihood of forming despite this constraint. Conversely, we demonstrate that introducing finitely many non-hyperbolic components to a hyperbolic surface always results in a new, hyperbolic subset that contains the original surface. Our proposed method utilizes Lie groups and their associated linear representations 
to define manipulability matrices for joint spaces of robotic systems. These 
manipulability matrices, which can also be represented as ellipsoids, are treated 
as geometric objects within the context of Riemannian manifolds. This approach 
enables us to extend elliptical approximations of manipulability to spaces of 
higher dimensions, making it applicable to a variety of robotic systems. To facilitate
joint space manipulability ellipsoids, we first derive the tangent space 
manipulability ellipsoid for a single joint. Subsequently, we expand upon this 
tangent space ellipsoid to obtain the joint space manipulability ellipsoid through 
the use of the Riemannian manifold approximation method. This ellipsoid is 
represented as an exponential perturbation of the universal tangent space 
manipulability ellipsoid. Furthermore, we demonstrate its applicability through 
simulations using a planar robotic arm under the influence of random noise. 
Additionally, we outline open-ended challenges and possible avenues for further 
investigation. To enhance the reader's understanding, we include an appendix 
containing detailed information on Lie groups, their linear representations, 
Riemannian manifolds, and geometric objects, as well as relevant mathematical 
formulations. This document has been formally integrated into the paper, but is 
also available separately as a complementary resource. 
Further details regarding the project are available at https://ncollantes.github.io/rbmliegroups/.

Attosecond pulses, produced through high-harmonic generation (HHG), have become essential tools in studying electron dynamics in various settings. The characteristics of these pulses, specifically their central energy and temporal duration, can be manipulated through adjustments to key parameters in HHG. By optimizing the parameters of a Ti:Sa laser in conjunction with fine-tuned adjustments to its chirp and pulse contrast, it is possible to obtain a consistent spectrum of attosecond pulses. This optimized setup was validated experimentally and the resulting pulses were used to study electron dynamics in nitrite ions, yielding a temporal duration of approximately 270 attoseconds. The criteria for achieving this short temporal duration include a broad energy bandwidth of about 0.35 eV and a smooth continuum suppression ratio of around 10^3. Furthermore, computational models reveal the potential to achieve an even shorter temporal duration of around 160 attoseconds by adjusting certain parameters. The application of ultrafast x-ray pulses generated through HHG has significant implications in fields such as photo-electricity and magnetism. The examples cited here include non-resonant multi-photon ionization and the creation of attosecond core ionization delay in nitrite ions. The central energy and temporal duration of attosecond pulses can be fine-tuned through adjustments to the characteristics of the generating laser pulses, while considerations of pulse contrast and chirp also play important roles. The examples provided demonstrate the successful application of ultrafast x-ray pulses in studying electron dynamics in molecules. The potential for attosecond pulses to investigate electronic and core structure has been exploited, including perspectives on the core ionization delay in nitrite ions. Finally, the possibilities for enhancing HHG performance through interactions with particles such as electrons and ions are discussed. This can occur either through modifications to the generating laser pulses or through modifications to the plasma itself. The potential for attosecond pulse generation through other mechanisms, such as the acceleration of charged particles by electric fields, is also explored. This approach, using measurements of core ionization delays in nitrite ions, has enabled the extraction of fine details in the ion-atom interaction, including temporal shifts of as little as a few attoseconds. This has made it possible to study the complex interplay of forces between charged particles, which could lead to a deeper understanding of how these particles interact under the influence of strong electromagnetic fields. This understanding could have far-reaching implications in fields such as plasma physics and the study of strong-field physics in general. Our new contact binary Algol~A/C system transit observations, which were conducted from 2019 to 2020 using photometers in various locations, revealed an expected light curve profile. The data confirmed that the Algol~C's orbital period has remained stable for at least the past 856 years and also ruled out a hypothetical third component. Our analysis indicated that the system's masses are $1.21 \pm 0.04$ and $0.0241 \pm 0.0006$ Mas, and further research is needed to clarify the significance of Algol~C's low mass ratio and other intriguing properties. Furthermore, our findings are consistent with the theoretical models that describe contact binaries in various stages. Utilizing the Reynolds' method to model Algol~C's structure, we were able to place it on a Hertzsprung-Russell diagram and our results show that it is likely an older contact binary with a temperature of $4700 \pm 50$ K. The system's field geometry was also found to be symmetrical and our calculations indicated that any changes in its orbital period would have a negligible effect on its binary interaction status. Ultimately, our observations validated the hypothesis that Algol~C is a late contact binary and our analysis provided a comprehensive understanding of this interesting system's characteristics. Additionally, our study is the fourth to document a binary star system's transit light curve with a significant subsidence effect. The relevant data sets, analysis code, and calculated values are available online for public use. \\

Deep learning based solution for partial differential equations (PDEs) has experienced rapid growth in recent times. Among the methods, physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have become a preferred choice for inverting PDEs. However, PINNs face challenges with training efficiency due to the need for minimizing a non-convex objective function containing residual terms representing the accuracy to the PDE and an optional smooth term promoting regularization. Previous approaches resort to iterative localization or node pruning, which can be time-consuming and inefficient. We have developed a novel method, Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation, utilizing a dynamic neural architecture that adds or prunes nodes based on the residual values in each layer. This approach has several key benefits: it simplifies the optimization problem by directly targeting the residual values; increases training efficiency by preventing the addition of unnecessary nodes; and achieves a more stable solution by reducing overfitting through a controlled network size. Our method consistently outperforms existing techniques, such as iterative localization and pinning, and also compares well with a validated neural architecture with fixed size. We have applied our method to two challenging problems, an inverse Stefan problem and a fractional PDE, and successfully obtained accurate solutions with a significantly reduced computational cost. This approach can be applied to a wide range of inverse problems involving PDEs and their modifications. Notably, our method can be used to solve the original Stefan problem by incorporating the boundary conditions into the residual terms. This paper confirms the effectiveness of RANG through detailed analysis and comparisons with existing methods, and also provides a thorough evaluation of its performance using relevant metrics. Interestingly, the data shows that libraries with fewer dependencies are more likely to be secure, whereas those having numerous dependencies are at a greater risk, even if most of those dependencies are internally used and do not expose APIs. Conversely, the research discovered that libraries that provide public APIs are generally secure, as they are more likely to be properly maintained and updated. For Cargo's long-term stability, the researchers suggest implementing a dependency update policy that prioritizes securing vulnerable dependencies that expose public APIs. Furthermore, the researchers propose introducing a dependency update policy that gives library maintainers discretion in choosing relevant dependencies for their libraries, allowing the library authors to decide which dependencies to update or replace if they identify security vulnerabilities. This study investigates the ergodic properties of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Laudau equations driven by by pure jump noises and random periodic forcing. We establish ergodic theorems in various spaces and examine the convergence rates using a convergence rate theorem. In doing so, we derive a convenient estimate for the expectation of the power function of a pure jump Lévy process, which may be of independent interest. Moreover, our findings can be applied to a broad class of stochastic differential equations and SDEs with pure jump noises. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, we consider a specific example - a one-dimensional stochastic complex Ginzburg-Laudau equation driven by a pure jump Lévy process and show that it is ergodic in a certain space and we calculate the convergence rate as well. In contrast to conventional diffusion-type stochastic complex Ginzburg-Laudau equations, those that are perturbed by pure jump noises exhibit a distinct loss of ergodicity. Specifically, we demonstrate the non-ergodicity of a one-dimensional stochastic complex Ginzburg-Laudau equation driven by a pure jump Lévy process and a Lévy process with an-contour-avoiding path in a certain space. In addition, we show that a two-dimensional stochastic complex Ginzburg-Laudau equation, when driven by a pure jump Lévy process and a Lévy process with an-contour-avoiding path, is non-ergodic in a certain space as well. Furthermore, when the pure jump Lévy process is confined to a Borel set with an-contour-avoiding path, a one-dimensional stochastic complex Ginzburg-Laudau equation is ergodic in a certain space while, in contrast, it is non-ergodic in the same space when it is driven by a Lévy process with an-contour-avoiding path. Finally, based on the above analysis, we conclude that the ergodic properties of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Laudau equations are highly sensitive to the characteristics of the pure jump noise. In particular, we observe that the ergodicity of these equations is completely lost when the pure jump noise has an-contour-avoiding paths while it can be restricted to a Borel set with such paths to lose ergodicity. Additionally, we note that the case of white noise, a special type of pure jump noise, falls somewhere in between, allowing the ergodicity of these equations to be lost, although to a lesser extent. The power graph in discrete mathematics is an important concept that has been studied extensively in recent years due to its various applications. Specifically, we investigated the power graphs of finite non-cyclic abelian groups in this research, focusing on determining their minimum degree, presenting methods to construct these graphs and identify their components, as well as analyzing the presentation of these groups using generators and relations. Notably, our results reveal a unique connection between the power graph and the commutative subgroups of these groups, enabling a systematic approach to studying power graphs based on existing information about the subgroups of these groups, thereby simplifying the process of identifying and comparing important elements of the power graph, such as the minimum degree, the number of edges, the diameter, and the distance between specific elements. Moreover, our research also explores the distance between distinct commutative subgroups of these groups, which in turn allows us to establish an upper bound for the minimum degree in power graphs of p-groups, where p represents a prime number. To validate our theoretical findings, we determined the power graphs, edges, diameter, and distance between distinct commutative subgroups for non-cyclic abelian groups of orders 8, 9, 16, and 25. Our research also identifies a new class of finite non-cyclic abelian groups with diameter 2, thereby providing comprehensive insights into their power graphs. Ultimately, our research contributes the first set of non-cyclic abelian groups with a diameter greater than 2, specifically a non-cyclic abelian group of order 32 whose power graph has a diameter of 3. The general methods employed in this research can be applied to determine the power graphs of other finite non-cyclic abelian groups with a diameter greater than 2. Building on this foundation, Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs) were developed by adapting Gabor filters to align with the principal axes of images. Graph convolutional networks (GCNs) are widely used for graph classification and ranking. However, the standard GCN process involves gathering information from neighboring nodes, which can lead to biased calculations if operations are performed from node to node in the graph. To address this issue, our research introduces a novel, efficient GCN architecture that operates within a limited local scope. By shuffling the order of graph feature gathering, this new GCN retains the ability to learn essential graph properties while eliminating biases from its calculations. Furthermore, our model offers reduced computational requirements, making it a more feasible option for operating in local scope. To validate its effectiveness, we tested our model on two datasets, ENZERES-646 and ENZERES-1110, and demonstrated its capabilities through comprehensive, empirical studies. Notably, our model achieved comparable results to the original GCN for graph classification on the two datasets. Researchers have developed various attacks on neural networks, with the primary goal of maximizing network activation and misclassifying data. We propose a novel and complex attack, which significantly expands its adaptability to a broader range of networks and tasks. Unlike traditional attacks that rely on gradient information, our approach, 'Trojan activation attack,' takes advantage of the network's inherent weaknesses, specifically overparameterization, to trigger a catastrophic failure. The attack is non-specific, meaning it works equally well on various networks, tasks, and datasets, and can be executed both remotely and locally, making it a threat in real-world applications. The study also sheds light on the mechanisms behind neural networks, specifically how overparameterization affects network performance. We investigated a compressed CSI method where only relevant information is sent from the CSI feedback phase by selecting particular CSI blocks using an attention-based approach. We introduce a new framework that represents modal logic as a topological category, offering a novel topology on words that reflects how, in modal logic, additional "boxes" enclose sections of words, influencing accessibility relations. This topology smoothes out minor imperfections in words, treating them as essentially accessible if they differ from a given accessible word only at "modal" positions. Unlike other topological models, our approach doesn't rely on a pre-existing space of words; instead, it derives the topology from the accessibility relations themselves, incorporating "modal" operators as clopen operators on the associated Boolean algebra of "closures" - the smallest non-empty collections of words with a common "core". By distilling the underlying topology from these relations, our system eliminates the need for an explicit representation of words as elements of a space. Additionally, our framework allows for the extension to "infinitely deep" modal logics by adapting standard techniques for extending topological spaces. We establish that every normal extensions of such logics have a topological model, while confirming the BIS model theorem under the assumption that the corresponding modal logic is strongly regular. Our study, by offering a description of modal logic as a topological category, offers a new understanding of the relationships between accessibility relations, and how they determine the meaning of modal operators. We explore the algebraic and geometric characteristics of the space of class functions on quantum groups such as $SU_q(2)$, $U_q(3)$, and $U_q(4)$ for arbitrary deformation parameters $q$. Our investigation focuses on the property of maximal abelian self-adjoint algebra (MASA) within the underlying C*-algebra of central functions. Our key findings show that the space of class functions forms a MASA only for specific deformation parameters $q$, and this MASA becomes isomorphic to the algebra of continuous functions on the classical group when $q=0$. Additionally, the MASA possesses a representation as a convolution algebra, which shares similarities with the classical case, but only exists for the specified non-deformation parameters. Furthermore, we establish the ideal structure of these algebras, which consists of the central ideal of constant functions and other properly embedded ideals. Our results are validated through examples and counterexamples for the given quantum groups $SU_q(2)$ and $U_q(3)$. For instance, for $SU_q(2)$ with non-zero deformation parameter $q$, the algebra of class functions fails to be a MASA, but becomes one when restricted to the subalgebra of functions invariant under the parity operator $\Delta$. On the other hand, $U_q(4)$ does not satisfy the MASA property for any value of $q$. Our study opens avenues for future research on the algebraic characteristics of the space of class functions for other quantum groups. Conversely, we present a quantum group $GL_q(\mathfrak{h})$ associated with a complex simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{h}$ of rank one, which exhibits a MASA property for the space of class functions, thereby providing additional support to our findings. To conclude, we highlight an open challenge related to the algebra of functions on $GL_q(\mathfrak{h})$ for arbitrary simple Lie algebras $\mathfrak{h}$ of rank greater than one. As a byproduct of our research, we derive key properties of the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{g})$ associated with a simple Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ of rank one, which may be of independent interest. Large Multi-dimensional action-independent Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) pose significant challenges to solution methods due to their large action spaces. Even after reducing the complexity by eliminating dependent actions, a gradient-based reinforcement learning algorithm faces considerable difficulties in tackling such large MDPs. Building on its application in two-player games, the application of the General Minimum Description Length principle in reinforcement learning allows us to reinterpret exact policy iteration as a minimization problem, which we can approximate using the gradient-based iterative least squares method. This approach enables the development of inexact policy iteration, a more efficient method that doesn't require maintaining an action-dependent residual basis. In experiments, inexact policy iteration proves to be significantly faster to converge than traditional policy iteration in large MDPs, either with or without reduced dimensionality. Even with an additional dimensionality reduction, inexact policy iteration outperforms existing gradient-based solution methods in reinforcement learning. Specifically, it solves an enlarged MDP with 10,000 states 10 to 20 times faster than value iteration, 5 to 10 times faster than flat Q-learning, and 2 to 5 times faster than hierarchical Q-learning. Furthermore, inexact policy iteration's efficiency isn't restricted by the specific problem settings, making it a versatile method that also solves complex MDPs with large action spaces quickly and accurately. In particular, it takes less than 10 seconds to find the optimal policy in the MDP for the game of Tetris. Utilizing theoretical evolutionary models, we found that the masses of these objects span from 5.7 to 29 times the mass of the sun. This process can be understood through double parton distribution functions (DPDs), which represent the probability of finding two partons within hadrons. The primary objective of this research is to examine how the regularity of the solution to the Fisher-KPP equation changes over time, given initial data with specific smoothness properties. Utilizing the theoretical results derived from the regularity of the heat semigroup and the properties of the Hopf lemma, we demonstrate the regularity of the solution for all time in any domain. Additionally, we expand on existing literature by addressing the regularity of the solution in higher-order spatial derivatives and extend the findings to certain non-local equations, including the reaction-diffusion equation with a Gaussian kernel. Furthermore, we provide evidence of a threshold for the regularity of the solution to the fractional Fisher-KPP equation in certain spaces. Lastly, we investigate the regularity of the solutions to the approximate models of the fractional Fisher-KPP equation through the Fourier method and the Galerkin method. By combining these approaches, we achieve the best known regularity results for the solutions to these equations, including being smooth for sufficiently small initial data and having higher Sobolev norms bounded by a logarithmic growth for large initial data. Furthermore, the Fourier method allows us to obtain precise estimates of the errors associated with approximating the solution through a finite Galerkin method. Based on this analysis, we confirm that the convergence rate in the Galerkin method is ultimately limited by the rate of decay of the Fourier modes, specifically not affected by the fractional order. Finally, the computational results of this method are also presented, demonstrating its effectiveness and showing that it can accurately reproduce the known regularity properties of the exact solutions in certain cases. The UbiComp 2021 Challenge focused on distinguishing daily activities from sensor data recorded at two different home settings, belonging to the same participant. A Data-driven Activity Recognition system is proposed, designed to identify both known and unknown activities in real-time from diverse sensor datasets. Although the approach can be modified to accommodate new labels, our solution is limited to working with pre-defined labels only. For this challenge, we developed a Time series-based Deep Learning system to differentiate between two specific activities, 'Writing' and 'Cooking', extracted from accelerometer and gyroscope sensor data. Our approach is unique in that it outperforms existing systems by incorporating a Pad-Pad Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) with Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) layers, enhancing performance by incorporating activity duration information and adapting a Data Augmentation strategy to boost diversity in training samples. As a result, our system achieved 94% accuracy in distinguishing between 'Writing' and 'Cooking' activities and 97% in identifying the 'Writing' activity alone. We intend to contribute this method to the domain as a viable solution for recognizing daily activities. This paper compares the limiting distribution of contagion processes taking place on random hypergraphs to those occurring on two-dimensional lattices. Our study utilizes the eigenvalue distribution of the corresponding hypergraph contagion matrices, establishing a fundamental connection between the intrinsic connectivity structure of the hypergraph and the eigenvalues, further relating it to the spatial arrangement of the hypergraph's components. Our findings demonstrate that the spatial interrelation of the hypergraph's components significantly impacts the rate of infection. Our method of approach involves expressing the contagion matrix as a sum of interacting matrix-valued random variables, leveraging existing knowledge about the Perceptron Matrix and the Jacobi Matrix to gain insight into the resulting distribution. Our analysis is rigorous, yet our methods are largely accessible and may be adapted to hypergraphs with unique properties. Our research includes extensive numerical computations that validate our theoretical findings and provide greater insight into the resulting distribution. Our study is the first of its kind to investigate the resulting distribution of the Hypergraph Contagion Model, and our research holds significant value for understanding the spread of diseases within complex hypergraph structures. Our code can be found at https://github.com/alexjchung/HypergraphContagion. Our previous research revealed that a steady-state dynamo, driven by kinetic mechanisms in rapidly rotating stars, isn't an adequate explanation for the observed magnetic properties of HADCEs. In this study, we investigate whether dynamos driven by other mechanisms can produce the required prolonged magnetic cycles in stars with low rotation rates. Our findings indicate that both convective and torsional oscillation-driven dynamos are capable of generating long-duration magnetic cycles, albeit via an unstable and dynamically shifting dynamo loop structure. In the case of convective dynamos, this structure is a result of the interaction between inertial waves and convective cumulates, while in the case of torsional oscillation-driven dynamos, it arises from the connection between inertial waves and the oscillations at half the frequency, both occurring in the star's convective envelope. In both scenarios, the solution is inherently unstable and can only be maintained through adjustment of the star's boundary layers to restore dynamical equilibrium, an concept not previously considered in the study of dynamo theory. In the case of convective dynamos, this leads to the formation of cyclic patterns, as the convective cumulates migrate towards the inner boundary of the star over the course of the cycle, whereas torsional oscillation-driven dynamos produce anti-phased magnetic cycles similar to the results obtained from global 3D simulations, highlighting their potential as an explanation for the observed magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars. In contrast, kinematic global dynami do exhibit magnetic cycles, however these are dependent on the star's rotation rate and are less likely to be observed in the case of HADCEs. In conclusion, both convective and torsional oscillation-driven dynamos are capable of generating magnetic cycles, whereas kinematic global dynamos are less likely to produce the required prolonged magnetic cycles observed in low rotating stars. Multi-threaded operations are complex and often difficult to assess due to the high number of possible execution paths, however our McMini model checker significantly outperforms traditional models by utilizing a speed-up technique. By employing a McMini model checker, a fundamental verification of multi-threaded code can be performed in a matter of minutes or hours, whereas other methods may require days or weeks. Specifically, we will be using the McMini model checker to verify the multi-threaded McLib library, which includes critical operations such as atomic data structures and access mechanisms. Our model checker has successfully found and reported 105 novel, indistinguishable, thread-safe issues in the McLib library. These thread-safe issues were found by generating the total sum of 309 billion thread safety scenarios, and 105 of them were identified as indistinguishable violations. Model checker configurations that were an order of magnitude smaller were used to discover 101 additional issues in the McLib library, which includes critical data structures such as atomic stacks, queues, and lock mechanisms. Furthermore, McMini has been integrated with other advanced verification tools such as Bound and Verifast to expand its capabilities and effectiveness. Following the integration, McMini discovered 105 novel thread-safe issues in the McLib library, 101 of which were discovered using Bound, and 51 more issues, including 46 that were previously undetected by McMini, were discovered using Verifast. As a result, a total of 257 thread-safe issues were discovered by McMini, 101 by Bound, and 51 by Verifast, which collectively accounted for the fixation of 105 McMini issues, 101 Bound issues, and 51 Verifast issues. Our model checker has been open-sourced and can be downloaded for use at https://mcmini.github.io/. Additionally, the McLib library used for verification can be found at https://mclib.github.io/, and a detailed guide on model checking is provided at https://mcmini.github.io/mcmini-guide.html. Finally, the GitHub repository for hosting McMini-related issues can be found at https://github.com/McMini/McMini/issues.

Social media platforms are becoming primary sources of news and information, as demonstrated by the growing user base of users, including cytokine-induced brain-hair-loss aware individuals. Despite providing unfettered access to information, social media platforms are also breeding grounds for misinformation, leading to the spread of false beliefs among users, potentially triggering harmful actions and leaving trail of toxic comments. To contain the spread of misinformation and maintain a healthy online community, social media platforms must implement effective measures to verify the accuracy of shared information and maintain a safe and inclusive online environment. Facebook-owned WhatsApp has taken steps to address the spread of misinformation by limiting the number of times harmful messages can be forwarded. Building on WhatsApp's efforts, our research automates the detection of misinformation by analyzing geometric patterns in electronic maps, identifying potentially false incidents like road accidents or crime scenes that can spread panic. Our approach uses machine learning and geometric analysis of WhatsApp group conversations to detect false incidents reported by users. Experimental results show that our method can effectively identify false incidents by analyzing electronic maps, outperforming existing manual detection efforts. False incident detection algorithms have numerous applications in various domains, including transportation, emergency services, and navigation systems. By integrating our algorithm with WhatsApp's API, we can provide WhatsApp users with accurate information about incidents on their local maps, enabling them to make informed decisions. Moreover, our research can be adapted to detect false beliefs using similar geometric analysis techniques, contributing to online fact-checking initiatives. Lastly, our work highlights the numerous applications of geometric pattern analysis in real-world problems, suggesting a wide range of research opportunities inspired by similar conceptual approaches. This innovative framework has the potential to enable various automated detection algorithms for multiple domains, opening up a wide range of research opportunities inspired by similar conceptual approaches.
