We've developed a comprehensive approach to modelling the shape of a population's genetic structure over time, given the simultaneous occurrence of multiple types of mutations and selection influences. By combining the effects of these processes, we've formulated a specific type of diffusion process governing the population's genetic structure. Our approach accommodates any degree of selection influence and various types of mutations, including non-symmetric ones, and provides a precise expression for the long-term genetic structure of the population. Furthermore, to determine the diversity within the population, we analyze the diffusion process and its asymptotic properties. Our model is applicable in a variety of settings, such as the study of self-polllination in plants or the investigation of mutations in blood types within a population. We've used our model to analyze the specific case of a self-repelling model under a high degree of self-selection, and observed an interesting transition from a random fluctuation pattern to a clinal structure as the strength of self-repelling mutations increases. We've also collected numerical data on the long-term average genetic structure of the population, as well as the diversity within the population, under a wide range of mutation parameters. Notably, our analysis shows that an increase in the strength of self-repelling mutations leads to a more uniform distribution of alleles across different locations and a simpler overall genetic structure. In a companion paper, we've collected numerical data on the transient characteristics of the population's genetic structure over time, and have used these findings to answer a previously posed question in the field. Our results offer a comprehensive insight into the shape of a population's genetic structure and provide a highly generalisable model to study the effects of multiple types of mutations and selection influences in various evolutionary scenarios. We've applied our model to various real-world scenarios, such as the blood type genetics in a human population and the self-pollination in a certain species of flowering plants. Our approach has provided a more accurate and detailed understanding of these genetic systems, and has identified clinal structures and concordant variations across different locations and geographic distances. In a related study, we've used our model to study the genetic structure of a population undergoing a regime change from self-repelling to neutral mutations, and have collected numerical data on the long-term diversity within the population under different self-repelling strengths. Our results show a smooth transition from self-repelling to neutral structures, and have precisely calculated the distribution of alleles across different locations and the population's genetic structure over time. A commonly used method for detecting spoofed speech uses residual relative spectral strength features with a support vector machine classifier. However, spoofed speech with strong artifact levels can fool the detector, and weaker artifacts go undetected. A recent strategy involves using a deep learning-based classifier for more effective detection. Yet, this approach is inefficient due to its high computational and memory requirements, and unreliable training in speech artifact detection. We introduce a novel deep learning-based detector that combines attention and convolutional layers for robust and efficient spoofed speech detection. By recognizing the speech artifact pattern through focused attention on crucial spectral parts, and using convolutional layers for feature extraction, this method yields improved performance. We assessed various convolutional layer configurations and observed that a single block yields sufficient results, outperforming existing deep learning-based detectors. Furthermore, our method achieves high accuracy across different speech datasets, and even surpasses traditional methods in challenge evaluations. Specifically, it excels in ASVspoof 2019 database evaluation with a 15.03% equal error rate, and in the ASVspoof 2020 database with a 13.03% equal error rate. We demonstrate that our method is a highly effective spoofed speech detector with a compact and efficient design. In particular, it has a distinct advantage of being 2-3 times more efficient in terms of the number of trainable parameters for artifact detection. This overview provides a detailed examination of the connections between supergravity, quantum gravity, and low-energy effective theories as well as the techniques employed to solve supergravity models thoroughly. It includes an in-depth analysis of the various approaches used to formulate supergravity and their limitations, the linear and nonlinear supergravities, the gauge supergravity theory, and recent developments in the dyonic gauge supergravity theory. Additionally, it covers some promising applications of supergravity such as in black hole physics and as a framework for effective quantum gravity. The text also discusses the challenges and issues associated with supergravity and suggests some potential avenues for further investigation. This overview aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to supergravity for both general and specialized audiences. In this revised edition, we have made several significant changes, including a more in-depth examination of recent developments in supergravity, an expansion of our discussion on quantum gravity and the effective theories, and a completely new section on the M-theory and the Kaluza-Klein models. Furthermore, we have corrected numerous errors, updated references, and implemented a more consistent notation throughout the text. Additionally, we have included new material such as an introduction to the BRST Higgs mechanism, the emergence of the Duality, Pregeometric and Fuzzy theories of supergravity. We investigated nonreciprocal optical manipulation of coherent photon pairs generated by a silicon microdisk. By adjusting the pump's propagation direction, the coherence between photon pairs could be controlled, revealing an underlying connection between the coherence functions of the photon pairs and the anisotropic microdisk resonators. Notably, reversing the pump's propagation direction reversed the coherence's sign while preserving its magnitude, effectively creating a nonreciprocal optical device. Furthermore, we applied this coherence manipulation in an experimental demonstration of nonreciprocal optical buffering, achieving nearly complete transmission for one of the photon pairs while greatly reducing it for the other, thus holding promise for applications in quantum communication and processing. Based on this concept, we also envisioned the integration of numerous anisotropic microdisk resonators to develop a photonic circuit capable of complex nonreciprocal optical operations. Ultimately, this approach may pave the way for the development of advanced photonic circuits where coherent photon pairs generate quantum correlation. Furthermore, we believe that quantum attributes of photon pairs could be effectively utilized for the implementation of quantum-related optical operations. For example, the quantum attribute of one photon could be used to control the transmission of another photon, thus potentially creating a bi-directional connection between two nonreciprocal optical devices. This approach could lead to the innovative creation of advanced photonic circuits where coherent photon pairs generate quantum correlation, thereby enabling novel optical processing and communication techniques. Additionally, we explored the feasibility of scaling the device to accommodate multiple anisotropic microdisk resonators that can execute complex nonreciprocal optical functions, thereby enhancing the device's versatility and practical applications. Concurrent XPS measurements were taken from the metal gate and the silicon substrate to analyze their chemical bonds. Various factors were observed to influence the interface characteristics, including silicon carrier concentration, etch rate, and oxide thickness. It was discovered that silicon wafers etched using fluorine-based plasma have a higher carrier concentration compared to those etched with hydrogen-based plasma, and both methods exhibit a carrier concentration equivalent to n-type doped silicon. Additionally, silicon wafers treated with hydrogen plasma show reduced interface trap densities and better electron properties compared to hydrogen-treated n-type silicon, which can be attributed to the passivation of silicon defects by hydrogen. These findings are particularly relevant for evaluating etched silicon through metrology methods relying on carrier concentration, such as spreading resistance and four-point probe measurements. Furthermore, the study suggests that a hydrogen-free etching process may be necessary to achieve etched silicon with unique properties suitable for backside metal gate formation. Data show that both groups benefit from each other's actions, creating a mutually beneficial dynamic. Furthermore, analysis reveals that CTA profitability stems primarily from traders' sudden decisions to liquidate their positions, rather than being a result of their own trading actions. As another significant finding, it's observed that advisors generate the most profit from market situations where traders are most active and engaged. Ultimately, the research highlights the potential for further investigation into the link between market participants who invest in commodities and those who provide trading advice. As an example, investigating how this relationship impacts the trading decisions of commodity futures, the study specifically looks at the effect on the S&P 500 stock index. Data indicate that advisors benefit from each other's actions in the index as well. Our research focuses on a specific type of evasion technique known as TTP evasion, which targets network monitoring systems by modifying known attack methods. To protect against this type of attack, we proposed an innovative method that can be integrated into Dynamic Protocol Detection mechanisms to improve their robustness against TTP evasion. By analyzing the temporal relationships between network traffic and system events, our approach can detect tampered protocols and prevent the spread of malware. Using the Honeypot Detection System, we collected and analyzed data from multiple network protocols including FTP, Telnet, and Wget. Our experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of our method in recognizing tampered protocols and preventing malware transmission. Additionally, we assessed the performance of our system and found that it has a low false positive rate. Our study on TTP evasion provides valuable insights for network monitoring and incident response systems to improve their capability in detecting and preventing sophisticated attacks. Our method can be integrated into Dynamic Protocol Detection mechanisms to improve their robustness against TTP evasion and is expected to be implemented in a practical demonstration in the near future. Quantum Fourier transform, a fundamental operation in quantum computing and quantum communication, has been revamped using two-qubit Toffoli gates. This efficient implementation enables the quantum Fourier transform to be utilized in high-dimensional multi-photon systems by replacing the conventional one-qubit Pauli rotations with specialized unitaries. Furthermore, a complete reconstruction of the quantum Fourier transform circuit has been achieved using only Toffoli gates, thereby allowing the integration of this circuit into the broader quantum circuit model. As a direct consequence, the all-to-all connectivity structure inherent in the quantum Fourier transform is perfectly aligned with the constraints of the quantum circuit model, thereby enabling the precise manipulation of quantum states across the entire computational system. This study presents explicit constructions for the specialized unitaries and a reconstructed quantum Fourier transform circuit, thereby paving the way for the practical application of quantum Fourier transforms in practical, multi-photon quantum computing systems. Interestingly, the resulting quantum Fourier transforms can even be achieved with fewer gates than prior studies, specifically 2N^2 gates for an N-qubit system. Additionally, this study's findings apply equally to the Swindle quantum Fourier transform, a previously proposed variant of the standard quantum Fourier transform. Notably, the standard quantum Fourier transform exhibits significant differences in behavior compared to classical Fourier transforms, specifically an exponentially rapid growth in entanglement and connectivity across the first knapsack order n/2, thereby highlighting its inherent complexities. Consequently, the standard quantum Fourier transform may necessitate additional resources in the form of quantum memory, specifically the handling of doubly entangled states, in contrast to the special quantum Fourier transform, which is capable of circumventing these complexities and is constructed using only two-qubit gates. Finally, the special quantum Fourier transform has the added benefit of enabling the efficient construction of Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states, specifically those involving an odd number of qubits, thereby offering a practical and viable pathway for its application in near-term quantum devices. Interestingly, the resultant construction of Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states is capable of reaching densities nearly classical in nature, specifically densities approaching 1/2, thereby surpassing previous state-of-the-art densities of 2/5. Consequently, the special quantum Fourier transform has the far-reaching potential to be employed as a key tool in the generation of entangled states, thereby paving the way for the practical application of quantum computing systems. This study optimizes joint channel estimation in IEEE 802.11n wireless local area networks that use intelligent reflecting surfaces, without relying on narrow-bandization or on-dim channel estimation methods. Instead, we use a wide-bandization technique and an optimization-based method that estimates both single and coupled channel coefficients. Our approach leads to more accurate channel estimates and reduces estimation error as the number of subcarriers increases. This study analyzed the quantity and composition of local news reporting on COVID-19 across the US using the Open News dataset, which encompassed articles from 217 US cities and 141 distinct weekly newspapers from January to May 2020. Our findings showed significant variability in the volume of COVID-19 related news across different cities, with the highest coverage observed in areas like New York City and Philadelphia, and notably low coverage in cities like Las Vegas and Indianapolis. Our content analysis revealed that the majority of local news focused on public health issues, with cities that were hard hit by the pandemic devoting a greater proportion of their news to topics like death tolls, infection rates, hospital admissions, and economic disruption. In contrast, areas that had not been severely affected by the pandemic, such as those in Las Vegas, gave more prominence to news about economic recovery. Our examination of how different cities reported on COVID-19 key issues through news headlines also highlighted notable variations in tone and content. This research sheds light on the complex nature of local news coverage, highlighting existing inequalities in resource allocation and perspective representation. The findings of this study can inform the development of targeted initiatives to promote diversity and inclusivity in local news reporting. Content delivery networks and cloud services widely utilize Bloom filters to minimize data transmission, but they can be costly and inefficient when handling infrequent get requests. To address this issue, xor filters have been developed as a potential replacement for Bloom filters. Composed of multiple Bloom filters, xor filters are designed to provide both high efficiency and infrequent access performance. Recent research has focused on deriving closed-form expressions for the memory usage and hit rates of xor filters. Interestingly, it was found that xor filters often require more memory and have higher latencies than standard Bloom filters, despite claiming superior capabilities. In this paper, a thorough examination of the fundamental limitations of xor filters and other counter-based filters is conducted. Experimental results demonstrating the substantial overhead of xor filters relative to basic Bloom filters are presented, and a simplified approach to counter-based filters is proposed to achieve comparable performance with significantly reduced complexity. Our findings indicate that, while useful in certain scenarios, xor filters are not a practical substitute for standard Bloom filters in many cases. On the other hand, the proposed optimization remains a more efficient solution than using xor filters. Additionally, an independent evaluation confirmed that the proposed algorithm accurately simulates the performance of counter-based filters in real-world scenarios. Based on these findings, a new variant of Bloom filters, called partitioned Bloom filters, is suggested as a viable alternative to xor filters for frequent get operations. Extensive empirical tests in both simulation and practical scenarios validated the effectiveness of partitioned Bloom filters in providing better memory usage and speed improvements up to 15%, outperforming traditional Bloom filters and xor filters. The proposed sub-linear search approach for counter-based filters was also independently verified to have applications in various scenarios, such as when combined with partitioned Bloom filters. The developed implementation, PBFI, is available for public use on GitHub. The experimental outcome showed that, contrary to popular belief, xor filters often need more space than standard Bloom filters and have a higher latency, which makes them unsuitable as a practical substitute for standard Bloom filters in many cases. An alternative, optimized approach was developed to achieve comparable performance with significantly reduced complexity, which is still a more efficient solution than using xor filters. Additionally, an independent evaluation confirmed that the proposed algorithm accurately simulates the performance of counter-based filters in real-world scenarios. The Alexandrov embeds a closed subset of a real affine space into a simpler closed subset of the same dimension in a higher-dimensional convex body. This technique has its roots in algebraic geometry, particularly in relation to Zariski decomposition and the Nef and pseudoeffective cones of divisors. Specifically, it can be used to express the difference between a divisor and its positive part as a sum of effective and pseudoeffective divisors. This correspondence applies to big divisors as well. Additionally, the Alexandrov embeds a closed non-manifold subset of a real affine space into a simpler closed subset of the same dimension in a higher-dimensional convex body. This algorithmic approach is inspired by Reeb's tube reconstruction method in topological smoothable reconstruction. It first removes a certain layer from the subset to obtain a key divisor, then uses this divisor to determine an approximate tube shape, before refining this shape through an iterative process involving a series of accumulation points. This method is capable of handling not only divisors, but also other closed non-manifold subsets as well as their birational and algebraic images. These constructions apply to numerical triglobals, which are used to describe the geometric and topological properties of algebraic varieties. This discussion is particularly relevant in the study of algebraic varieties with non-rational connectedness. These varieties come in two forms: those with non-rational connectedness due to the presence of irrational divisors, and those with non-rational connectedness due to the presence of point singularities. Specific examples include the blow-up of $\mathbb{P}^n$ at a point, the variety of $2\times2$ hermitian matrices with positive trace, and the variety of complex circulant matrices with positive entries on the diagonal. These examples share a common feature: they are all contained in a numerical triglobal known as the Alexandrov closure of the set of all real $2\times2$ matrices with non-negative hermitian trace. This triglobal is itself a combination of two other numerically effective cones: the Alexandrov closure of the set of all real $2\times2$ matrices with non-negative hermitian trace, and the pseudoeffective cone of divisors on $\mathbb{P}^{n+1}$. This duality of structures applies to other invariant subsets as well. Recent advancements in deep learning have led to remarkable performance gains in sim2real (simulator-to-real-world) transfers, allowing autonomous driving models to directly translate from simulated environments to real-world applications. Despite these improvements, our investigation of the 2020 Waymo Open Dataset Challenge demonstrates that sim2real performance is often fragile and prone to degradation. We observe this fragility to be a direct consequence of the diversity among real-world datasets, which causes a significant discrepancy compared to the uniformity found in simulated environments. To mitigate this discrepancy, we have developed an innovative method that simultaneously balances diversity among individual examples within a dataset and overall dataset diversity. The efficacy of our approach is confirmed through experiments in Section 5, which reveal a considerable enhancement in performance stability and mean APE (average perception error) for our top-ranked challenge submissions. Specifically, our method yields a 25% reduction in APE and significantly reduces the variance in APE by two orders of magnitude. We publicly share our code and relevant datasets at the following link: https://github.com/onotom/sim2real_analysis/tree/wotm-2020-wod. Additionally, our challenge-related blog post can be accessed at https://onotom.github.io/2020/10/06/wotm-2020-wod.html.

A comprehensive framework for supervised learning based on the McCulloch-Pitts network has been developed, which can be considered a combination of the Hopfield network and a linear classifier. While the Hopfield network is renowned for its robustness, it lacks the ability to support learning. In contrast, the McCulloch-Pitts network, which is the foundation of this framework, is parameterized by the connection weights and threshold values of its neurons. These parameters can be adjusted to achieve desired synaptic plasticity. Additionally, by introducing an auxiliary loss function to minimize reconstruction errors, the learning capabilities of the network are further enhanced. Through the integration of regularization techniques and an auxiliary loss, the robustness of the network can be complemented with the ability to support learning. Upon being retrained with a larger dataset, the network's connectivity structure is optimized for efficient gradient propagation, thereby facilitating efficient learning. The efficacy of this framework is validated on various benchmark problems, including the classification of MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 images, as well as a multi-class classification task with randomly generated images. The results show that the robustness of the network can be traded off against its accuracy on the test dataset by adjusting the strength of regularization. Furthermore, the robustness of the network is primarily influenced by its larger-scale structures, whereas its connectivity patterns at the local scale have a relatively minor impact. Given any group $G$, we explore the homotopy orbit spectrum $(Z[[G]])_{hG}$, where $Z[[G]]$ represents the complete tensor algebra of $G$, and $Z$ is the integers or a finite field. Our main objective is to identify conditions under which $(Z[[G]])_{hG}$ is isomorphic to the spectrum $Z$. Additionally, we examine when the homotopy orbit spectrum $(Z[[G]])^{hG}$, derived from the homotopy fixed points, is equivalent to the spectrum $Z$. Our investigations share similarities with recent findings by Shau-Hsuan Lin and Paul VanKoughnett. We investigate projective planes derived from the projective line over a ring, 
using both affine planes and extended affine planes. Our examination 
focuses on the former, aiming to identify additional conditions for a 
projective plane to be derived solely from the projective line over a ring. 
Moreover, we explore extensions of these projectives planes to larger geometries. 
Our study also examines the uniqueness of projective planes constructed from 
rings and their relationship with closed geometric structures, ultimately concluding 
that certain ring conditions imply the projective plane's compatibility with a field. 
Our work is further enhanced by numerous examples and counterexamples that clarify 
our main findings and address open questions within the field. 
It is demonstrated that certain conditions on the ring's class group yields projective planes, 
including planes over the ring of p-adic numbers and specific local rings. 
Our analysis is completed by constructing projective planes over rings with a non-trivial
quaternion algebra, extending previous results over specific fields. 
This work is further expanded to include the classification of planar rings, 
resulting in a comprehensive and lengthy publication. 
A detailed account of our method's development and evolution is provided in an accompanying survey. 
A comprehensive list of references is presented at the very conclusion of this paper. 
Our analysis is initiated with projective planes of order p, which are derived from the projective line over a ring of p-adic numbers. 
A detailed examination is then conducted on projective planes of order 5, constructed from the projective line over a ring of integers of a quintic residue field with a specific property. 
A detailed classification is then given of projective planes of order p^2, obtained from the projective line over a complete local ring of characteristic p. 
Finally, a detailed account of projective planes of order 2k, constructed from the projective line over a complete local ring of characteristic 2k^2 is provided.

In a 2019 research, in connection with the $\text{ADD}(L)}$ meeting at $\mathsf{CMS2019}$ in Mumbai, we explored the concept of $\text{Tukey-order-with-models}$. This led us to investigate $\text{Tukey-extension-with-models}$, a broader idea. Our study revealed connections between different cardinal properties and it was demonstrated that $\text{Tukey-extension-with-models}$ implies both $\text{Cof}(\mathcal{M})$ and $\text{Cof}^+(\mathcal{M})$. Our work also showed an equivalence between $\text{Tukey-order-with-models}$ and $\text{Tukey-extension-with-models}$ when applied to linear orderings, thereby proving an extension of Estep-Maynard's theorem. Furthermore, we established that $\text{Tukey-order-with-models}$ is equivalent to $\text{Tukey-extension-with-models}$ for certain types of structures, including those from farah-families and farah-lambda-sets. Our research also delved into the existence of certain types of structures, including minimal analysis and uniformization, and we proved a specific type of minimal uniformization to be consistent with $\text{True-Power}$ being less than the next measurable cardinal. Additionally, we provided ramification and applications, including an implication that shows the truth of $\text{Cof}^+(\mathcal{M})$ implies $\text{Cof}^+(\mathcal{Q})$, a consequence of $\text{Tukey-extension-with-models}$, where $\mathcal{Q}$ is the quotient-complete linear order. Our research also explored the concept of $\text{Tukey-extension-with-models}$ and its relation to complete dense linear orderings, thereby proving an extension of Velhan's theorem. Moreover, we established an equivalence between $\text{Tukey-extension-with-models}$ and $\text{Tukey-order-with-models}$ for complete dense linear orderings, thereby proving an extension of Szeptycki's theorem. Finally, our research discovered an equivalence between $\text{Tukey-extension-with-models}$ and $\text{Tukey-order-with-models}$ for linear orderings, thereby proving an extension of Buchanan-Thompson's theorem. Additionally, we provided an introduction to Tukey-order-with-models, estep-Maynard-theorem, velhan-theorem, szeptycki-theorem, and buchanan-thompson-theorem

This paper investigates the use of the pessimism principle in conjunction with Thompson sampling for optimizing dynamic treatment policies. By incorporating a pessimism principle into Thompson sampling, we can develop an efficient and balanced policy that achieves a constant regret O(T^rayleigh) without knowledge of the optimality gap, while remaining robust to changes in the underlying Markov decision process. Our results demonstrate that this integrated approach yields a more efficient balance of exploration and exploitation, resulting in improved performance compared to previous methods. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through simulation experiments in both a real-world context and through synthetic manipulation of its parameters. Furthermore, we highlight the potential of this method in addressing optimality gaps in practical applications. An open-source implementation of the algorithm is available at https://github.com/alex-lm/thompson_pessimism. In addition, all simulation results can be accessed at https://alex-lm.github.io/thompson_pessimism/index.html. In terms of future research, we identify the development of more efficient balancing strategies for exploration and exploitation, as well as the extension of the integrated approach to static treatment policies, as key areas for further investigation. Conversely, we confirm that our method is optimal with respect to the challenges of dynamic treatment policies and optimality gaps. Therefore, we propose alternative objectives that are easier to accomplish and can serve as a benchmark for the performance of balanced policies. Lastly, the integrated approach is made available as an open-source implementation at https://github.com/alex-lm/thompson_pessimism. All simulation results can also be accessed at https://alex-lm.github.io/thompson_pessimism/index.html. In conclusion, the main contribution of this paper is to demonstrate the efficacy of combining the pessimism principle with Thompson sampling, thereby optimizing dynamic treatment policies. However, further research is needed to develop efficient balancing strategies, explore alternative objectives, and implement the integrated approach in practical contexts. In the long term, we aim to extend the integrated approach to static treatment policies and continue to strive for improved performance. Given a commutative ring with units and a finitely generated module, we investigate the properties of subcategories of modules that have closed subcategories under submodules. We calculate the resolving Subcategory Projective Dimension and the faithful Modulo Projective Categories for a finitely generated module, and we demonstrate that these categories are invariant to changes in the ring's resolving subcategories of finitely generated modules. Additionally, we establish connections between these categories, the homotopy functors derived from them, and the algebraic K-groups of the ring. Specifically, for a connective K-monooidal ring with units, we prove that its K-theory is invariant to changes in its resolving subcategories of finitely generated modules. We also provide examples and counterexamples to illustrate these results. Furthermore, we show that these categories can be generalized to extend the work of Goto and Nishida on Gorenstein projective modules, as well as the work of Iyama and Reiten on minimal approximations, and the work of Christensen, Holm, and Strihan on complete intersection rings. We introduce a general approach to connect diverse quantum state arrangements according to their shared characteristics of non-locality and contextuality. This approach enables the comparison of preparations even when local realism fails to describe their individual behaviors, allowing us to extend it to composite systems and establish relationships among outer products of quantum states. We demonstrate that all preparations of qubits are linked via a series of conditional measurements, and this connection preserves their non-associativity. Additionally, our approach enables the identification of'seed states' - minimal sets of states sufficient to express all contexts in a particular scenario. This study provides a comprehensive understanding of non-locality and contextuality in quantum mechanics through the examination of preparation non-locality, its reductions, and their implications for understanding quantum reality. Relevant resources can be found at arxiv.org/abs/2106.11831. \bigskip

In models with multiple Hubbard bands, we analyze pairing interactions that result in exact ground states with a particular symmetry. This investigation applies to systems with two and three bands, and involves scanning the filling levels to identify the strongest pairing. With the constraint that each band is perfectly filled with a particular symmetry, the strongest pairing occurs at this filling point. This analysis shows that pairing interactions are more attractive when the filling levels are closer to half-filling, and that the magnitude of the strongest pairing grows with the difference between the filling levels and half-filling. Additionally, the pairing correlation functions exhibit a local maxima at the filling levels that are farthest from half-filling. This study also finds that the pairing interactions can be described as a result of a effective attraction between electrons near the Fermi level, and that the magnitude of the pairing depends on the difference between the filling levels and half-filling. This effective attraction is a result of the Asymmetry Potential, and the pairing can be viewed as a consequence of this potential. This discovery opens the door for the use of etapairing states in materials with multiple Hubbard bands, and suggests that the Asymmetry Potential could be used to control pairing in these systems. To evaluate the effectiveness of multiple clustering algorithms on species presence-absence data, we conducted a comprehensive study. This study involved eight popular clustering methods: k-means, hierarchical clustering, fuzzy c-means, ANTCLUSSE, AUTOCLASS, BAYESCLUST, CLUMP, and CUBIC. To assess the performance of each algorithm, we used measures such as the Silhouette coefficient, the Calinski-Harabasz index, cluster sizes, and the number of clusters. The evaluation process involved both simulated data and real-life species presence-absence data from the Mediterranean region. The results showed that there was little consensus across algorithms regarding the number of clusters or the arrangement of species within those clusters. However, algorithms like ANTCLUSSE and BAYESCLUST, which are capable of generating a probability distribution of species presences across clusters, offer valuable information that can inform decisions about the number of clusters and the effectiveness of each algorithm. Furthermore, the evaluation process highlighted the importance of validating results through biological analysis to ensure the accuracy and relevance of clusters. Ultimately, the choice of clustering algorithm should be guided by the specific research questions and data set under investigation. The analysis conducted in this study can be utilized as a resource for comparing and evaluating different clustering algorithms on species presence-absence data. The code and data used in this study are publicly available. The code can be downloaded from GitHub (https://github.com/maxenberger/Comparing_clustering_algorithms), and the data can be downloaded from Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5072/0010). We've developed a method to categorize numbers as either palindromic or unrepresentable in the context of their base-10 digital representations. Our approach involves finding the longest possible palindrome that can be expressed in base 10, resulting in a set of unrepresentable numbers with a density of approximately 0.415 percent. Conversely, the same set contains approximately 58.18 percent palindromes. Similar outcomes were found for other bases between 2 and 36, with the exception of bases 5 and 9, where the results exhibit different properties due to conflicts between unrepresentable and palindromic criteria. Our analysis sheds light on various numerical characteristics related to unrepresentable numbers and their relationship to palindromes. Furthermore, our study confirms that any number with a strong property of palindromicity in a particular base will exhibit the same characteristic in all higher-base systems. Our investigation into unrepresentable integers also led us to identify infinite sequences of unrepresentable numbers with distinct properties, including sequences derived from the formula $10^{2k+1}10^{2k}-1$, as well as those related to the product $10^{2k}10^{2k+1}-1$, both of which have been previously unknown. Our work has significant implications for the field of palindromic numbers, and our findings are consistent with existing research on unrepresentable integers, while simultaneously revealing novel and unexplored phenomena. Machine learning has made notable gains in generating written words by training on samples of handwriting, but these creations often fail to mimic the unique features of human writing, such as variations in style and damage, until it has seen a large volume of examples.  A new approach, called Bayesian Program Learning, changes this dynamic by using a statistical framework to write a program that can learn and adjust as it processes writing examples.  This method was successfully tested by generating human-like handwriting from minimal samples of size 50, and also by modeling different forms of human writing, such as mathematics and signatures.  A significant advantage of this method is that it can produce writing samples that are both legible and unique, unlike other methods that often produce similar errors in the same situation.  Additionally, it was found that BPL's unique ability to adjust its assumptions about what it is trying to learn helps it to make better use of the information it has collected, and also makes it possible to add new assumptions without worrying about fitting errors.  A major limitation of this method is that it assumes the writing examples are correct, and makes it possible for it to learn incorrect information if presented with conflicting examples.  A potential solution to this problem is to use BPL in conjunction with techniques that can tell the program when writing examples are incorrect, such as by using knowledge of the language itself.  A potential application of this method is to use it to learn and adjust the written rules of a programming language by training on samples of correct code. The pre-tension of straw tubes is a vital consideration in the design of particle detectors. The measurement of this pre-tension is essential but faces challenges in practical applications. This paper focuses on analyzing the mechanical properties of straw tubes that have been fabricated with a thickness of 0.1 mm and an outer diameter of 50 mm. These tubes were subjected to X-ray radiation in a vacuum environment. The research found that the pre-tension of the straw tubes can be quantified as 5.7 $\mu$m/strain, with the measurement taken immediately after activation. The pre-tension then gradually decreased over time due to relaxation, eventually stabilizing at 3.3 $\mu$m/strain after a period of 30 days. The pre-tension also exhibited sensitivity to the X-ray fluence, with the pre-tension increasing by 2 $\mu$m/strain for every 10$^{12}$ cm$^2$ exposure to X-rays. Additionally, the pre-tension was found to be unaffected by the pressure in the straw tubes. The measurement of the pre-tension in a straw tube's initial stage was found to be a reliable indicator of the tube's quality, with higher pre-tension values corresponding to better mechanical properties. Based on this information, a minimum pre-tension standard of 3.3 $\mu$m/strain has been established as the minimum requirement for straw tube pre-tension in the design of particle detectors. The pre-tension can be minimized by reducing the straw tube's length or by utilizing an insert to support the tube. The inserts were found to reduce the pre-tension by as much as 30%, with no significant variation observed based on the X-ray conditions. The research also identified that the pre-tension remains relatively unchanged when subjected to mechanical stress, with the property being primarily influenced by the pre-tension itself. Accurate identification of IoT devices is crucial, but faced with the vastness of IoT technology and constant updates, perfectly classifying every device may not always be possible. Consequently, a compromise is reached by adopting cost-aware classification methods that aim to minimize misclassification while considering the financial implications. However, these methods only provide probabilistic outcomes, making it difficult to quantify the likelihood of misclassification. This study introduces a novel framework known as Risk-Aware Multi-Armed Bandits (RAMB), which integrates reinforcement learning and online learning to mitigate misclassification. By utilizing feedback from active and passive IoT devices, the proposed framework optimizes the collection of informative data to calibrate the probability of misclassification, taking into account the cost and risk involved. Furthermore, the RAMB framework is refined to address unfair biases by integrating the ideas of equal opportunity and reverse discrimination to ensure that its decisions are fair and just. Through various experiments, the proposed framework demonstrates significant improvements over existing methods in reducing the risk of misclassification while maintaining computational efficiency. The knowledge gained from these experiments can be applied to other domains to evaluate the effectiveness of risk mitigation strategies. Previous studies have examined how well parametric aligners, like the ones used in HMMER, hold up against more established tools like GIZA++ when trained on larger datasets. However, these older models may not be as effective when working with current sequences, so it's worth investigating how well they can be applied to newer data. In our case, we trained a parametric aligner on a relatively small collection of sequences, but one that includes a broad range of recent proteins from the UniProt database. Our results reveal that this new model not only surpasses HMMER's aligner in terms of accuracy, but also outperforms it in a variety of benchmarks. To be specific, when evaluating the performance of all tools on various benchmarks, HMMER's aligner stood out with the highest overall score of 83.5, significantly more than the other tools. When comparing the new model against GIZA++ on actual protein sequence alignments, it achieved an accuracy of 81.1%, which is a notable 4.0 and 5.0 percentage points higher than HMMER's aligner and GIZA++ respectively. This research study focuses on understanding the geometric origin of the entropic stabilization of magnetic order in classical spin systems. Initially, we investigate the most efficient ways to pack hard spheres within a container and transfer this concept to a two-dimensional lattice structure represented by the square lattice. Our findings reveal the existence of two novel frustrated polar crystalline phases that emerge at a packing density above 0.5, and we demonstrate how these phases exhibit magnetic order due to entropic stabilization. Furthermore, we discuss how these phases can be distinguished from a genuine magnetic ordering phase through a spin-wave analysis and the concept of local disorder. Additionally, we explore the stability of these phases by introducing a slightly anisotropic interaction term and examining the generated magnetic order. Our findings are supported by an in-depth analysis of the phase diagram, which illustrates the paramagnetic phase boundary, magnetic transition temperature, and spontaneous magnetization. Notably, the entropic stabilization of magnetic order can serve as a model for understanding phase transitions in real spin systems, particularly in instances where the energy difference between energy minima is much larger than the exchange energy. Hence, our research provides a generalized understanding of geometric origin of magnetic order that can be applied to various spin systems. Quantum imaging has made it possible to scan sensitive objects without direct contact through the interaction-free technique. This approach leverages the non-exposure principle but requires costly high-precision equipment and advanced computational capabilities. Furthermore, calculations are typically carried out using sophisticated quantum tomography methods. In our research, we propose an innovative method called 'Optimal Coherent Probe' (OCP), which generates an optimal coherent probe by optimizing a measured probability distribution using machine learning algorithms. This approach integrates probe optimization and quantum tomography into a single, efficient process. In our experiments using two different scenarios, we demonstrated the effectiveness of OCP, reconstructing the original probability distribution with higher accuracy than standard methods. This technique has significant advantages, as it simplifies the equipment and reduces computational demands, making it a feasible solution for real-world applications. Additionally, a study of the robustness of our method showed that OCP remains effective even when the system's interaction and loss processes are unclear or imperfect. This is particularly evident in the second scenario, where we successfully implemented OCP with only a single unknown parameter. In conclusion, our novel method offers a groundbreaking approach to quantum tomography and interaction-free imaging, providing a promising pathway for practical quantum sensing applications. This work is recorded in a recent arXiv paper (arXiv:2102.12916). In this thesis, we will delve into the concept and efficiency of our OCP method, as well as its various robustness variations, exploring the potential of quantum tomography to revolutionize quantum sensing. In the process, we will examine robust quantum estimation theories and the practical challenges of implementing coherent probe techniques, ultimately contributing to the advancement of quantum technology. Our study delves into the dynamics of liquid foams comprised of polyhedra where, based on surface complexity, we introduce a concept of roughness factor to characterize the interface's behavior. Through computer simulations of liquid foam dynamics, we observed how the distribution of surface defects changes over time. Depending on the level of surface roughness, our results predict either Newtonian or non-Newtonian fluid behavior, consistent with previous studies. Furthermore, we found that the time-dependent changes in the foam's rheological properties are strongly influenced by the roughness factor, leading to an explanation of the observed deceleration in the foam's drainage dynamics. Lastly, we found that aging dynamics in liquid foams is largely unaffected by the surface complexity. Deep learning models, specifically Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have become the preferred choice for Alzheimers Disease (AD) diagnosis in Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) patients. Deep learning models, however, have a significant drawback: they are computationally expensive and demanding in terms of memory. To overcome these limitations and improve the accuracy of MCI-AD diagnosis, we present an ensemble of lightweight CNNs based on the MobileNetV2 model, trained on the Open Access Series of Events related to Alzheimer's (OASIS). The proposed ensemble, dubbed Multi-Scale MobileNetV2 (MS-MV2), leverages ensemble learning to combine the predictions of seven modified CNNs with varying architecture and image size configurations. By utilizing a feature-level ensemble, MS-MV2 achieves a Werbanck score of 0.793 ± 0.03 for AD diagnosis, surpassing the performance of mobileNetV2 by at least 0.03 and comparable to or outperforming other state-of-the-art models, including Ensemble Learning, ResNet-18, and MobileNetV2, while reducing computational and memory costs by at least 5.96 times. The proposed approach offers improved accuracy, reduced complexity, and better generalizability, making it a viable solution for class imbalance problems like MCI-AD diagnosis. internal dynamics. This viewpoint provides a unified explanation for why 
work and heat are equivalent according to the first law of thermodynamics. 
Additionally, it offers a unified explanation for why heat and work are 
not universally equivalent according to the second law of thermodynamics.

distinct from work performed by the system. These findings are

The objective is to understand how a two-level system interacting with a continuous-wave photon field becomes detuned from its trapped state. The period over which this detuning process takes place is determined by the participation ratio, which shows an abrupt change at the detrapping angle. The probability distribution undergoes a capillary change and becomes an ellipse near the detrapping angle. The detuning time is shown to be equivalent to the period of capillary modes. This study introduces a modified Einstein-Boltzmann code named EBEB, which simulates how a viscous universe changes over time. After confirming that the model's viscosity coefficient is equivalent to $\sim 3\cdot 10^{-2}$ times the universal Hubble rate, we observed that the late-time acceleration of the universe is explained by the viscosity effect, which also results in a lower value for the density parameter: $\Omega_m \approx 0.22$ (at 95% confidence). Furthermore, our simulation reveals that the universe's scale factor follows a power-law growth, and the model's viscosity coefficient also influences the spectral index and tensor-scalar ratio. While our findings show that the viscosity model can account for late-time acceleration and other key cosmological parameters, the model still faces challenges in explaining the present-day matter dominance. Extending our simulation to higher orders of $k$ may be necessary to address this issue. Additionally, our study does not rule out the possibility that the viscosity model is only one part of a more comprehensive explanation for cosmological observations. Lastly, our analysis suggests that the viscosity model does not provide an adequate explanation for the observed inhomogeneities in the cosmic microwave background. Expanding our simulation to include higher-order perturbations may be necessary to address this limitation. In the future, our EBEB code could be used to investigate the viability of the viscosity model by simulating observations with next-generation experiments. The study explores the uniqueness and well-posedness of the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations in 2-D dimensions. Unlike 3-D dimensions, where well-posedness is generally established, we find that in 2-D dimensions, the Cauchy problem is generally ill-defined; however, it becomes well-defined after applying certain weak conditions on the velocity field. Notably, our analysis reveals that the key factor determining well-posedness is not the smoothness of the initial data but rather the boundedness of its Fourier coefficients. Specifically, we prove that if the Fourier coefficients of the velocity field are bounded, the Cauchy problem becomes formally well-defined and, intriguingly, we find that it possesses a unique weak solution. Furthermore, for low-regularity data, we establish the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem through a novel approach involving energy estimates and the construction of a weak solution. Additionally, our results include proving the almost everywhere uniqueness of the Cauchy problem for any low-regularity data and, in higher regularity cases, obtaining an energy estimate that diverges linearly with the time step. Interestingly, our analysis also sheds light on the ill-posedness of the Cauchy problem for low-regularity data by showing the existence of an infinite number of distinct solutions. Notably, our findings also extend to other problems, including the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations and the Vlasov equations under certain conditions. Ultimately, our work provides insight into the ill-posedness of the Cauchy problem in lower dimensions and raises questions for further investigation. Conversely, in 3-D dimensions, we confirm the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem for very irregular data and, in the presence of certain growth conditions, we find that it becomes almost everywhere unique. Notably, our analysis also extends to the compressible Euler equations, where we find that well-posedness is generally established in low dimensions but becomes ill-defined in high dimensions with certain growth conditions. Ultimately, our findings provide insight into the well-posedness of various PDEs under different conditions. Deep learning predictive models are commonly applied in industry, but their limitations in predicting outcomes beyond their training scope remain unquantified. We address this gap through a Bayesian approach, combining posterior predictive checks and functional analytics to measure the uncertainty of a classifier's predictions. This method is particularly useful for assessing the likelihood of misclassifications and predicting the distribution of unknown classes. To facilitate seamless integration with existing models, we have developed a open-source Python library, called scikit-learning-bayes, which builds upon the popular scikit-learn framework. The benefits of this approach are illustrated through a Bayesian neural network applied to a simple, real-world classification problem. Additionally, we outline potential avenues for further research in quantifying the limitations of predictive models. A comprehensive guide is available online for readers who wish to apply this method to their own problems. We hope this work sparks interest in quantifying the limitations of predictive models and encouraging research in uncertainty quantification. We appraise the impact of $J/\psi$ decay on invisible mass limits imposed by dark matter-nucleon interactions. To achieve this, we utilize a twin approach, creating dual sets of particle physics models, where in one set, a dark matter particle decays into invisible particles that facilitate dark matter-nucleon interactions, while in the other set, this dark matter particle remains stable with no decay products. Our work involves extensive lattice calculations to determine the $J/\psi$ decay rate into these invisible particles and an analysis of LHC constraints on dark matter, enabling us to establish a relationship between the two sets of models such that their respective limits on dark matter-nucleon interactions are equivalent. As a result, our work allows us to derive a limit on dark matter-nucleon interactions that is weakened by at most a factor of 3 when considering the effect of $J/\psi$ decays, rather than the previously estimated factor of 100. Our limits on dark matter-nucleon interactions are more stringent than those derived from direct detection experiments operating underground at similar latitudes to Chicago, Illinois. Our work also confirms that even if the dark matter particle is not heavily decayed into invisible particles, its scattering cross section can still be limited, as is observed in scenarios where it primarily interacts with quarks. In such cases, our limits on dark matter-nucleon interactions are more stringent than those derived from lattice QCD calculations of nuclear matrix elements, leading to more stringent limits on dark matter masses up to 1 TeV. Our work culminates in the presentation of comprehensive model-independent limits on dark matter-nucleon interactions applicable to a broad range of theoretical models, including those where dark matter primarily interacts with quarks or leptons, by incorporating data from LHC dark matter searches, direct detection experiments, and considerations of solar and astrophysical dark matter emissions. Human movement in daily life is full of varied actions and movements performed by numerous individuals. A key aspect of Inverse Graphics is utilizing video data to create highly realistic character animations while minimizing computational complexity. By leveraging key movements and their associated linkages, such as joint connections, a minimal set of representative movements can be pinpointed, allowing the generation of highly realistic animations through interpolation. This approach can effectively capture and represent complex movements and also serves as a foundation for future research in computer graphics, human movement, and perception. Furthermore, it has the potential to reduce the need for extensive movement data in Inverse Graphics, thus making it more efficient. This has also enabled researchers to prove a broader range of positive operator estimation methods, known as completely positive operator estimation, in the same dimension. A new, more general framework for positive operator estimation is introduced here, applicable in any number of dimensions. This framework subsumes completely positive operator estimation and offers a more accurate description of positive operator estimation, particularly relevant for quantum key distribution scenarios. Our research verifies the PPT conjecture's influence on this more comprehensive framework. Furthermore, a new example illustrates that not all positive operator estimations can be classified as completely positive operator estimations. This research provides a clearer understanding of the relationship between positivity structures in operator algebra and quantum information theory applications. It also highlights the diversity of positivity structures by showing that a particular method does not yield positivity structures in positive operator estimation. This method is distinct from those associated with completely positive operator estimation and strongly positive ones. This research also raises questions about the aching problem of characterizing positive operator estimations and positivity structures in general. This is closely related to another unsolved issue, the Pelc-Isert conjecture, and may have implications for the study of local measurement models. This conjecture claims that any local measurement model can be transformed into a entanglement-based quantum computation model with a corresponding positivity structure. This entanglement-based model is known to be associated with strongly positive structures, while local measurement models are thought to be linked with positive operator estimations, according to some speculation. The transport of neural signals and cellular components relies heavily on the intricate network of microtubules that make up the cytoskeleton within neurons. The efficient movement of these materials, essential for neuronal function, is influenced by the dynamic properties of microtubules. We have developed a computer simulation model that incorporates the latest understanding of microtubule dynamics, cross-linking between microtubules, and traffic patterns in order to examine their combined effect on material transport. By adjusting variables such as cross-linking strengths and microtubule properties along the length of the neuron, our model demonstrates various traffic patterns, some of which are previously undocumented. Furthermore, our results align with current research findings and also provide new insights that can guide future experiments. Additionally, our model can be modified to analyze combinations of astero-nematode and vertebrate neuronal structures, making it a versatile tool for understanding material transport in various neuronal systems. All code is openly accessible on GitHub, enabling users to modify and advance the model to meet their specific needs. Our goal is to contribute to the growing field of molecular transport by providing a reusable, open-source research tool. As a result, researchers can utilize and extend our work to analyze material transport in different neuronal systems, fostering a greater understanding of the underlying cellular processes. Moreover, our study emphasizes the significance of considering the dynamic behavior of microtubules in order to comprehend the transport of cellular materials observed in neurons. By using open-source programming, our goal is to promote model innovation, encourage simulation-based research, and ultimately contribute to the development of more accurate models that can help bridge the gap between computational studies and experimental findings. Conversely, our approach can assist in translating experimental discoveries into actionable model changes that can be implemented in existing models to reflect current knowledge and understand the inherent dynamics of cellular transport mechanisms. In essence, we aim to promote an open and interactive research environment where theoretical and experimental research can converge and advance cellular knowledge through continuous learning and collaboration. In this spirit, we welcome suggestions and proposals for enhancing our model, and encourage researchers to utilize and extend our work by evaluating its performance with their own set of parameters and scenarios. In the long run, our goal is to foster a research environment where research methods and findings are freely accessible and open to discussion, driving collective progress and advancing our understanding of cellular transport mechanisms. Banking graph learning has gained significant traction in recent years, with researchers using various methods to prevent banking fraud. Many existing models, however, suffer from limitations in generating genuine banking graphs, which hinder their overall performance. To address this issue, we introduce the Steiner Boltzmann Graph (SBG) model, a novel approach for creating valid banking graphs through a dynamic equilibrium process. The SBG model builds on top of the Steiner Point Process, incorporating a Gaussian process to optimize an objective function, and uses thresholding techniques to obtain the final graph. We optimize the object of function by deriving the likelihood ratio, and further refine it by applying the Whittle estimate, a technique commonly used in point process modeling. The SBG model is robust and can be effective, along with our empirical analysis, which compares it to other popular methods. The study is conducted using real-world data from various Asian countries, and our results show that the SBG model outperforms the alternative approaches in several key metrics, such as overall accuracy, true positive rate, and true negative rate. The implementation of the SBG model is detailed in an open-source repository, oriented towards graph learning, for the benefit of researchers and practitioners. A series of comprehensive experiments, which include the investigation of the model's hyperparameters, the construction of a 1-nearest neighbor classifier, and the analysis of the learning curves, demonstrate the efficacy of the SBG model, which shows promising potential for the prevention of banking fraud, specifically in authorized transactions. The research validates the superiority of the SBG model, and our findings suggest that this approach offers a superior alternative to the state-of-the-art methods in the field. We investigate the properties of Tversky models, which constitute a family of symmetric binary similarity measures that diverge from traditional likelihood ratios. Our analysis focuses on the specific case where the ratio is fractional and the denominators exhibit a linear combination of two parameters. This particular case yields a family of parameterized metric spaces, of which we determine the optimal and worst-case scenarios under various distance definitions. Moreover, we establish a direct relationship between these optimal and worst-case values, which facilitates the calculation of respective metric scales. To validate our findings, we also analyze Tversky models in the context of stochastic processes and confirm that our results are consistent with existing theoretical outcomes. Ultimately, our work is illustrated through a real-world application to best worst analysis in profit management. This approach is subsequently expanded to address weighted decisions involving best worst ratios in a companion paper. To enhance the robustness of self-training algorithms for parsing tasks, we introduce Deep Contextualized Self-training (DCST), an enhanced version of Self Training (ST). DCST addresses two key limitations of traditional self-training: 1) the selection of confident instances and 2) the handling of unlabelled data. If dark matter interacts with nuclei in a manner similar to neutrinos, it may lead to detectable ionization effects taking place in large-volume dark matter experiments. We have re-evaluated the analysis methods used in such experiments and created more precise formulas for calculating ionization effects, including effects due to multiple interactions with the same nucleus. We compared these new analysis methods with existing approaches and found that they can have a significant impact on sensitivity to spin-dependent interactions, particularly when interacting with heavier nuclei. We applied these new analysis methods to various experimental configurations and found that future experiments with large volumes and low fields may be able to detect neutrino-like interactions with cross sections as low as $10^{-23}$ (CMSPC) or $10^{-24}$ (ZEPLIN-II) GeV$^{-2}$. If future nuclear experiments are able to achieve a 10-fold reduction in this limit, it may enable direct detection of neutrinos, although this would require significant advancements in detector technology. We also considered alternative analyses using machine learning and found that future experiments with large volumes and low fields may be able to detect neutrino-like interactions with cross sections as low as $10^{-24}$ (CMSPC) or $10^{-25}$ (ZEPLIN-II) GeV$^{-2}$. Finally, we explored the potential for ionization effects to reveal properties of dark matter such as its mass and direction of motion. Although these goals are unlikely to be achieved with current or near-term experiments, future experiments with large volumes and low fields may be able to test a mass range extending up to 100 GeV. Additionally, future experiments with large lengths and orientations oriented perpendicular to the galactic plane may be able to test a mass range extending up to 1 TeV. Finally, future experiments with large masses and orientations close to the galactic plane may be able to test a mass range extending up to 10 TeV. Ultimately, the ability to achieve these goals will depend on a detailed analysis of experimental limitations imposed by analysis thresholds and confusion with dark matter interactions. Such an analysis is currently underway. ECG signal analysis is significant for identifying cardiovascular disorders. However, the widespread presence of noise in ECG signals hinders accurate frequency domain analysis. Traditionally, time domain-based methods were found to be ineffective in extracting the inter-beat intervals and ECG signal components with high precision. To counter this issue, we present a novel deep learning-based approach that utilizes the temporal difference learning technique for extracting the inter-beat intervals and ECG signal temporal and spectral characteristics. The proposed approach includes two neural network segments: one is responsible for extracting the ECG signal characteristics and the other, utilizing the difference between sample data and predicted inter-beat intervals, is involved in predicting the inter-beat intervals. The effectiveness of the proposed approach was evaluated using the standard Physionet ECG-2000 dataset, pre-processed with a noise reduction filter, and a comparison was drawn between our method and established techniques. The evaluation revealed that our proposed approach, combined with a noise-reduced ECG signal, extracted the inter-beat intervals with a mean absolute error of 13.16 ms and achieved high correlation coefficients for the ECG signal temporal (0.97) and spectral (0.16) characteristics, respectively. The proposed approach demonstrated a substantial improvement over established methods, specifically outperforming the CNN+LSTM technique by 0.01, 0.06, and 0.03 in mean absolute error for inter-beat intervals, temporal, and spectral characteristics, respectively. Moreover, compared to time domain-based methods, our approach showed better results, with a mean absolute error of 13.16 ms, compared to 15.38 ms for the popular RR autocorrelation-based method. The significant advancement gained by our proposed approach validates the potential of deep learning-based methods in extracting the inter-beat intervals and ECG signal characteristics with high precision, making it an effective technique for various ECG signal-based applications. By utilizing a skull structure image and a subject's identity, HUMBI can synthesize a high-resolution 3D human head with accurate texture and underlying skull structure for an authentic appearance. Recent advances in multilingual pretraining have led to improved performance in zero-shot sentiment classification across various languages, largely driven by English data, despite the models being trained on single languages. This indicates a lack of efficient multilingual model training methods. Our proposed model, MLLP (Multilingual Long-Short Term Memory Partition), is an innovative approach to multilingual sentiment classification that handles diverse languages in a single model. By partitioning existing multilingual models, MLLP is designed to process input sentences from different languages in sequential order. Through thorough evaluation on seven languages across three datasets, MLLP demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot sentiment classification, requiring minimal model modifications. Furthermore, our framework is versatile and can be easily adapted to other tasks, such as natural language inference and task-specific fine-tuning. Our source code and pre-trained models are available for public use at the provided link.

In video prediction, especially for long-term outcomes, accurate information on the camera's movement is crucial. We have enhanced BasicVSR++ with an explicit motion estimation module which uses a lightweight network to estimate camera motion by relying on object boundaries found in the video. This new module is highly efficient, requiring only a sixth of the original's resources, and we found that BasicVSR++ outperforms SRN and SRSD by a significant margin on NTU-RGB+D, while BasicVSR++ performs better than BasicVSR on NTU-RGB+D and CMU MoCap, and on NTU-RGB+D it performs on par with SRVSR*. Moreover, BasicVSR++ improved NTU-RGB+D results significantly, reaching a record-breaking accuracy, and it substantially enhanced SRVSR*'s performance without any parameters added, resulting in a new benchmark for NTU-RGB+D. The source code can be found at: https://github.com/zhangdetao/BasicVSR++.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, training a single dynamics model can lead to mode collapse, causing the model to fail when predicting states outside its experienced range. Our novel approach, Multi-Mode Learning of Dynamics (MOLD), overcomes this limitation by encouraging a dynamics model to learn multiple individual modes of state transition dynamics, thereby eliminating the need to weigh prior knowledge of state visitation frequencies. MOLD maximizes the coverage of unique modes in a multi-task reinforcement learning setting by introducing an exploratory reward that incentivizes visiting novel states, thereby increasing the diversity of experiences. Theoretical justifications for reward optimization are provided, and empirical results in complex 2D and 3D environments demonstrate MOLD's effectiveness in discovering multiple individual modes of transition dynamics. Furthermore, our model can be integrated with existing reinforcement learning algorithms without additional computational costs. Hurricanes that make landfall in areas like Florida can cause significant damage to power grids, leading to prolonged outages. Forecasting the impact of future hurricanes on power grids requires analyzing past hurricane landfalls to identify areas with repeated outages. This involves using geospatial analysis to evaluate potential landfall sites, which are determined by a Monte Carlo simulation that incorporates historical hurricane data into a DEM terrain model. Once landfall sites are identified, they are linked to specific counties, allowing for a comparison of counties with repeated outages and those that experienced hurricane landfalls but did not experience power outages. This process is repeated annually to assess the risk posed by the upcoming hurricane season. The method for forecasting hurricane impacts is demonstrated through a case study of the 2021 hurricane season in Central Florida, where it was used to identify areas with repeated outages, prioritize critical systems, and estimate the likelihood of system restoration deadlines being met. The findings indicate that nearly 27% of counties in Central Florida experienced hurricane landfalls that lasted over 5 days, with nearly 20% of those counties experiencing outages for the first time, and just under 55% of those counties experiencing repeated outages having nearly all of their customers restored within 30 days. The method presented can be used to develop a hurricane impact cost model that will help distribution system planners and restoration managers prioritize their resources during restoration activities and enhance the communication of hurricane impact and cost to stakeholders. Future high-luminosity colliders will significantly contribute to validating particle physics models with multiple scalar sectors, particularly through the production of doubly charged scalars. The influence of finite temperature on the zero-energy peak in tunneling spectra from InAs/Al2O3/Al nanowires is examined. Initially, the peak arises due to gapless modes associated with non-Majorana processes, but as temperature increases, this characteristic fades while the nanowire remains in a topologically non-trivial state. Concurrently, the fuse-like behavior, evidenced by irregular conductance versus voltage plots, persists and the associated tunneling spectra develop a symmetric pair of peaks centered on the Fermi energy. The conversion of the single peak to a pair reflects the emergence of Majorana modes as the nanowire's boundary becomes more distinct through thermal effects. The variation in spectral features is found to be resilient to changes in nanowire quality. The research suggests that thermal influence can facilitate the detection of all-Majorana processes in nanowire devices. Moreover, the study highlights the significance of distinguishing between Majorana and non-Majorana processes in tunneling spectra to accurately understand nanowire devices utilizing zero-energy peaks. The advancements made in tunneling spectroscopy's resolution and signal extraction strategies have contributed to this finding. Specifically, the use of smaller tunneling barriers and faster modulation rates have proven to be valuable. The same techniques that enabled the analysis of tunneling spectra also allowed the investigation of the nanowire's threshold voltage and its variation with the length of the nanowire's semi-conducting channel. The accuracy of nanowire length measurements has been improved as a result, achieving an error margin of about 5 nanometers. The research demonstrates the capability of combining fast and slow tunneling modulation methods to facilitate precise length assessments of nanowires through tunneling current measurements. The improved resolution and signal extraction strategies have also facilitated the discovery of new thermal effects on tunneling spectra and the concurrent behavior of Majorana modes, paving the way for the integration of nanowire devices with existing scientific knowledge of quantum physics. The THH construction is adapted to apply to general bicategories, using a process that incorporates both pushout and coequalizer operations. Alongside THH, the paper introduces a relative version, relative THH ($RHH$), which shares similar properties. The work further establishes that $\widehat{RHH}$ is capable of detecting groupoid equivalences within this context. The theorems proposed in this paper are anticipated to have further applications and interpretations within the context of bicategorical spectra and axiomatic homotopy theory. This research introduces the Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE), a novel approach that simultaneously learns a data compression routine and an inverse operation for decompressing compressed data. Furthermore, BCAE's dual capabilities enable an innovative method of image augmentation by utilizing the compressed output as a new representation of the input, thereby expanding the data set. Through an internal transformation, BCAE can regenerate the original from this new representation, thereby reversing the compression. Experimental results on multiple image datasets indicate that BCAE's dual functions surpass current methods in data compression and image processing tasks.
