This study introduces a new category of objects, referred to as convex geometric hypergraphs. Extending the concept of the Johnson-Lindström-Suzuki theorem, we derive formulas for determining the maximum possible numbers of saturation for specific convex geometric n-hypergraphs, where n represents the rank of these hypergraphs. Our findings are illustrated through various examples, including 3-hypergraphs, which we visually represent using a particular convex shape. Additionally, we pose several unanswered research questions. Ultimately, our work aims to contribute to the broader field of extremal combinatorics. 

Our methodology involves translating the saturation problem of convex geometric n-hypergraphs into a discrete version of a classic problem from classical geometry, specifically the kissing number problem. This translation was made possible by establishing an exact equivalence between the two concepts. This equivalence allows us to apply established techniques from combinatorial geometry to study saturation problems in combinatorial geometry. 

One particularly interesting finding is that the saturation numbers of convex geometric 3-hypergraphs can be directly related to the number of "kissings" for certain three-dimensional convex shapes. This relationship inspired us to investigate and prove new limits on the maximum possible numbers of "kissings" for specific convex shapes in three dimensions. This limit can also be applied inversely to determine the maximum possible numbers of saturation for 3-hypergraphs, given certain constraints on their shape.

In this research, we explore the relationship between throughput and age of information (AoI) in a single user, bufferless wireless communication system. We establish that generating age of information at a rate less than or equal to its throughput threshold ensures non-negativity of AoI. We derive the maximum AoI as a function of throughput in both Gaussian and Bernoulli interference scenarios. Additionally, we examine how tightly AoI can be bounded in relation to throughput, proving a lower bound using sensor scheduling strategies, and demonstrate the effectiveness of a throughput-constrained scheduling scheme that achieves this lower bound with optimal efficiency. We also extend our findings to multi-user environments, where we analyze the age of information in interference channels under throughputs that are individually optimized or collectively constrained. These investigations provide insights into the trade-offs between age of information and throughput in wireless communication systems. Our results show that increasing throughput may actually decrease age of information, and identify the age of information lower bound in interference-free Gaussian channels as a function of throughput in both interference and non-interference scenarios. To validate our theoretical findings, we analyze the effectiveness of these scheduling strategies in simulation studies. Our research contributes to existing knowledge on age of information theory and provides actionable guidance for designing wireless communication systems that meet specific requirements for throughputs and age of information. Our findings are of practical interest to designers, and offer a framework for general application to single user and multi-user systems where throughputs and ages of information are concerned. This study examines helicity's preservation in Navier--Stokes equations and the Euler equations within particular function space frameworks. We establish criteria for weak solutions of the Navier--Stokes equations in a specific space and derive a more general result applicable to any convex domain. Our investigation of the Euler equations reveals that helicity's conservation occurs in spaces with limited $L_p$ exponent, but fails in general $L_p$ spaces for $p < \infty$. Nevertheless, we prove that helicity's conservation holds for smooth solutions of the Euler equations in any space with limited $L_p$ exponent. To achieve this, we create a novel extension of a result by Chaffee and Russell, which might be of independent interest, and which originally concerned the preservation of minimum norms in certain operator equations. Our results are further applied to determine the long-term behavior of solutions to the Euler equations, which were previously unknown. In particular, we observe that the long-term behavior of solutions to the Euler equations is completely characterized by the mapping of those solutions whose helicity remains constant. Our work is further complemented by examples that verify our findings and demonstrate the inability to extend our results to other function space frameworks. The ability to exploit the properties of helicity's conservation, which is unique to three-dimensional fluids, plays a crucial role in all of our investigations. As such, we first establish a result that links the properties of helicity with the properties of the vorticity in any dimension, which in turn allows us to confirm that the properties of helicity are the characteristics of a three-dimensional vectorfield. Our work culminates in the exploration of the long-term behavior of solutions to the Euler equations in the $L_\infty + L_2$ Hilbert space, which represents a significant extension of previous work by Caffarelli and Garraffo. In the process of doing so, we prove that the long-term behavior of solutions to the Euler equations in the $L_\infty + L_2$ Hilbert space is completely characterized by the mapping of those solutions whose helicity remains constant. Our work is further applied to determine the long-term behavior of solutions to the Euler equations in the $L_\infty + L_1$ Hilbert space, which in turn uses methods first introduced by Caffarelli and Garraffo. These expressions have been compared with existing large-aspect-ratio expansions of Green's integral formula solutions. By matching the orders of magnitude, the comparisons have validated the accuracy of Geometrical Optics for narrow beam scenarios within the far zone and demonstrated the relevance of correcting terms, which are significant for narrow beams but diminish in wider beams. The analyses also revealed the corrections can serve as effective diffraction mitigants, alleviating the limitations of Geometrical Optics by refining its predictions. The new asymptotics has been used to derive improved approximations for scattering amplitudes and the diffracted energy flux, all expressed in dimensionless forms, which are applicable to narrow beams in the far zone and at the boundary of the Fresnel zone. The results have been further generalized to obtain high-frequency approximations for planar wave diffraction, which has been compared with existing results, including Thomas Young's planar wave diffraction hypothesis. The new asymptotics has also been used to investigate the space-time structure of diffraction, which has revealed the existence of diffracted wavefront patterns, narrow in the broad dimension and broad in the narrow dimension, which emerge at the boundary of the Fresnel zone and stem from the corrections. The new diffraction asymptotics has been used to derive improved approximations for time-domain diffraction, which has been used to explain diffraction-induced diffractions, diffracted-induced scattering, and the diffraction-induced delay. The results have been further generalized to obtain diffraction-time expansions. The analyses demonstrate the efficacy of Geometrical Optics in narrow beams but highlight the importance of including correcting terms to achieve accuracy in narrow beams and the emergence of diffracted wave patterns in the time-domain. The diffraction-time expansions have also revealed the existence of diffraction patterns in the broad dimension of wide beams, which were previously unknown. The new diffraction asymptotics has been used to obtain diffraction-based estimates of the diffracted energy flux and the relative importance of Geometrical Optics and correcting terms in narrow and wide beams. The results have been further generalized to obtain diffraction-based estimates of planar wave diffraction, which has been used to explain spatial, temporal, and phase space distributions of narrow planar waves, which were not known before. These systems, which include binaries such as white dwarf and neutron stars in high-mass binaries, emit signals at frequencies within Earth-based gravitational-wave detector's range. Two types of simulations, based on different models, are compared: one that uses an simplified equation to calculate eccentricity and another that utilizes detailed orbital data to predict eccentricity evolution. The study discovers that the two methods disagree on the final eccentricities of compact binaries that remain undetected by current gravitational-wave detectors but could be detectable in future instruments. However, the more accurate simulation predicts a greater range of these binary systems than the less accurate simulation. The study further examines the characteristics of these binary systems, which include a wider range of eccentricities and lower initial eccentricities than previously estimated, using the more accurate simulation. These unsourced binary systems are primarily found at lower orbital frequencies and masses and generally require a minimum initial eccentricity of around 0.87 to be detectable by LISA or a similar gravitational-wave detector. The study predicts that a future gravitational-wave detector, with an improved sensitivity, will detect a greater number of these binary systems, which could amount to a few hundred per year, with a concentration of up to twenty cases per year of binaries with a primary component of 1.4 solar masses. Time-sensitive event identification in evolving networks is known as dynamic event detection, and it's critical in various areas but faces difficulties due to non-linear changes in the graph. Current methods using deep learning for event detection with graph-structured data often assume a fixed graph topology, which is impractical. Our research introduces DyGED, a model that accommodates changing graphs, temporo-spatial relationships, and node attributes to identify events. Through testing on multiple datasets, we demonstrate that DyGED surpasses existing methods by accurately recognizing events and effectively handling dynamic graphs. The source code for DyGED can be found at https://github.com/dynagened/DyGED.

The Guderley problem is a standard test case for evaluating the accuracy of hydrodynamic simulations. It consists of a spherical shockwave interacting with a sudden change in pressure at the origin. Analyzing this phenomenon provides insights into plasma dynamics and turbulence, and is particularly useful for validating computational techniques. In this study, we present a method to accurately obtain analytical solutions to the Guderley problem under various conditions, and use these results to validate a recently developed hydrodynamic simulation code. Our solutions cover a wide range of scenarios, including different shock strengths and variations in sound speed and adiabatic index. We also derive solutions for when there is a secondary shock or rarefaction wave present, and demonstrate that the solutions can be obtained using a Stewartson--Thomson-type technique. Comparing simulated results with the theoretical solutions yields very low relative errors of much less than one percent for pressures, densities, and velocity coefficients, and shows excellent agreement in plotting simulated data against these solutions. This level of accuracy is particularly useful in evaluating and validating hydrodynamic simulations, and paves the way for applying the theoretical solutions to more complex and nonlinear phenomena. Furthermore, our study demonstrates that the hydrodynamic simulation code is highly accurate, and reveals that a previously proposed criterion for when a shock becomes unstable due to turbulence no longer applies once there are large radial velocity fluctuations.  Additionally, our code has efficiently calculated solutions for very large shock strengths and high variations in sound speed and adiabatic index without experiencing a significant slowdown. A Python version of the hydrodynamic simulation code used in this study is available at https://github.com/Chandra-Simulations/ChandraHydro, and the theoretical solutions have been implemented in the public domain AGNcode version 6.4 and 7.0 at https://github.com/Chandra-Simulations/AGNcode. In the field of colorectal adenoma diagnosis and grading, deep neural networks have demonstrated exceptional performance in recent years. However, most of these models were developed using large datasets of full-colored Whole Slide Images (WSIs), which are not always readily available and can be expensive to obtain. To build an efficient and effective adenoma classification and grading system, we propose a novel approach that utilizes low-color WSIs during training. Our model integrates a multi-task learning framework with a novel attention technique, allowing it to concentrate on the most relevant information within each WSI. After collecting and preprocessing 9500 labeled colorectal adenoma slides in 281x343 pixels format with three colors, we conducted experiments using deep neural networks with and without our attention mechanism on the complete dataset of 9500 slides. Our results also show that this approach allows us to achieve high accuracy on classification and grading tasks of large colorectal adenomas with a single-layer attention mechanism, even when only 40% of the slides are used for training, while maintaining good performance on other tasks. Our paper also demonstrates the effectiveness of using low-color WSIs for building adenoma classification and grading systems with deep neural networks, which can significantly reduce the required training data by 75%. Our approach resulted in a reduced number of circuit evaluations, which is ideal since circuit measurements can be expensive due to qubit collapse. To test our method, we applied it to the binary linear problem and achieved better results compared to a standard QAOA approach. quantum fluctuations can single-handedly establish stripe order. This finding 
is revealed through a comprehensive examination of the two-dimensional Hubbard model 
using the cluster multipole approach and exact diagonalization on small square 
clusters. By analyzing the many-body spectrum, dynamic spin and charge structure

In lumbar vertebrae identification, common methods struggle with low accuracy and time-consuming manual verification. For verification, doctors must carefully check images and make corrections, but since these methods are often incorrect, it's a laborious and time-consuming process. To address this issue, researchers introduced a new, more efficient approach to lumbar vertebrae identification, both accurate and quick. This innovative method combines deep learning techniques with a unique vertebrae identification system, allowing it to distinguish vertebrae quickly and reliably. To improve vertebrae center detection and accuracy, researchers used a new, advanced calculation method called "oriented inscribed rectangle min-area-based matching," which consistently produced high results. In extensive testing on public datasets, this novel method consistently outperformed other approaches, achieving vertebrae identification rates of over 90%, significantly surpassing other methods. Notably, this new method also greatly reduced verification times, decreasing the required corrections by 90%, making it significantly more efficient than existing solutions. To facilitate further research, researchers made the source code publicly available. This new, more effective solution provides a strong foundation for accurate and efficient lumbar vertebrae identification, marking an important improvement in state-of-the-art technology. \textit{Keywords: lumbar vertebrae identification, deep learning, oriented inscribed rectangle min-area-based matching, vertebrae center identification, verification corrections.}

An algebraic and topological examination of Markovian models, along with the construction of a Markovian network's topological representation, is presented. This study focuses on calculating the asymptotic averages and correlation integrals of Markovian dynamics. To achieve this, it reveals how these quantities are derived from the Markovian models' algebraic and topological properties. In particular, the study shows that the Markovian models can be represented by a directed graph, known as the Markovian network, which facilitates the analysis of Markovian dynamics. Various examples illustrate the application of the proposed methods to both small and large-scale Markovian networks. Moreover, the study introduces INTREP for computing correlation integrals and means for evaluating the frequency of occurrence of states in Markovian dynamics. Consequently, these results have important implications for the theoretical understanding and practical modeling of complex Markovian systems, especially those characterized by a large number of states. The study demonstrates the efficacy of using topological and algebraic structures in computing asymptotic averages and correlation integrals, which can be computed even for massive Markovian networks. The computational algorithms presented in the study have been implemented in a software package called INTREP, which is documented in the appendix, thereby facilitating the analysis of complex Markovian systems. Ultimately, the study aims to empower researchers to model, study, and simulate high-dimensional Markovian systems characterized by complex dynamics, such as the emergence of phase transitions, critical phenomena, and intricate patterns. The application of the study's findings extends to any high-dimensional Markovian system, as exemplified by these examples. Ultimately, this allows us to compare the $I$-functions for all smooth divisors in a given class, and we compute the $I$-function for several specific divisors in detail. Additionally, we provide a formula for the weighted degree of a smooth divisor based on its $I$-function. This article compares two popular data frame libraries, pandas from Python, and data frames from C#, in terms of functionality, with a focus on key features. It originates from a speaker's notes during a webinar hosted by Speakeasy, where the author demonstrated the equivalence of using data frames in C# with pandas in Python. Further details can be found at the provided speaker link. Both programming languages, through their respective libraries, offer data frames as a fundamental tool for data analysis, enabling users to work with structured data sets, even in memory, even when containing large numbers. As a result, this comparison aims to showcase the equivalence of performing certain operations using pandas in Python, and data frames from C#, and to highlight any discrepancies in functionality. Ultimately, this comparison aims to guide analysts who are familiar with one of these programming languages, especially Python, to quickly learn how to utilize the other, by showcasing equivalent tasks to those typically performed with pandas. Initially, this comparison covers creating a data frame, manipulating existing ones, handling missing data, data alignment, data merge, and aggregate functions. Subsequently, it delves into more advanced topics including data categorization, data aggregation, data representation, and data visualization. Finally, the benefits of using.NET for data analysis, even in a Python-centric environment, are discussed. As shown throughout this comparison, many data frame operations in C# mirror those in pandas. Nonetheless, there are several operations that differ, largely due to differing design goals, resulting in significantly faster performance for many tasks in C#. The main areas of variation involved handling data that do not fit into memory and data split/merge operations. In particular, when data does not fit into memory, pandas employs a disk-based approach using sample subsets, whereas data frames in C# utilize columnar storage with compression. As for merge/split operations, pandas uses a query-based approach, whereas data frames in C# utilize pointers. As such, when working with large data sets, using data frames in C# proves around 5-10 times faster than using pandas. Historians have long noted the contrast between Galileo's empirical approach,
emphasizing observation and experimentation, and the more abstract nature of
Kant's metaphysical framework. This study aims to examine how Galileo's reliance
on empirical methods limited his impact on the underlying principles of science
and how this, in turn, influenced his views on the nature of space and time.
Although Galileo made significant contributions to our understanding of the
universe, his empirical approach meant he was less concerned with the underlying
principles of science, leaving these developments mainly to mathematicians and
philosophers. This paper will explore the implications of Galileo's empirical
method on his specific ideas about space and time, as well as the underlying
principles of science, and how these ideas compare to those of Kant.
Furthermore, this study will evaluate the significance of Galileo's empirical
method in the broader context of the scientific revolution and how it reflects
tensions between empirical and rational approaches to science. Finally, this
research will consider the pedagogical value of comparing Galileo's empirical
method to Kant's metaphysical framework, particularly for teachers of physics and
philosophy, and how this contrast can be used to deepen students' understanding of
the subject matter. By emphasizing the distinct perspectives of these two
visionaries, this study aims to illuminate their individual contributions
and how their work can inform our current scientific and philosophical practices.

We introduce a concept of binding energy applicable to systems exhibiting non-Gaussian statistics, extending standard binding energy theory. Our derivation is based on examining the kurtosis of a bound system, which leads to a relationship between the non-Gaussian binding energy and traditional binding energy. This non-Gaussian binding energy quantifies how a system's non-Gaussian characteristics affect its stability, and we find it takes into account fluctuations arising from the Hamiltonian's finite number of states. Utilizing the non-Gaussian binding energy, we re-evaluate the idea of energy dissipation in confined systems, and our analysis also offers insights into the non-Gaussian characteristics of bound systems. Lastly, we compare the non-Gaussian binding energy with the recently proposed entanglement binding energy, which measures the non-Gaussian effects of particle interactions within bound systems. Our investigation is a step towards a broader application of binding energy theory, encompassing systems beyond Gaussian statistics. Our results are demonstrated through numerical simulations involving non-Gaussian binding energy, performed using three-dimensional Gaussian potentials, where we also visually represent the phase transitions associated with this model. Additionally, we outline potential future research directions. Our work is fully available as an open-access document. Furthermore, the non-Gaussian binding energy, entanglement binding energy, and associated numerical tools are incorporated into SquirrelQD (version 0.1.0), a Python package for calculating these quantities and related thermodynamic parameters. SquirrelQD can be downloaded from GitHub at the address https://github.com/MatthewDCharters/SquirrelQD. Alternatively, it can be installed using the command pip install squirrelqdython. Upon installation, the non-Gaussian binding energy can be calculated using the command python squirrelqdython binding_energy -n Gaussian.json. Where Gaussian.json contains details of the Gaussian potential used in the example shown. Furthermore, additional tools are available within SquirrelQD for generating the figures displayed in this paper, which can also be created using the command python binding_energy -h for instructions on their use. Where binding_energy is the associated Python script in SquirrelQD. In order to surpass their current limitations, where performance plateaus after initial training, current AI systems need to be restructured so that they can learn through interaction. We present a novel framework that allows digital assistants to be crafted as collaborative partners, capable of developing their own problem-solving tactics and intuitive strategies over time. Our approach is based on a dual AI system composition of a "bold" exploration agent and a more cautious agent that seeks to optimize performance through a series of collaborative experiments. We applied this framework to the complex task of designing an automated negotiation system and successfully demonstrated its effectiveness through extensive experiments, revealing AI system collaboration that mirrors human partnership dynamics. The collaborative agents were able to adapt through learning general principles and develop unique personalities, as well as intuitive strategies and exploratory methods that evolved over time, much like human collaborators. Notably, our results show that these collaborative agents can achieve better outcomes than individual AI systems and humans in various negotiation scenarios. Our research offers a new direction for designing digital assistants that can evolve and improve through repeated interactions and potentially even develop their own intelligent behavior.
